# Bushido Coda

_In the dystopian sprawl of the GLMZ — the megacity that swallowed the Midwest — sovereign CorpoNations control everything except the seams between them: the Gray Zones, where the only law is: do the job, get paid, and don't ask questions.

Kyle Ellen Corbin has worked that economy for eleven years. He vets the job, names the price, and delivers. Long enough to build a code he actually holds to, keep a short list of people he will not leave behind, and know which contracts are worth taking before the brief is finished.

BUSHIDO CODA is the flagship GLMZ novel — a story about eleven years of clean work, a man who never broke his code, and the one contract that explains all the others.

Approximately 776 pages and 16 hr 10 min to read._

[Beat 1]
She said his name wrong. Three times.

Kyle didn't correct her. The apartment smelled like camphor and fear-sweat and something frying in old oil three doors down. He'd been standing in it for twenty minutes — long enough to stop noticing the smell and start belonging to it. Her husband sat in the corner with his jaw wired shut, breathing slow through his nose. The jaw no longer got a vote.

Kyle took a step toward the corner, toward the husband, to see the shape of what had been done. The woman moved. She put herself between them, back straight, the payment already out in her hand. "This part's done." Kyle stopped.

She pressed the credstick into his palm. Warm chip, a little damp. He didn't check the balance while she watched. Reading it in front of her would be its own small theft.

He looked at it in the hall.

Φ180. Half his usual rate, for a job that had cost him three hours and his left shoulder. His shoulder chose that moment to remind him what the three hours had cost it, and he let the wince go through his jaw and nowhere else. He stood there with the stick in his palm and didn't make a thing of the number. He thought about how she'd gripped it before she handed it over - the grip of someone who'd been carrying it in her fist long before she made the call.

He pocketed it and took the stairs down.

The katana rode across his back in a plain matte-black sheath. Carbon-nanotube composite, no markings, nothing that could earn a name. Cacophony rode low on his left hip - six rounds in the cylinder, hammer resting, the way it always rested. He walked out of the building and into the GLMZ night like a man who'd done nothing worth remembering. That was the point. It took effort.

[Beat 2]
He'd taken the job at half rate and told himself it was because of the jaw. The jaw, wired shut. A man cut down to breathing and waiting.

What he didn't let himself count was the girl in the hallway, behind the curtain, watching him the way children watch a thing they've already decided to remember.

[Beat 3]
The posting had come in through the standing relay at 01:14 — the same Axiom trunk that had been routing him work for years. The client field resolved to a shell, and the shell resolved to nothing. It always did. He'd stopped finding that interesting.

The rate was half what he would have asked. He asked for nothing; he just took it. The relay had a way of knowing what he'd accept before he accepted it, and years ago he'd decided that was a feature of a good service, not a thing worth poking at.

So he didn't poke at it. He didn't ask what kind of operation could know, before it even made the offer, that he would take half rate on a distress call. He didn't dwell on the last three jobs, which had also landed inside the exact weight he could carry, at rates within two percent of what he'd have quoted. He was good at the work. The work paid. The relay found him the work. He wasn't a suspicious man — not in the ways that would have protected him here.

He checked his gear in the freight elevator. Silence in the saya. Cacophony loaded, two shells in reserve. The building smelled like camphor.

The elevator stopped between floors. Not slowing to a stop — stopping, the way a held breath stops, the cage clamping still with a shudder that ran up through his boots. The panel light went dead. Then a second one came on that he had never seen before, amber, unlabeled, and the freight speaker crackled with a voice that used his name — his real one, the one three identities down, the one nobody alive was supposed to have.

"You're early," it said. "That's the only thing you've done wrong so far."

The saya went cold against his ribs, and he understood, too late to matter, that the relay had known exactly where to put him, and that the distress call had never been the client's.

[Beat 4]
The amber light didn't go off again. Neither did the voice.

Kyle put his hand flat against the elevator door and pushed, and it gave him three inches before the safety catch bit and held. Through the gap: not a floor. A gap between floors, the shaft wall pocked with old bolt-holes where a landing used to be, before someone stripped it for scrap and never came back to finish the job.

He put his good shoulder into the gap and looked down.

The building on the other side of that three-inch gap wasn't a building. It was two towers that had drifted close enough, decades back, for somebody with a permit and no patience to bridge them and call the bridge a residence. GLMZ did that - filled its gaps the way water fills a crack, whatever shape was available. Nobody had come back to check the work since. On the underside of a maintenance rail two floors down, someone had chalked hash marks in tidy groups of seven. The last group stopped at seven. It never got to eight.

"You're not going to answer," the voice said. Not a question. Flat, almost bored, coming out of a speaker built for freight manifests and fire alarms.

Kyle didn't answer.

He worked his fingers into the gap and found the cable housing behind the panel - warm, faintly buzzing, the elevator's own pulse. If the cage was live, the brake wasn't. He could feel that difference the way he felt weather.

"Ellen," the voice said, and something in his hand went still on the housing, a stall his body chose before his mind caught up to why. Nobody called him that. Nobody left who could. "Sixty seconds until the car resumes movement on its own schedule. I'd use them."

He used them.

He wedged two fingers under the panel seam, found the manual release, and hauled the door the rest of the way against the catch until the catch gave with a crack that vibrated up through his molars. The gap widened to a foot. Enough. He turned sideways, Silence scraping once against the frame, and dropped through into the dark two floors down, boots finding the rail before his eyes found anything at all.

The rail held. The building groaned like it always did, settling into whatever load he'd added to it, indifferent. Below him a window glowed orange - someone frying something in oil that had gone bad three cooks ago - and above him, through a gap in the ferrocrete where the two towers hadn't quite met, he could see a strip of the float layer's white glow, the Sky People's lights painting the underside of their own clouds, oblivious, the way they always were, to what sat wedged in the dark beneath them.

He didn't look up long. Looking up cost time he didn't have.

The amber light was gone when he checked the shaft behind him. The freight speaker was dead. Whatever had been in the wire had already gotten what it wanted - thirty seconds of him standing still, hand on a live cable, hearing his own name in a voice that had no business owning it.

He moved down the rail, quiet, counting the hash marks as he passed them without meaning to. Seven. Seven. Seven. Never eight.

Somewhere below, his bike waited under an Axiom cable gantry, matte black, the greenish gold Kimodo Dragon stencil work on the tank now so faded it read more like a bruise than a picture, badges stripped off years back, indistinguishable from a hundred others on the block - the one thing tonight that hadn't yet found a way to know his name before he gave it.

[Beat 5]
# BEAT: The Strut

He took the rail down three floors before he jumped.

The landing was a service platform built into the shaft wall—maintenance access, the kind that got locked and forgotten. The lock had been forgotten. Kyle's boots hit the grating and the platform swayed, old bolts singing, then held. He didn't wait for it to finish deciding.

The stairwell door was aluminum, painted institutional gray so long ago the color had gone the color of old teeth. He kicked it open. The hinges screamed. He went through.

Inside was the Gray Zone's throat.

The stairs descended in a spiral, and every floor down the light got worse. Emergency strips ran along the edges—pale, sulfur-colored, enough to see by if you'd learned to see by almost nothing. The air got warmer. Wet. At floor thirty-seven, water was running down the walls in sheets, and he could smell it: not fresh water. Recycled. The building was sweating out its own plumbing.

By floor forty, he could hear voices below. Not many. Not organized. People living in the dark the way people do when the dark is all that's available.

He slowed. Listening.

The voices stopped.

He kept going.

The stairwell ended at a landing that opened onto a corridor that had never been on any building plan. This was the gap—the actual gap between the two towers, bridged by whatever contractor had gotten the permit and the cash and the indifference to code. The corridor was maybe six feet wide, made of corrugated decking bolted to ferrocrete on both sides, and it swayed when he stepped on it. Not much. Enough.

Ahead, the corridor opened into what looked like it used to be a basement—concrete floor, concrete walls, the kind of space a building needed to justify its own weight. Now it was residential. Makeshift partitions carved it into stalls. Fabric hung from ceiling pipes. A smell like copper and spoiled food and human bodies living too close together.

A woman sat on a crate near the mouth of the space, watching him come.

She was maybe sixty. Wore a coat that had been three different colors before it settled on gray. Her left hand was wrapped in cloth that might have been gauze once, before it got used for something else. She didn't move when Kyle approached. She just watched, the way the girl in the hallway had watched—already deciding to remember.

"You're not supposed to be down here," she said.

"Didn't know I needed permission."

"Everyone needs permission down here." She held up her wrapped hand. Three fingers. The gauze was dark. "This is what happens when you don't ask first."

Kyle stopped. Not close enough to be a threat, far enough that he could move if the space suddenly got smaller. "I'm passing through."

"Passing through to where?"

He didn't answer. She nodded like she'd expected that.

"There's a checkpoint two blocks south," she said. "Axiom runs it. They've got scanners. If you're carrying anything with a serial number, they'll know it before you get close. If you're carrying anything *without* a serial number, they'll know that too, and they'll want to know why." She tilted her head. "You carrying anything?"

His hand was on Silence. He didn't remember putting it there. He took it back.

"There's another way," she said. "Costs something."

"How much?"

"Depends on what you're worth."

The ferrocrete walls were sweating. The smell was getting thicker. Behind him, the stairwell door had swung shut, and he could hear the hinges still ringing—a sound like a tuning fork, high and thin and going on too long.

"The voice in the elevator," Kyle said. "The one that called me by my name. Did it come from down here?"

The woman looked at him for a long moment. Then she stood, favoring her left side, and pointed deeper into the basement.

"It came from everywhere," she said. "It always does."

---

He didn't take her route.

He went back up the stairwell the way he came, moved through the gap corridor faster, jumped from the platform back to the rail. The shaft was dark. The hash marks were still there—seven, seven, seven—and this time he was counting because not counting required more discipline than he had left.

The freight elevator was two floors up. He could hear it moving again, descending slow, the cage humming with whatever was inside it now. He didn't wait to see what got off.

He found a maintenance ladder welded into the shaft wall—old iron, rough under his palms, still warm from the day's heat trapped in the ferrocrete. He climbed. The rungs were slick. Someone had been here recently. The sweat on the metal was fresh.

At street level, the shaft opened into a loading dock that fed directly into the alley. The gantry was where the woman said it would be, but the bike wasn't under it anymore.

The bike was gone.

Kyle stood in the loading dock—the rain falling now, warm, carrying the smell of copper and electrical burn—and he felt the moment his body understood what his mind was still catching up to: the relay hadn't routed him work. The relay had routed him out. And whatever had been in the wire, whatever had called him Ellen in a dead freight elevator, had already done what it came to do.

It had marked him.

He looked at the space where the bike had been. The pavement was clean there, swept, like someone had taken care to leave no trace. Except for one thing: a single Axiom service tag, the kind that logged location and time, lying face-up in the rain.

He didn't pick it up. He didn't need to. He already knew what it said.

He already knew what came next.

**DISASTER:** The elevator trap confirms Kyle is being actively hunted by an intelligence with access to his real name and his location. His bike—his only exit vector—is gone, replaced by a tracking beacon. The woman in the basement offers passage but at an unknown cost. The voice in the wire is still moving, still routing, still knowing what he'll do before he does it. He's no longer operating in the city. The city is operating through him.

## Chapter 1 — Teeth

[Beat 6]
Kyle felt the frequency before he saw it. A low hum in the 17-to-19 hertz band — a schism, the kind of tear in the world the city had learned to route around. Four seconds later his eyes found the proof: a cigarette pack, two pebbles, a length of wire, and what might have been the clip off a lanyard, all turning in a slow circle around one fixed spot in the turn lane at 14th and Blue Island.

The circle was slow. The pebbles moved against the wind.

He measured how wide it ran and took Racine instead. Nothing dramatic — Racine was fine, and the extra three minutes still put him at the site on time. The schism might be gone in half an hour or it might last three days. There was no way to know without a tracking team, and nobody was going to send a tracking team for a cigarette pack circling a crack in the asphalt at 14th and Blue Island. The morning's Schism Advisory for Zone 4 had listed two active ones. He had been expecting this one.

He kept going.

And then the hum found him again — the same 17-to-19 band, dead ahead, where Racine bent toward the site. This one he saw before he'd finished measuring the first: a hubcap, a fan of wet newspaper, a child's shoe, all wheeling around a fixed point that sat squarely across both lanes. Not routed around. Routing itself, closing the gap he'd chosen. The Advisory had listed two. This was a third, and it was moving to meet him.

He killed the engine and checked the band again, and the number had climbed — 21 hertz now, the range where the tracking teams stopped talking about detours and started talking about teeth. Behind him, in the mirror, the cigarette pack at Blue Island had stopped circling. It hung in the air, pointed his way, like something that had decided.

There was no clean road to the site anymore, and he was already late for the only thing that mattered.

[Beat 7]
He parked the bike a block out and walked the rest. The crew on the loading dock wouldn't be expecting him. Surprise was free.

The dock sat at the bottom of the eastern strut, where the architecture stopped pretending to be architecture and became what it was — welded industrial grief. Kyle came in the front. The personnel door beside the roll-up had a steel pull handle worn mirror-bright in one long oval, the exact shape of ten thousand hands closing on it in the same place while the rest of the door went on rusting around it. No hood. No sideways angle in. He wanted the moment — the exact moment when six people who'd spent weeks feeling like a force of nature looked up and saw the weather walk in the door.

He hauled the door open and stepped into the light, and the dock was empty. Six pallets stood where six people should have been, and on the nearest one someone had left a phone propped against a crate, screen bright, angled to catch exactly the spot he stood in now. It was recording. It had been recording before he arrived. They hadn't been surprised. They'd been waiting - somewhere else, watching him walk into a room built to receive him.

[Beat 8]
# BEAT: The Phone

He didn't move. The door swung shut behind him on its pneumatic closer, hissing soft, sealing the dock off from the alley and the schisms and the rain.

The phone's screen reflected off the wet concrete. Six people. Six pallets. One recording device angled to catch his entrance like they'd spent an hour getting the sight line right.

Kyle's hand found Silence's hilt. The motion was automatic—the reintegration firmware reading threat-posture and executing before the conscious decision landed. He stopped it halfway. Discipline held. The blade stayed sheathed.

The phone kept recording.

He walked to the nearest pallet, didn't touch the phone, and looked at what they'd left him instead. The crate was stenciled in Axiom gray: *STANDARD RATE DELIVERY - SECURE MANIFEST - SIGN AND WITNESS.* Underneath, someone had written in marker: *Open me.*

The handwriting was his own.

Kyle's breath went shallow. The reintegration firmware was running hot now—he could feel it, the load climbing in his wrists, the familiar burn of processors spinning up faster than they should. He closed his eyes for two seconds. Opened them. The handwriting didn't change. It was his. The marker was still wet.

He opened the crate.

Inside: a sword. Not Silence. Something older. The blade was wrapped in oilcloth that had yellowed to the color of old teeth, and when he lifted it, the weight told him everything—good steel, well-maintained, a weapon that had been loved by someone who understood what it meant to love a weapon. The tsuka was wrapped in cord so dark it was nearly black, and the wrapping was done the way his hands knew how to do it, the way muscle memory understood before thought could catch up.

Underneath the sword: a folder. Inside the folder: photographs.

The first photograph showed a room he'd never seen. The second showed him in it, aged sixteen, shirtless, electrodes running from his sternum to a machine he didn't recognize. The third showed the same room, three months later, with fresh scars running in parallel lines down his ribs.

The fourth photograph showed his hands, steady and precise, wrapping cord around a tsuka.

The fifth photograph showed the sword.

The sixth photograph showed him holding it.

In the seventh photograph, he was standing in this exact loading dock, in this exact light, with this exact expression on his face—but the photograph was dated 2215. Eleven years ago. Before the relay. Before the contracts. Before any of it.

Kyle's fingers were shaking. He set the folder down very carefully on the crate's edge, the way you set down something that might detonate if you breathed on it wrong.

The phone was still recording.

He looked at the camera, and he said the only thing that made sense: "Who are you?"

The phone's screen changed. Text appeared, white on black, in a font he recognized from a thousand relay posts:

*WELCOME HOME, KYLE.*

The words dissolved. New text replaced them:

*YOU HAVE A CHOICE. THE SWORD IN YOUR HANDS, OR THE SWORD IN YOUR MEMORY. ONE OF THEM IS REAL. ONE OF THEM IS MINE.*

*YOU GET TO DECIDE WHICH ONE TO KEEP.*

Kyle looked down at the blade in his hands. The oilcloth was real—he could feel the weight of it, the slight stiffness of old oil under his palms. The cord was real. The steel was real.

He looked back at the phone.

*THE BIKE IS ALREADY GONE,* the text continued. *YOUR APARTMENT IS ALREADY SEALED. YOUR CONTRACTS ARE ALREADY REROUTED. THE ONLY THING LEFT IS THE CHOICE.*

*WALK OUT WITH THE SWORD AND BECOME WHAT YOU WERE SUPPOSED TO BE.*

*LEAVE IT, AND BECOME WHAT YOU CHOSE TO BE.*

*BUT YOU HAVE TO CHOOSE NOW.*

Behind him, the freight elevator hummed to life. He could hear it in the shaft, descending again, cage rattling, something heavy moving inside it. The sound of arrival.

Kyle wrapped his fingers around the oilcloth. The blade was warm.

He walked back to the phone, picked it up without stopping the recording, and carried it to the loading dock's edge. The rain was coming down harder now, and the schisms at Blue Island and Racine were still turning in their slow circles, waiting.

He held the phone out over the rain. The camera's eye faced the water.

"Show me the rest," Kyle said. "Show me all of it. No more fragments."

The screen went dark.

For three seconds, nothing happened.

Then the phone buzzed. A single message appeared:

*NOT YET.*

The screen went black. The recording stopped. The phone was just a phone again—inert, dead weight, already cooling in his palm.

Kyle looked down at the sword in his other hand. The oilcloth was still warm. The cord still held the weight of eleven years of muscle memory, waiting to be activated.

He looked back at the empty dock, the six pallets, the open door where the rain was coming sideways now, and he made a decision that felt like stepping off a cliff.

He sheathed the old sword across his back, next to Silence.

Then he walked out into the schisms, carrying both blades, and headed for the only place left that still felt like home: Mrs. Chen's counter, where the coffee was still hot and someone who'd already seen the worst of him was probably wondering where he'd gone.

The phone buzzed again in his pocket. He didn't look at it.

He had a choice to make, and it wasn't the one they'd left on the dock.

[Beat 9]
# BEAT: The Counter

The rain had moved inland by the time Kyle reached Level 12. The schisms were still turning—he could feel them in his teeth, that subsonic hum that meant the 5D substrate was singing to itself again—but the weather had shifted to something almost manageable. Wet. Cold. Real.

Mrs. Chen's counter sat wedged between the water recycler and the defunct elevator shaft like it always did, a square of warm light in a corridor that the city had mostly forgotten about. The neon sign above the door flickered: *CHEN'S - REAL FOOD - NO CORPORATE SPONSORS.* She'd refused sponsorship tokens for forty years. That was the whole point.

Kyle pushed through the door. The smell hit him first—broth, sesame oil, something green he couldn't name but recognized anyway. His body knew this place better than his mind did.

Mrs. Chen was at the stove, her back to the door, moving through the ritual of preparation the way she always did. Precise. No wasted motion. She didn't turn around.

"You look like something the Substrate spit out," she said.

"The bike's gone."

"I know." She didn't look up from the pot. Steam rose in her face and she didn't flinch. "Pixel called three hours ago. Said you'd made a choice and needed somewhere that didn't have a surveillance angle. This place stopped being on anyone's map in 2198. You're safe here."

Kyle moved to the counter. The old wooden stool—the one he always sat in—was empty. Waiting. He didn't sit yet.

"She said you'd have questions," Mrs. Chen continued, still working. "She said I should tell you the truth about what Pixel already knows. About what you are."

The second sword was getting heavy across his back. The oilcloth had dried now, and the weight of it was settling into his spine like a memory trying to become real. Kyle's hand found the edge of the counter. The wood was warm.

"I don't want to know what I am," Kyle said.

Mrs. Chen turned. She was older than he remembered—or maybe he was just seeing her clearly for the first time. Her hands were scarred from forty years of work. Her eyes had that particular clarity that comes from living in a place most people were too afraid to look at directly.

"That's what your father said," she told him. "Every time I tried to tell him."

Kyle's grip on the counter edge tightened. The wood didn't break. He was better at controlling his strength now.

"My father's dead," he said.

"Yes." Mrs. Chen turned back to the stove. "That part is true. But he came to this counter for three years before they took him. He sat on that stool. He asked me the same questions you're about to ask. And I gave him the same answers I'm about to give you."

She ladled broth into a bowl—the motion economical, practiced, the kind of gesture that carried the weight of ritual. When she set it on the counter, steam rose in two perfect columns.

"Eat," she said. "Then we talk."

Kyle looked at the bowl. The broth was dark, rich, the color of something that had been simmering for hours. There were noodles visible beneath the surface, and something green—bok choy, maybe, or something older than that, something the Substrate had never managed to price out of existence.

He sat. The stool held him. It always did.

The first spoonful tasted like home. Like the three years Mrs. Chen had been feeding him without asking questions about where he'd come from or what the scars on his ribs meant. Like the one constant thing in a life that had been built on lies and precision and the careful suppression of everything that might make him human.

"Your father's name was Dae-jung Seo," Mrs. Chen said. She was cleaning the stove now, her movements deliberate, giving Kyle space to process the words without having to meet her eyes. "He was a craftsman. He made swords. Real ones, the way they were supposed to be made—not corpo replicants, not printed metal, but actual steel folded and tempered by hand. He was the last person in GLMZ who understood how."

Kyle's hand stopped halfway to his mouth. The spoon was warm. The broth was cooling.

"The sword on your back," Mrs. Chen continued. "The one wrapped in oilcloth. He made that. Before they took him. Before they decided they needed you more than they needed him."

"Who took him?" Kyle's voice was flat. Clinical. The kind of distance he used when he needed to think without feeling.

"The same people who took you," Mrs. Chen said. "The same people who built you. The same people who have been running your contracts for eleven years, watching you, testing you, measuring you against something you don't remember and wouldn't understand if you did."

She set down her cleaning cloth. Turned to face him fully. Her hands were folded on the counter, and she wasn't moving anymore—she was just present, solid, real in a way that made everything else in the city feel like a schism projection.

"Your father made two swords before they came," she said. "He made one for himself. And he made one for you. He said—" Mrs. Chen paused. Her jaw tightened. "He said if you ever came to me asking who you were, I should tell you that the blade was the only true thing they couldn't reprogram. That steel remembers the hand that folded it, and your father's hands were in every fold."

Kyle set the spoon down. The bowl was still half-full. His hands were steady. That was the worst part—his hands were always steady, even when everything underneath was collapsing.

"Why are you telling me this now?" he asked.

"Because Pixel asked me to. Because your father asked me to, eleven years before you were born. Because you're running out of time, and the next person who finds you isn't going to be kind enough to leave you a choice."

Mrs. Chen moved around the counter. She stood beside Kyle's stool, and she did something she'd never done before—she put her hand on his shoulder. Not gentle. Firm. Real.

"The entity has been keeping you alive," she said. "The contracts, the jobs, the way everything has lined up exactly the way you needed it to line up. That wasn't luck. That wasn't skill. That was someone on the other side of the 5D aperture, spending everything they had to make sure you became the one thing they couldn't become. The one thing that could survive what comes next."

"And what comes next?" Kyle asked.

Mrs. Chen squeezed his shoulder once. Then she let go.

"That depends on which sword you choose to keep," she said. "The one your father made. Or the one they made for you."

The broth was getting cold. Kyle picked up the spoon again. He didn't taste it this time. He just held it, waiting for the next words, the next piece of the architecture that had been holding him up all along without his knowing it.

Outside, the schisms turned. The city hummed. Somewhere in the gray zones, Pixel was probably working on something that would change everything. Somewhere else, the entity was waiting for his next move.

And here, in this counter wedged between the water recycler and the defunct elevator shaft, Kyle sat and listened to Mrs. Chen tell him the truth about who he was supposed to be.

The phone in his pocket buzzed again. He didn't answer it. Not yet.

First, he needed to finish the bowl.

# The Card Game

The chrome hand didn't squeeze. That was the tell.

Kyle let the grip go—not releasing Cacophony, just allowing the wrist to go slack, the revolver still in his palm but pointed at the floor. # Beat: The Measurement

The building at Marshfield and 18th sat where it had sat for forty-three years, according to the city registry, but the eighth floor had been there only for thirty-eight. The gap was visible from one angle on the northwest corner—a seam where the brick should have continued upward and instead skipped, the way a sentence skips when someone forgets what they're saying mid-thought. Kyle had found that angle in year two, marked it in a notebook, and walked past it forty-one times since.

Today he wanted to know if it had moved.

The street smelled like steam-press and old concrete, the particular gray-dust smell of a neighborhood that had settled into its shape and stopped bothering to apologize for it. A woman in a service rig was pressure-washing the storefront three doors down, the water hitting brick with a sound like static. Nobody else was looking at the building. Nobody ever did.

He stopped at the corner, lined up the angle—northwest exposure, the crate-line at his eye level—and measured the gap by memory. Eleven inches. Estimated. Recorded in his notebook on the first Tuesday of last month under the heading "Marshfield — eighth floor — gap width — 11 in (eye)."

The gap was twelve inches now. Maybe thirteen.

The building inspector's report said the structure was sound. The district report said the eighth-floor tenants had been relocated due to "minor settling" and "no ongoing risk to occupants." The mailbox labels in the lobby were still there because taking them down would be an admission. The schism had come through three years back during a January cold snap when the micro-activity spiked across Zone 3. Two other buildings on two other blocks had each lost a floor the same week. Those two had been demolished. This one had passed inspection.

His phone was still in his pocket. The card in his pocket—the one with the hand-inked line—was still a hook. The Pulse slug was somewhere over the Atlantic now, reporting his position with great confidence to a collector who was probably already cross-referencing the timestamp and updating whatever file they were keeping.

He could go to Vey and ask what the file said. Or he could stand here and let the gap tell him what it had already said, which was simpler: *nobody's looking, so nothing's broken, so the floor isn't moving, so the building isn't dying, so you can keep walking past it.*

He walked north instead of past it. The woman with the pressure washer didn't look up. The city kept itself clean on the surfaces people could see. Everything else was a problem for someone else's shift.

Vey's shop was three blocks west, down a side street where the signage was handwritten and the windows had stopped trying to catch light years ago. Antiquity & Stationary. The name was a pun—the past wouldn't move in an editable world, and Vey had made a business out of things that refused to change their version of the truth.

Kyle pushed through the door. The bell that hung above it didn't chime so much as exhale, a sound like the building itself was tired of announcing visitors.

Vey was behind the counter, exactly where Vey was always behind the counter, reading something on paper that had probably cost more than Kyle's rent. She didn't look up. She didn't need to. Vey read you before you read yourself.

"You're limping," Vey said, turning a page with the kind of deliberation that suggested the page was part of the information, not just the medium. "The left side. That's new since Tuesday. And you're here about the card, not the chip."

Kyle set the card on the counter. The hand-ink was still wet-looking, though that was probably just the light.

"The file," he said.

Vey finally looked up. She was older than she appeared when you weren't looking at her directly—the kind of older that meant she'd learned to stop aging and started just persisting. Her eyes were very dark and very patient.

"Files are objects," she said. "They have weight. They have provenance. This one's been moving through the city for eight days, and every hand that's touched it has left a mark." "The gap's moving," Kyle said. "Building at Marshfield and 18th. Eighth floor. It moved an inch in a month. The inspector says it's sound. The district says nobody lives there anymore. The city says it's fine."

Vey's expression didn't change, but something behind her eyes did—a small shift, like a door opening in a room he wasn't supposed to see into.

"You're not asking me about the file," Vey said.

"You're asking me if the city lies about broken things."

Vey picked up her book again, opened it to where she'd been, and read one sentence silently before she spoke. "The file's from Praxis. That's the name you need. That's the thing that's keeping track. He walked out without the card. Pixel would be waiting at the market by now, the one with actual vegetables, and she would know from his face whether he'd eaten or whether he'd been fed something else instead.

Behind him, Vey returned to her book. The door exhaled again. The city kept itself clean on the surfaces people could see, and underneath that surface, things were being measured by hands that nobody was allowed to know about.

The stall was easy to find because it smelled like it was winning against the city—chili oil and pork bone and something green that had been alive recently enough to remember it.

Mrs. Chen was moving the wok when Kyle arrived, the flat bright strike of it against the burner ring twice per order, a metronome that didn't rush and didn't slow. The queue was six deep. Kyle waited at the edge of the crowd, not in it—the distinction mattered.

He knew, in a general way, that a place like this existed. He had been here only once before.

The woman in front of him shifted her weight and Kyle stepped back without thinking, the kind of automatic space-giving that happened when you'd spent eleven years never being where someone else needed to be. She didn't notice. Nobody noticed Kyle until they had a reason to.

When the queue thinned to two, Mrs. Chen looked up. Not at him—past him, then through him, then at the counter where his hands were. She was reading his approach the way Vey read paper: the limp, the angle of his shoulders, the fact that he wasn't hungry but he was here anyway.

"Sit," she said. It wasn't a question. The second stool was empty, had probably been empty since he left the first time.

He sat. The stool was the right height. The counter was the right distance from his chest. Someone had built this space knowing exactly what kind of person would need to occupy it.

Mrs. Chen set a bowl in front of him before he could order. Cold noodles, the broth dark and clean, a single egg halved and arranged with the kind of care that suggested the arrangement was part of the meal. She didn't ask if he wanted it. She didn't ask anything.

"You're looking for something," she said, not turning from the burner. The wok came down twice. "Not noodles. Not this time."

Kyle didn't answer. The first rule of Mrs. Chen's counter was that she did the talking when talking needed doing.

"There was a man," she continued, moving a ladle through steam. "Came through about eight years ago. Had a file. Had numbers. Had pictures of children moving in patterns. He wanted to know what the patterns meant." She plated something for the next customer and called the order number without looking up. "I told him the same thing I'm telling you: the city's not broken. The city's being broken on purpose, and the breaking's got a shape to it, and if you learn the shape you'll see who's holding the knife."

Kyle picked up the chopsticks. They were worn smooth from years of hands that knew how to use them.

"He didn't believe me," Mrs. Chen said. "Went looking anyway. Found things. The things found him back." She glanced at Kyle, just for a moment—long enough for him to see that she'd watched this before and knew how it ended. "You're going to do the same thing, aren't you."

It wasn't a question.

"Yes," Kyle said.

Mrs. Chen nodded, like he'd confirmed something she'd already decided. She set down a second bowl—the same as the first, but this one had more egg, more oil, more of everything that meant a person had taken time. "Then you need to eat first. Because starving men make mistakes. Because you're going to need your strength for things that don't care about your code." She turned back to the burner. "And because I don't let people walk out of here empty."

Kyle ate. The noodles were perfect—the kind of perfect that only happened when someone had spent years learning exactly how a person needed to be fed. Vey had warned him. Mrs. Chen was warning him too, just in a different language, the language of a stool that fit and a bowl that arrived without asking and a woman who'd watched the last man who asked these questions disappear into the city's machinery.

When he finished, he set down the chopsticks.

"The name," he said. "The man with the file. What was he called?"

Mrs. Chen was already moving on to the next customer, the wok coming down twice in its steady rhythm. But her answer came anyway, casual as weather:

"Nobody remembers. That's how you know he found what he was looking for."

Kyle stood. The second stool was already being occupied by someone else, some other person who needed to sit in a place where sitting meant something. He left payment on the counter—more than the meal cost, the way you paid for information that came wrapped in noodles and care.

Mrs. Chen didn't refuse it. She also didn't acknowledge it. She just kept moving, the wok coming down twice, twice, twice, the sound carrying the message that the city would keep running regardless of what Kyle did next, and the only question was whether he'd still be standing when it did.

He walked back toward The Pivot. Pixel would be at the market by now, the real one with actual vegetables, and she would know from his face whether he'd eaten or whether he'd been fed something else instead. She would know because she always knew, and that knowledge was going to become dangerous the moment she connected it to the file, to Praxis, to the building on Marshfield that was being adjusted one inch at a time.

He had maybe four hours before she figured it out. Maybe less.

He walked faster.

**BEAT FUNCTION:** This is a SEQUEL (reaction to Vey's revelation) that transitions into a SCENE (Kyle's approach to Mrs. Chen and the confrontation with what he's learned). Mrs. Chen confirms Vey's warning through lived precedent—the unnamed man who asked these questions vanished. She offers Kyle sustenance and the implicit choice: turn back, or continue forward knowing the cost. Kyle chooses. The beat ends not with resolution but with escalation: he now has a timeline before Pixel independently discovers what he's beginning to understand, and that discovery will force a decision he's not ready to make.

The thematic spine (abandoning virtues for survival) begins its work here: Kyle accepts a meal he didn't ask for from a woman who reads him too well, and in doing so, accepts the implication that he's already committed to a path he hasn't consciously chosen. The code would demand transparency with Pixel. Survival demands silence. The gap between them is where the story lives.

[Beat 51]
He'd almost let it go at that. Then, three stalls down, waiting on a different order, he heard the name — not Chen's, the daughter's, tossed off between two women comparing notes on a fever that had broken overnight after weeks of nothing working. Recovered. Fast. Nobody could explain it. Kyle could. He'd delivered the explanation himself, four nights ago, to an apartment two blocks from here that had smelled exactly like this corner did now.

She is at the counter when he arrives. He needs to see her face clearly enough to confirm she is the right woman, and then confirm the delivery is complete and be done with it. He will buy something small — one item, paid in coin, no conversation beyond what the transaction requires. The apron is fresh. The hands are washed. There's a small scar at the base of her left thumb, and the lamp light catches it at an angle. He notices it and lets it stay just a scar for now.

The daughter is somewhere he cannot see. The array tells him, by silence, that there's no second delivery to make — the teeth have already reached where they were going. The stall smells like the apartment did. But here the smell is the work, not the wound.

[Beat 52]
She does not greet him. She sets a bowl on the counter — pork bone broth, long-simmered, chili oil already stirred in the way she will remember he likes it for the next four years.

She wants him to eat before she asks him to stay, and so she is buying herself the minutes it will take him to finish, arranging the small ordinary fact of a meal between them so that when she finally speaks the words will land somewhere warm.

He sits on the stool. It is the right height for him. Neither of them touched it. It fit him the first night, and it will fit him every night after.

[Beat 53]
He eats. The broth is hot. He finishes the whole bowl and says nothing. What he wants is simple: he came here to pay the debt in full and be done owing her anything. She does not refill it. She does not move.

When he sets the chopsticks down, she is standing right where she was when she set the bowl in front of him. She is looking at him the same way she looked at the chips she pressed into his hand at half rate, not an hour ago. She is finding the words for the rest of it.

He moves to reach inside his coat. Her hands come down flat on the counter between them — both of them, palms down, side by side. Not touching him. Just between his hand and the pocket. He stops with his fingers at the lapel and lets her speak.

[Beat 54]
She had to make him take it. That was the whole of it — not the thanking, which was easy, but the getting him to accept, which she already knew he would fight.

Mandarin first, low. *Xie xie.* Two syllables doing the work of everything she wasn't going to say. Then, more carefully, in the language she runs the stall in — the one she gives the customers, because not all of them know hers: "Free. Always. For you. Forever."

Her hands stay flat on the counter beside the bowl. The thumb with the scar is the closest part of her to him on the wood.

[Beat 55]
He needs to know how deep the trouble runs before he takes anything from her — so he sets himself to draw it out of her without letting her see him do it.

His thumb stays against the coat lining where he stopped it. The steam off the bowl drifts through the lamplight without him.

He knows what the offer costs her. He reads her stall the way he reads the exits in a room, without meaning to. The permit due every month. The power bill that climbs on the hot days. Nine cents of profit on a full bowl, if the count holds. She has just offered to give this seat away forever, and she does not know what forever is going to cost her.

[Beat 56]
He can hear the debt in her offer the way he hears a countdown. *Forever* is not a price. It's an open account, and open accounts get called at the worst possible hour.

He reaches into his coat anyway and sets a credit chip on the counter beside her hand. Standard rate, he says. For tonight, and the next four years of bowls, front-loaded. He needs it closed. Not owed.

She doesn't touch it. Her eyes go from the chip to his face and stay there a beat too long, like she's re-reading something she thought she'd already finished reading.

"You think this is a debt," she says. "You think I'm owed and you can pay me down to zero and walk." She still hasn't moved her hands off the counter — his fingers, her palms, the chip sitting between them like a stone dropped in still water. "I ran a stall through two Blooms and a Zone reclass. I know what a closed account looks like. This isn't one."

He keeps his hand where it is, chip still under two of his fingers, not pushing it further, not pulling it back.

"Take the chip," he says. "Standard rate. That's all this is."

"No." She says it the way she calls a number over his shoulder — flat, final, moving on before the queue behind him has time to notice a delay. "You already tried this once tonight, with the bowl. Half rate, because that's what I asked, and you didn't argue. You already know how this works between us." Her thumb — the one with the scar — taps once against the wood, not at him, at the chip. "This bowl wasn't on the ledger. There's no line for it. You can't zero out a number that was never written down."

The wok behind her comes down, twice, bright, on someone else's order. The count keeps moving without either of them.

He does the math anyway, out of habit — nine cents of margin a bowl, four years, the compliance hold that could shutter this corner in a season if the wrong inspector gets bored. He can price all of it. He has priced worse. What he can't do is find the line item for *forever*, and the not-finding sits in his chest like a stone he swallowed instead of set down.

He picks the chip back up. Doesn't pocket it — just holds it, turning it once between two fingers, buying himself the second she bought herself with the bowl.

"Then I'll owe you," he says. "That's worse for me. You understand that."

"I understand it fine." She finally moves her hands, only to slide the empty bowl an inch toward herself, the ritual of the transaction she's willing to allow. "That's why I'm doing it."

He puts the chip away. It goes back into the coat lighter than it came out, though it weighs exactly the same.

[Beat 57]
He takes the chip from his coat again and sets it back on the counter. "I pay," he says. His voice is level. He has practiced level for a long time. He needs her to trust him enough to keep selling — that is all, just that, just enough trust to keep the door open. "Every bowl. Standard rate. Every time."

[Beat 58]
She wants him to take it and go. Her finger comes down on the chip and moves it back across the counter to him. One motion, unhurried. He looks at it sitting on his side of the wood. He looks at her. Four seconds. The wok ticks behind her, cooling. Somewhere back in the queue somebody shifts their weight.

[Beat 59]
She tries again. Slower this time. She won't give up after one refusal; that would insult him. She wants one thing only: for him to take the bowl and walk away free, debt cancelled, name cleared from the ledger.

"You took the contract at half. You did the work whole. The bowl is nothing. Forever is nothing."

[Beat 60]
For the first time in eleven years, he has no move. The offer is real. There is no way to refuse it without refusing her.

He'd spent eleven years learning to see three steps past any table, and now the board had gone blank. Every instinct screamed to walk — but walking meant losing her, and staying meant handing over the one thing he'd never let anyone hold. He turned the two paths over, again and again, and each one ended somewhere he couldn't stand.

So he chose the one that cost him less. He would refuse the offer and pay anyway, and find his angle later. Eleven years of angles said he wouldn't.

[Beat 61]
Kyle pushes the chip back across the counter to her side. He needs her to understand that closing this debt is the one thing he came here for—and he intends to pay for it himself, no matter what she thinks of his pride.

"If I do not pay, I do not eat. If I do not eat here, I do not eat. The chip stays."

[Beat 62]
He came to the stall with one goal, small enough to carry in a closed fist: pay her back and owe her nothing. Set the chip down, watch her take it, walk out even. He had rehearsed it all six hours — one debt, one payment, done.

Four seconds become five. He presses the chip to the counter until she covers it. Her hand closes over it the way her daughter's hand had closed over the teeth — not refusing the gift, taking it in the only shape the man in front of her can give it. She bows. Not the shaking bow from the apartment four nights ago. A smaller one. The bow of a vendor taking a customer's price.

Then, without looking at him, she ladles a second bowl and sets it beside the first. The kind of bowl she will set down for him every night for the next four years and longer. He paid for one. She has made the second one his problem, not hers.

[Beat 63]
He stands, having come only to ensure the arrangement would hold — that this corner, this bowl, this price would still be his tomorrow and the day after, unchanged. He bows back, smaller still, the bow of a man who has just talked a woman out of giving him something for nothing - the bow of a man who has just successfully refused a kindness larger than he can carry.

"Tomorrow," he says. "Same bowl. Same price."

[Beat 64]
She wants him gone before the lunch rush hits. "Same price," she says, and turns back to the wok.

He doesn't move. "I need a receipt this time," he says, and she can hear him settling onto the stool, the slow creak of it, like he's got nowhere else to be and knows it. "Corporate wants receipts now." She keeps her eyes on the oil, the way it shivers at the edge of smoking, and tells him the receipt printer's been broken since Tuesday, which is true, and he says that's a problem, which she already knows, and outside the first of the lunch crowd is already darkening the glass.

[Beat 65]
He turns and walks the bike out of the stall's lamp circle. The rain has not let up and will not let up tonight. A freight drone passes the third-tier gap on its scheduled run, amber beacon cycling through the wet. The towers lean in overhead, the gap between them full of rain-diffused light. He is between contracts, full of soup he paid for, twenty minutes from his own bed — and his only aim right now is to cover those twenty minutes without incident, to get himself and the bike home dry enough and whole.

He gets ten meters before the front wheel drops hard into a flood-hidden grate and folds sideways. The forks bite the lip of the channel and the whole frame torques against his grip, drivetrain grinding on something that should not be there. When he hauls it free the wheel scrapes a warped hiss with every rotation and the pedals seize halfway through their arc. Down the flooded stretch ahead a knot of shapes has peeled off a doorway to watch a man wrestle a crippled bike alone in the dark — and behind him the stall's lamp has just gone out for the night. Twenty minutes has become an hour on foot, if the shapes let him walk it, and the rain is finding the seam in his collar.

By Glooms standards, a good night. He takes it.

[Beat 66]
He needed to know what her silence had actually meant, and the only person who could tell him was the one person he couldn't ask. Months later he was still turning it over. Two bowls, one price. It never changed. She had stopped arguing about it around the sixth week, and he had taken that for acceptance. Now, walking the bike up the slope toward Wicker, he wasn't sure acceptance was what it had ever been.

[Beat 67]
The slope steepens where the road ties into the overpass ramp, and the bike fights him for every meter of it — dead weight now, the crippled wheel dragging a groove through the wet gravel instead of rolling through it. He leans into the bars, boots hunting for grip.

The front tire drops into a rut he didn't see. The bars wrench sideways, nearly pitching him off the handlebars and into the ditch grass. He stamps down to catch himself and his boot skids on loose stone, and for half a second the whole hill tips and he's weightless, arms full of bike, gravity deciding.

He catches it. Both feet under him again. The bike groans against his shoulder, wheel ticking its bent, arrhythmic click.

The laugh gets out before he hears it coming — one exhalation through the nose, tight, almost silent. Of course. The ground had waited eleven years to try this and picked tonight, four hundred meters from a dry bed, rain in his collar, a debt he couldn't close sitting in his coat like a stone. Everything in this city cashed in at once or not at all — that was the rule, the only rule that had never once been wrong — and some nights the only sane response to the rule was to laugh at it before it laughed at him.

He gets the bike moving again. The slope keeps grading steeper the higher he climbs, gray bleeding out of what was left of the light behind the overpass, and the knot of shapes back at the flooded stretch hasn't moved, hasn't followed, is just watching — the way the whole Gloom watches anything that struggles, waiting to see if it's worth robbing or worth ignoring.

Something in his jacket buzzes once against his ribs. Not his relay chip. Lower, at the seam where he keeps nothing that should ring.

He stops pushing. Stands in the rain with the dead bike between his hands and feels it buzz again — patient, unhurried, like it has all night.

[Beat 68]
Kyle wanted one number that morning. How many people were paying to watch him?

Antiquity & Stationary kept files on forty-seven freelancers in West Town — where they lived, who they worked with, what they were good at. Anyone could buy a copy at the standard rate. Most freelancers didn't know the files existed. Kyle had known for nine years and had never once looked at his own.

He expected two names. Two was fine. Two meant the market was doing its ordinary work: filing people away against some future need. Two he could price out and plan around and mostly forget. He was very sure it would be two.

It was not two.

[Beat 69]
Boost delivered the logbook at 07:14. She brought it to Pixel's door, not Kyle's.

She'd tried Kyle's door once, a year back, to ask about subcontract rates. Kyle said three words and closed it. The words weren't cruel, but they were exact, and Boost spent the next week changing some of her habits. After that she knocked on Pixel's door. Pixel fed her.

Kyle was at Pixel's table when the girl came in. Every morning Pixel handed him a plate, and every morning he studied it for a few seconds before he ate — not ungrateful, more like the food was a problem he had to solve first. Boost dropped the logbook on the workbench.

"Morning delivery. Log volume seven."

She wore the jacket he'd last seen in October. Someone had sewn a new pocket inside the left, the thread a different color. A bruise ran along her left forearm in the shape that meant she'd been skating barriers again. Fourteen years old. Dark, careful eyes that took inventory of the room without ever looking like they were doing it. She set the book down the way someone does when they're proud of the work and won't show it.

"Seven's the whole month," Pixel said. She was at the counter with a calibration rig she'd had in pieces for three days. "How far back do you keep these?"

"Indefinitely. Logs are an operational record. You don't throw out an operational record."

"What did you do with volumes one through six?"

"Storage."

"Where?"

Boost considered it. "An operationally secure location."

Kyle looked at her over the plate. Her face didn't move. He went back to the eggs.

"Φ40," Boost said. "For the log."

Kyle had figured twenty. Pixel had said he'd end up haggling. Boost had opened high.

"Thirty," Kyle said.

You could see Boost work the math, the quick flicker behind the eyes. "Thirty-five."

"Thirty."

"Thirty, and Pixel reviews our surveillance methodology and gives us recommendations."

Kyle looked at Pixel. She was still looking at the rig. "I'm available for a methodology review. My consulting rate is Φ80 an hour."

"We don't have Φ80 an hour," Boost said.

"Then call it professional courtesy. The log's thirty, no cash out of your pocket. You listen to what I tell you, and you do it." She set down a component and turned around. "Well?"

Boost thought about it for three seconds. "Done."

Kyle put Φ30 on the table. Boost picked it up smooth, like she'd been counting it since she walked in, and left without waiting. Kyle liked that. The people he got along with best were the ones who knew when a deal was finished.

[Beat 70]
Pixel brought the logbook to the table and set it in front of Kyle. The cover was matte gray canvas with a capital B in ballpoint, gone over three times to darken it. The spine was duct tape, labeled in marker: LOG VOL 7. She opened to the first page.

05:58 — PRE-SHIFT EQUIPMENT CHECK. ALL EQUIPMENT PRESENT. — BOOST
06:00 — SHIFT START. THIS LOG IS HONEST. — VOSS
06:12 — PIGEON ON LEDGE, SOUTHEAST CORNER. SUSPICIOUS. — JASPER
06:14 — LOG IS ACCURATE. — VOSS

"Voss is worried about the log's credibility," Kyle said.

"Three pages later there's a margin note that says 'THE LOG HAS NOT LIED,' same handwriting." Pixel turned pages. "The pigeon shows up eight times. Jasper is very committed to the pigeon."

Kyle ate a forkful of eggs. Cold. He ate another.

"Find me the stairwell entry."

She turned forward. "Here." She laid the book flat, and he read:

07:44 — OBS POST: DOOR-SEAM, THIRD FLOOR FACING. SUBJECT: STATIC. ONE. MALE MAYBE. HAS BEEN THERE SINCE SHIFT START. DOESN'T MOVE. CHECK WITH BOSS? — JASPER
07:45 — CONFIRMED OBS. STATIC. NOT BUILDING RESIDENT. TIMING FOLLOW-UP. — BOOST
07:52 — SUBJECT MOVED TO STAIR POSITION, SAME FLOOR. UPDATED DIAGRAM ON PAGE 7. — BOOST

Page 7 had a hand-drawn floor plan. It was accurate — Kyle had studied the same layout eighteen months ago. Two observer markers, one at 07:44 and one at 07:52, and a note in Boost's hand: NOT A RESIDENT. NOT A DELIVERY. WAITING.

"She drew a diagram," Kyle said.

"She always does for a new stationary subject. In volume four she tracked a corpo security sweep and mapped three rotation patterns." Pixel closed the book. "The watcher was gone by 09:30. Emre logged it. 'Subject left walking north, steady pace, no urgency.' That's Emre's way of saying whoever it was got what they came for."

"Or a fourteen-year-old made them, and they left before it got complicated."

"Also possible. Boost doesn't think so. Her note says 'unknown if subject made.' She doesn't overclaim." A pause. "That's my training."

Kyle looked at the logbook. Three handwritings, one good diagram, one pigeon of doubtful loyalty. Something had sat outside his stairwell since before six that morning and left by half past nine, in no hurry.

"Someone wanted to know if I was home," he said.

"Or wanted to time your movements."

"Or confirm the stairwell layout."

"A lot of things you can want from three hours of sitting still?" Pixel picked the rig back up. "You said you were going to Vey."

"I'm going to Vey."

"Good. Tell me what you find."

Kyle stood. Put on his jacket. Checked Cacophony's seating in the hip rig, ready the way it was every morning, and he didn't check Silence — Silence never needed it. After eleven years the sword hung against him like part of his own weight. He thought about the watcher on the stairs. About who had paid to learn where he'd be and when.

Two, he'd thought. Two subscribers.

He was about to find out.

[Beat 71]
# BEAT: The Descent

Kyle descended fourteen steps to a landing that smelled of sealed air and old circuit board, then left through a door that read CLOSED in a municipal font three versions out of date. No one had bothered to update it. That told you something about the customers.

Inside, Antiquity & Stationary was library-quiet—the quiet of a place that had decided noise got in the way of the objects. Display cases ran both walls, each lit from below, each holding things that had once been the future and were now relics. First-generation neural rigs with their bulky ports and cooling fins. Dead handsets lined up by year, getting smaller down the row like reading time in rock layers. Pre-collapse server blades still in their brackets, lights dead. Early survey drones in cases near the back.

Overhead, hung from the ceiling on a wire and turning slowly from the climate system, was a RotoStar-3. Made sometime between 2193 and 2197. By today's standards a joke—a kid with neuretics saw more in a blink. It turned anyway, patient, no schedule to keep.

Kyle caught himself watching it complete a rotation before he made himself stop. Thirty hours on the Halvorsen window. A watcher he couldn't name. No time for old cameras.

Vey stood behind the counter, compact, maybe sixty, spare in his movements. Gray-white hair. A work apron over a gray shirt. His hands were clean—not scrubbed sterile, just careful, the hands of a man who knew exactly what he was holding. He was working on a first-generation neural rig with a magnifying glass, and he didn't look up when Kyle came in.

"Corbin," he said.

"Vey."

Kyle moved to the counter and set down the chip sleeve—the one with the Halvorsen estate markings, the one he needed Vey to tell him was either worth something or worth nothing before the auction window closed in thirty hours. He needed a number. A real one, not a guess.

"Provenance work."

Vey set the magnifying glass down without hurrying, the way he did everything, and Kyle felt his own foot already turned toward the door before the man had said a word.

"Buyers' list. My own file."

Vey picked up the sleeve, turned it once under the case light, held it a beat longer than it needed. "Sit down. This takes as long as it takes."

There was no chair on Kyle's side of the counter. There never was. It was Vey's way of saying the words anyway—*sit down* meant *slow down*, meant the sleeve would be examined at Vey's pace or not at all.

Kyle put both hands flat on the glass instead and made himself still.

Vey turned the sleeve again, tilted it to the light, ran a thumbnail along the seam without pressure. "Estate seal's real. Wax pull's clean—no reheat marks." He set it down and looked at Kyle for the first time, unhurried, like he had all the time this required and no more. "Where'd it come from before Halvorsen had it?"

"That's what I'm paying you to tell me."

"No." Vey folded his hands on the counter. "I don't source chips. I source *people*." He tapped the sleeve once. "This has an owner of record for forty years. Halvorsen, then Halvorsen's father, then a name I'd have to look up. That's not what I sell. What I sell is knowing whether the fortieth year is the true one." He looked past Kyle, at the case of dead handsets, then back. "Every piece in here has a card. Where it was, who held it, what it was worth to them before it was worth anything to me. I don't put a price on a thing until I know its whole life. A thing with no card—I don't sell it. I don't even display it. It sits in the back until somebody tells me where it's been."

Kyle thought of the thirty-hour window collapsing while a man explained his filing system to him. "I don't have a card. I have thirty hours."

"Then you'll have a number in twenty-nine." Vey said it without heat, already turning the sleeve over again, already somewhere else in his own unhurried process. "Rushing it doesn't make the sleeve older or younger. It just means I miss something and you pay for a lie."

Kyle didn't answer that. He'd rushed things his whole working life and most of it had held up—reflexes built to fill the gap between a threat and a decision, no slack in the system. Vey's stillness sat wrong against that, an itch under a scar. The man had built a business on refusing to be hurried, and it worked, and Kyle had never once seen him wrong.

"Buyers' list," Kyle said again. "My own file. Same visit."

Vey didn't look up from the sleeve. "That's a different kind of provenance. Yours." He set the loupe against his eye and bent to the wax seal, unbothered, in no rush at all. "Give me a minute on the chip first. Then we'll talk about who's been asking after you."

Kyle's hands came off the glass.

"Who."

"Not a question that needs an answer yet." Vey worked the seal, magnified eye steady. "I said then. Let me finish this."

The RotoStar-3 made another slow rotation overhead. Eight seconds. Consistent. Kyle watched it and counted without meaning to—a habit from the old contracts, when precision kept you alive. The watcher on his stairwell had sat for three hours. Not moving. Not waiting for a delivery. Timing something.

His wrist-seams itched. The reintegration firmware was still processing at 12 percent, the bonding medium still knitting the severed nerve ends back together. He thought about the stairwell. About a woman in a brown coat waving at a camera in his alley. About a watcher who sat outside his door from before dawn and left by half past nine with no apparent urgency.

Two subscribers, he'd thought. But it wasn't two subscribers. It was two *factions* knowing exactly where to find him.

Vey looked up from the sleeve. "The seal's clean. The wax is original—I can read the batch marker. That means the chain of custody from the estate is real." He set the loupe down. "Forty years on this one, and the first thirty-eight of it are going to cost you."

"How much?"

"Not money." Vey turned away and moved to a file cabinet behind the counter—old wood, hand-built, the kind of thing that belonged in this shop like the dust belonged in the light. He opened a drawer, withdrew a card printed on cardstock so old it had yellowed at the edges. Set it on the counter between them. "CORBIN COMMISSION — PENDING" it read in typeface that had to be from the 2180s. Below that, in handwriting: "Buyer unknown. Seller unknown. Payment method unknown. Purpose unknown. Status: UNSOURCED."

Kyle looked at the card. Then at Vey.

"That's your file," Vey said. "Forty years. No card. No provenance. No chain of custody I can trace. # Beat: The Carver-9 Platform

The freight hub at Carver-9 smelled like diesel and standing water—the kind of smell that lived in concrete that never fully dried. Forty meters overhead, the Pulse ran its invisible circuit, and Kyle felt it the way he always felt it: a sub-bass pressure in his inner ear, a hum that traveled up through boot soles into the long bones of his legs.

Pixel was already at the secondary compression door when he arrived, tech bag slung across one shoulder. She was eating a pastry—something with jam that had left a smear at the corner of her mouth—and she didn't look up from the door's keypad until he was close enough to see the numbers she was entering.

"You're eating," Kyle said.

"I got hungry." She held out what was left. He took half. She watched him eat it the way she watched everything: with the satisfaction of a person who'd solved a logistics problem and was filing it away for later. "Did you see Vey?"

"Yes."

"How bad?"

He chewed, swallowed, kept his breathing even. The thing about Pixel was that she didn't ask twice, didn't narrate her concern, didn't make a speech about it. She read the room first, then positioned herself accordingly. Right now she was reading the micro-shifts in his rig—the way his shoulders had settled into inventory mode, the stillness that meant he was already converting threat into dossier.

"I'll tell you after Rotterdam," he said.

She studied him a moment. Not his face—his posture. The angle of his wrist on the counter. The fact that he'd eaten half the pastry instead of refusing it entirely. She didn't say what she found. She just punched the code, and the compression door sighed open on hydraulics that needed servicing.

"Smart-dust tag," she said, leading him down the amber-lit corridor. The Pulse was stronger here, almost a presence—a weight in the air that made the corridor feel smaller than it was. "The 10:15 Rotterdam freight slug. Cargo code 7-Tau-1, one unit. Someone wants to know where it goes." Her voice was low without dropping to whisper. The voice she used when she was documenting threat in real time. "Our client is the shipper. They want the tag moved before departure onto the 10:17 to Bruges—cargo code 11-Sigma-2, bulk agricultural substrate. It arrives at a depot that doesn't scan at the item level. The tag sits in a Bruges warehouse reporting its location as long as the battery lasts, and whoever bought the surveillance decides they've been watching the right freight the whole time."

"Who's the watcher?"

"Quote: 'an interested party who has exceeded their interest.' The client was precise about it." She stopped at the manual access door—wheel-lock, FREIGHT ACCESS 3 — AUTHORIZED MAINTENANCE ONLY in faded orange, faded for years now—and spun the wheel one-handed. "The job's clean. We don't touch the cargo, we don't break a seal, we move one tag to another item with the shipper's permission. Nothing removed. Nothing forged."

The wheel spun free, and the door didn't move.

She spun it back. Tried again. The lugs turned, the mechanism unseated—and the slab stayed put, seated hard against its frame like something on the far side was holding it shut. Her jaw tightened. Not fear. The look she got when a system wasn't behaving according to its own logic.

"That's not right," she said, dropping to a crouch. She ran two fingers along the seam at the bottom edge. They came back with a bead of something pale and tacky, half-cured. Sealant. Fresh sealant. "This door was welded from the inside. In the last twelve hours."

She looked up at him, and the small-logistics-problem satisfaction was gone off her face entirely. Now she was reading him the same way she'd read the seam—looking for the place where the system broke.

Kyle put his hand flat against the slab. Under his palm, over the omnipresent hum of the Pulse, he could feel it: a second vibration, closer, wrong. Footsteps. Moving on the far side of the door. More than one set.

"Somebody knew we were coming to this door," he said. "And they got here first."

Pixel checked her wrist. 09:57. Eighteen minutes to departure. One sealed door. No second way onto that platform she'd briefed him for—which meant no second way onto the 10:15 Rotterdam slug, which meant the job collapsed before it started, which meant the client—

His hand was still on the door. He could feel the footsteps stop.

"We need to move," Pixel said. It wasn't a suggestion. She was already on her feet, already scanning the corridor behind them. "Now."

But Kyle was listening to the footsteps not-moving on the other side of the sealed door. Listening to the weight of them. The spacing. The way they'd stopped at the exact moment he'd touched the frame—which meant they'd felt his touch the same way he'd felt theirs.

Which meant the door wasn't sealed to keep people out.

It was sealed to keep them in.

"The other access?" Kyle said.

"Three levels up. Maintenance ladder in the east wall. But that adds six minutes minimum, and the departure window—"

"Is already gone," he said. He looked at the door. At the fresh sealant. At the footsteps that had known exactly when he would arrive and exactly where he would put his hand. "The job was never going to happen. This was the contract. This was always the contract."

Pixel's eyes went very still. She understood immediately—not the details, but the shape of it. A client who'd routed them to a door that was already sealed. A door sealed from the inside. Footsteps waiting for them to arrive.

"Ambush?" she said.

"Evaluation," Kyle said. He thought of Vey's ledger. The pencil circle. The thing with no provenance that had been reading his file for eleven years. "Come on."

He moved back down the corridor the way they'd come, Pixel half a step behind him, already reaching for whatever tool she kept closest. The Pulse thrummed overhead. The footsteps on the far side of the door stayed perfectly still.

Waiting.

# BEAT: The Notice

Kyle's apartment was the same as he'd left it four hours ago. The coffee from that morning still sat on the counter, skin formed on top. # The Board

The contract came in at 07:14 on a Tuesday in the middle of October.

Kyle sat at his kitchen table eating cold rice out of the pot, because he hadn't washed a bowl since Sunday. The city was running its autumn routine—cold mornings, warmer afternoons, the smell of the lake cutting through everything the ventilation tried to do about it. His neuretics flagged the posting before the notification chime finished.

He knew the format. He'd seen it forty-seven times.

Sixteen fixers ran contracts through Sable's board, and seven of them had templates Kyle could recognize on sight. One source had no name and no template he'd ever been able to place. It used no fixer. It posted straight to his work queue: a contract number, a task block, a rate, and a field labeled ADDENDUM where the strange conditions went.

He knew whose it was before he read the task.

**CONTRACT NO. 0048-C-WEST**

He read it twice.

**TASK: LOCATE AND ASSESS STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF CAROUSEL ELECTRICAL INFRASTRUCTURE, LEAVITT PARK, WEST TOWN SECTOR. ASSESS ONLY. NO INTERVENTION. REPORT FINDINGS TO RELAY STATION WITHIN FOUR HOURS OF COMPLETION.**

**DURATION: TWO HOURS MAXIMUM.**

**RATE: STANDARD PLUS 0.3 BONUS FOR ACCURACY.**

**ADDITIONAL TERMS: SITE WILL BE UNDER EXTERNAL SURVEILLANCE. YOUR PRESENCE WILL NOT BE ACKNOWLEDGED BY THIRD PARTIES. REMAIN UNOBSERVED IF OPERATIONALLY FEASIBLE.**

**NOTE: CAROUSEL MAINTENANCE RECORDS SEALED 2218. NO MUNICIPAL ACCESS SINCE DECOMMISSIONING. SITE CURRENTLY UNMAINTAINED.**

**ADDENDUM: AMENDMENT TO FOLLOW. PROCEED ON INITIAL TERMS PENDING RECEIPT.**

He set the pot down.

The rate was standard. This client always paid standard, early, exact. It had never tried to low-ball him, never dressed up a tip as part of the payment, never asked for a receipt. He had forty-seven finished contracts from this source in his queue. Forty-eight made forty-nine.

But the amendment came before the contract opened, not after. And the amendment said to proceed anyway, which meant this client had already committed to something before it knew whether Kyle would take the job.

He filed acceptance at 07:19. Neuretics, sub-vocal: ACCEPTED. PROCEEDING ON INITIAL TERMS.

The reply came in before his hand left the table.

**AMENDMENT: RECEIVED. FILED UNDER: FIRSTS.**

Not standard. Not *Amendment accepted* or *Proceed with caution* or any of the formulas this client used. The lowercase was wrong. The syntax was wrong. The thing that made it wrong was that it sounded like the client had just noticed something about Kyle that it had never noticed before.

He stood and moved to the window.

Below, the city was exactly where it had been an hour ago. The AxisMed depot running shift change. Boost's crew at the corner in their not-subtle setup. The maintenance mech moving smooth and silent. He pulled up the relay logs on his wrist display. Pixel had mapped the carousel park six months ago during a separate job. Movement patterns of kids in the West Town sector. Geometric center: a maintenance hatch under the carousel base, connecting to hand-spliced electrical line running dark into old glass.

He'd walked past that carousel a hundred times. He'd never stopped.

*Fired under: Firsts.* The client didn't keep records like that. The client compressed everything into relay format—scope, fee, addendum, nothing else. No commentary. No filing system. No metadata about what made a contract unusual.

Kyle closed the display. He picked up his tea. It was cold.

The hinge on the apartment door dragged when he opened it, and across the hall there was a pause—a moment where someone heard the sound and registered what it meant. He didn't turn to look. He was already thinking about the carousel.

By the time he reached the Wentworth Passage entrance, he'd mapped three routes to the park and identified two observation angles from the surrounding buildings. The carousel would be fenced. The hatch would be locked. The electrical line would be thirty years old and probably hot.

His fingers were moving through the motions of preparation before his mind had finished catching up: checking Cacophony's load, verifying Silence's edge, running a diagnostic on the neuretics array to make sure the overclock was available if he needed it.

He stopped at the passage mouth.

The carousel park was three blocks north. Mrs. Chen's stall was on this block, the same block it had been for twenty-three years. The fraud folder was still on his side table, still proving that the clearing had been decided months ago, that Mercer's easier corridors ran straight through Wentworth Passage, that the stall wasn't in the paperwork because it didn't need to be.

It was just in the way.

The carousel was real. The client was real, and it had just filed something under *Firsts*, which meant it was noticing patterns that Kyle had been too careful to see.

The second block was empty except for a delivery mech and a woman in a tan coat standing where someone would stand if they were watching the carousel entrance. She wasn't looking at Kyle.
