*What does this client see that I'm supposed to find?*

He reached the carousel perimeter at 07:47. The fence was institutional grade, posted with decommissioning notices dated 2218. The carousel itself was still beautiful in a way that abandoned things sometimes were—the horses frozen mid-gallop, the paint faded to soft colors, the whole thing waiting for something that wasn't coming.

He found the hatch.

The lock was old but maintained. Recent maintenance. Someone had been here, recently, and they'd cared enough to keep it functional. He worked the mechanism with his right hand while his left stayed on Silence, and the hatch opened on a smell of copper and old electrical insulation.

Below was darkness and the faint hum of active line.

He descended.

The wiring was older than the city's official records. Spliced by hand. Routed around the carousel's original infrastructure in a way that suggested someone had wanted it hidden but hadn't wanted it to fail. The electrical signature was hot—19.4 Hz, maybe 19.8. Close to the schism resonance but not quite. Close enough that his implants registered it as a warning.

He documented it. Photos. Readings. The geometry of the installation. The care taken in the splicing. The fact that this line had been live for decades, powering something, doing a job that the city didn't know about.

He was halfway back to the hatch when his neuretics flagged motion at the park entrance.

Not the woman in the tan coat. New players. Three of them, moving with the precision of a crew that had trained together. They had equipment. They had a writ. They had the bearing of people who expected the park to be empty.

They were heading for the carousel.

Kyle climbed. He sealed the hatch behind him. He moved to the fence line and watched them work.

The lead one—a man with a salvage crew badge—was reading the decommissioning notice with what looked like genuine surprise. The second was already photographing the carousel structure. The third was checking a handheld scanner, looking for access points.

They didn't know about the hatch. They didn't know about the line.

They were here for the carousel itself, which meant someone had filed a work order. Which meant someone had decided that the carousel needed to be taken apart, and that decision had been made without any consideration for the electrical infrastructure that had been running underneath it for thirty years.

Kyle's neuretics were running hot now. The overclock was available. His hand was on Silence's hilt. The rational move was to leave—get the data back to the client, file the report, let the chips fall where they would.

The rational move was to walk away.

He was already moving toward the fence.

He was halfway through his climb when the salvage crew lead looked up and saw him, and the whole thing changed from observation into something else.

"Hey," the man called out. "This is a sealed site. You need to clear the perimeter."

Kyle dropped back to the ground on the carousel side of the fence.

"Not my perimeter," he said.

"Doesn't matter whose it is. We've got a writ. You're trespassing."

Kyle could see the writ from where he stood. He could see the seal. He could see the signature block, and the authorization code, and the date that proved this crew had been dispatched this morning, which meant the decision to clear this site had been made before Kyle's client sent the contract at 07:14.

Which meant his client had known this was coming.

Which meant his client had sent him here to see it.

"The electrical line under the carousel is live," Kyle said. "You start cutting without understanding what's powering it, you're going to have a problem."

The second crew member—the photographer—looked at the lead. The lead looked back at his handheld.

"Our writ covers structural salvage only. Electrical's a separate permit."

"Then get a separate permit."

"Not your call."

Kyle was quiet for a moment. The carousel horses waited. The hum from below was still there, still 19-point-something, still close enough to the schism frequency that his implants couldn't quite stop registering it as wrong.

"I'm telling you what I know," Kyle said finally. "The line's been running for thirty years. It's connected to something. You cut it without understanding what, you're going to hurt someone."

The lead crew member smiled the way people smile when they're about to do something they've already decided on.

"Not my problem," he said, and turned back to the carousel.

Kyle climbed the fence.

He didn't draw Silence. He didn't pull Cacophony. He moved between the crew and the carousel, and when the lead man tried to step around him, Kyle stepped back, and they did that dance once, twice, three times, until the man's patience ran out and he radioed for backup.

"We've got a civilian interference at the site," he said into his wrist unit. "Send the enforcement team."

Kyle heard the sirens start.

He wasn't thinking about the carousel anymore. He wasn't thinking about the client or the amendment or the fact that his client had seen this coming. He was thinking about the fact that he'd spent six weeks coming to Mrs. Chen's stall, and she'd never explained the absences and never apologized for them, and he'd never asked, because asking would have made it a thing that needed his permission.

And now someone was clearing the passage where she stood.

And his client had sent him to watch it happen.

He climbed back over the fence—the sirens were still two blocks out—and ran north without looking back.

# Beat: Carousel Defense

"It covers the original installation. The original copper is still there — you can take it. The circuit runs on the secondary now. Pulling the original copper doesn't touch the lights."

That was true. Pixel had been very precise about it. The original copper conduit was still in the base housing; she'd rerouted the lighting circuit off it, not removed the copper. If the crew wanted the original copper, the lights would stay on.

The front man didn't like that. He conferred with the man behind him. Kyle waited. The October wind moved through the park and the horses didn't move with it. One of the men in back started toward the east wall with the cutter, the blade already spun up, whining thin and electric.

The girl was back. She'd drifted off from her father along the retaining wall, following the pigeons that had resettled on the fence the moment the argument stalled. Now she stood almost in the cutter's path, chin up, watching the birds instead of the blade. Her father was twenty feet behind her, eyes lost in a neuretics feed — a man who'd told a kid to stay close and thought that was the same as keeping her close.

"That secondary junction box," the man with the cutter said, pointing at the gray metal housing on the east retaining wall. "We cut that, the whole circuit falls back to the primary."

He was right. Pixel hadn't put that in the documentation.

Kyle looked at the box. It was mounted six feet up the east wall, installed 2218, never once serviced. Inside were three circuit relays and the connection to the secondary line. Cut it, and the secondary would drop back to the primary conduit, and the salvage writ would cover everything the lights were drawing from. To reach it, the man with the cutter would pass within a few feet of the girl.

He drew Cacophony.

It was the first time this year in West Town he'd drawn a weapon on a job that wasn't a demonstration. The gun sat familiar in his hand, always there, never the thing that mattered until it was. He didn't aim at anyone. He aimed at the junction box.

[Beat 98]
"That box is city property," he said. "So is the secondary line. Your writ doesn't cover either one. Cut that junction box and you're destroying city property outside your writ authority — and I'm a witness."

"You've got a gun pointed at a junction box?" the front man asked.

"I do."

"That's—"

The man with the cutter was almost at the wall. The girl still hadn't looked away from the birds. There was a version of the next two seconds where Kyle finished the sentence — told them what was coming and why, gave the men in front of him the beat it took to know a shot was coming instead of just hearing one, the way he'd done it every time before this. There wasn't time for that version.

He fired.

The first shot hit the relay housing dead center. In the enclosed park the sound was enormous, a hard crack that sent two pigeons off the far fence and made all three of the crew step back at once. The box didn't explode. It made the flat metallic sound of a thing that had been broken open and would not work again.

He fired again.

Four rounds remained.

The second shot went into the conduit housing below the relay, where the secondary line connected. The housing shattered. There was nothing left to cut now, because there was no junction left in any real sense. The secondary line ran from the city grid straight to the base circuit, no box in between — a less tidy solution, but it worked just as well and was much harder to get at with a portable cutter.

The carousel lights stayed on.

Behind him, the girl's father had her by the shoulder, hauled in against his leg at the sound of the shot, saying her name twice in the voice of a man checking his own pulse as much as hers. She wasn't hurt. She was mostly annoyed that the pigeons had gone.

Kyle held Cacophony at his side — not holstered, not raised.

"The secondary line's in the wall," he said. "The writ doesn't cover the wall. You want the original copper, it's in the base housing. You can have it. But you're not cutting to the lights."

The three men stood in the October morning looking at the wrecked junction box and the carousel lights burning clear and steady above them.

The front man folded the writ and put it in his jacket pocket. He looked at Kyle for a long moment, like a man recalculating what the day was going to cost him.

[Beat 99]
"DominionReach is going to want a damage report," the front man said.

"File it," Kyle said. "The address is on the writ."

They left. The van pulled out of the access lane and turned north, back toward wherever day-labor salvage crews went when a job stopped making economic sense.

Kyle holstered Cacophony and stood a moment in the quiet, listening to the city. Across the park the father was walking the girl back toward the east gate, already talking too fast, his relief curdling into a mild anger. She twisted around once for a last look at the wall where the birds had been.

He didn't go over. There was nothing to give them that wasn't already true: she was fine, and she'd have been fine either way, and the only difference between the two ways was a sentence he hadn't said. He had never fired without finishing that sentence first. Not once, not in eleven years of exactly this kind of work — the two extra seconds that turned a gunshot into a warning instead of a surprise. He'd skipped it this time. Nobody in the park had noticed. He had.

The gun had worked exactly the way it always worked. Walking back toward Pixel, he wasn't sure he had.

Pixel sat on the carousel's running board, cup in hand, watching him.

"You shot a junction box," she said.

"Yes."

"On purpose."

"It seemed efficient."

She thought about it. "It was efficient," she allowed. "The circuit runs cleaner without it, actually — the relay was pulling a 12% resistance load on the secondary draw."

"I didn't know that."

"I did. I was going to recommend pulling it anyway." She drank. "You could've just told me to."

"I needed the noise."

She nodded slowly. "How many rounds left?"

"Four."

She nodded again — not impressed, not unimpressed, just noting it. She kept count of things without turning the count into a comment on you. Kyle liked that about her, the way he liked a level that read true and said nothing about it.

"I need to get into hatch B-7," he said.

"The one the contract said not to touch until the crew left."

"Yes."

"What's in it?"

"I don't know yet."

She finished her coffee, stood, and handed him a flat-head driver from her satchel. "B-7 locks are compression latches. Counter-clockwise."

He took the driver. She didn't follow him.

[Beat 100]
The hatch sat in the park's northwest corner, flush with the ground. A concrete rim, a painted green stripe gone the color of old moss. Kyle knelt beside it. Counter-clockwise, two turns, then lift. The hatch rose on a hydraulic last serviced in 2209. It still worked.

Below was a crawl space, half a meter high, running under the carousel's foundation. He clicked on his hand light, lay flat on the concrete lip, and looked.

The space was not empty.

The old copper conduit ran along the left wall, right where the records said. Two water shutoffs — one working, one frozen with rust. An access panel for the base circuit, dead now since Pixel's reroute. And one more thing.

A cable. Hand-spliced. It ran from the city data line in the corner of the crawl space to a box the size of a hardback book, bolted to the foundation. The work was old — hand-soldered, taped, done by someone who knew what they were doing in a tight space with no room for power tools. The install date stamped on the box read 2215.

Eleven years old.

Kyle lay on the concrete and looked at it.

The amendment had told him: you will recognize it.

He didn't, not exactly. He didn't know what the cable connected to, or what signal it had carried, or why. But he knew the hand that made it. Careful. Deliberate. Built without paperwork, because paperwork would have made it visible — and the whole point was that it stayed invisible.

He reached in to get a closer look at the box, and that was when his hand light died.

Not dimmed — died. The beam snapped off mid-sweep, and the crawl space went black. He thumbed the switch. Nothing. Shook it. Nothing. In the dark he could still feel the cable under his fingers, and he became aware of something he'd missed in the light: it was warm. Faintly, but unmistakably. Powered. Carrying current, right now, in a line that eleven years of records swore was dead.

Then his earpiece crackled — Pixel's channel, the one that should have been silent this far under the foundation — and a voice that was not Pixel's asked, very quietly, "You shouldn't have opened that?"

Kyle went still. The voice hadn't come from the earpiece. It had come from the box, six inches from his face, in the dark.

He fumbled the light, smacked it hard against the concrete, and the beam stuttered back to life. The box sat exactly where it had been. Bolted. Sealed. Silent. No speaker grille he could see. Nothing that could have spoken.

But the amendment had said he would recognize it. And now, cold under the carousel with his hand still tingling from the warmth of the cable, he understood what it wanted him to recognize was not the wiring.

It was that the thing on the other end had been waiting for someone to come looking.

Someone had run this line in 2215 and kept it alive for eleven years by never touching it and never filing anything that would call in a salvage crew. The copper salvage writ — filed in 2214, a year before this cable went in — had only ever covered the conduit. Not the signal line. If the copper had stayed on the main circuit, sooner or later a crew would have found the cable and asked what it fed. Pixel's reroute had killed that risk. It stripped the copper of its salvage value and gave the crews no reason to open the base housing.

The entity had kept a physical line here for eleven years, and no contract explained why. If Kyle had to name it, the closest word was sentimental.

[Beat 101]
Kyle pulled the amendment back up on his neuretics queue.

TERMINATE LINE AT NEAREST JUNCTION. NO RECORD.

ADDENDUM: AMENDMENT: NO. PROCEED ANYWAY.

He lay flat in a crawl space under a carousel in West Town, October 2226, reading an order that argued with itself — from an employer he had never met or spoken to, over a signal line installed the same year he took his first job from that employer. The contradiction was plain. He looked at it a moment longer anyway.

He pulled himself forward on his elbows. The ceiling was six inches above his head. He reached the box, found the junction, and cut the cable.

He used the flat-head driver, not a cutter — levered the cap open and worked the splice apart by hand, clean, no frayed ends. The line went dead in his fingers. A small indicator light on the box, one he hadn't noticed until it died, had been green, barely there in the dark.

He backed out, came up through the hatch, and stood in the park.

The carousel was running.

No music — the calliope was silent — but the mechanism had started to turn. Slow. The painted horses came around in the October light, heads down in a frozen gallop, the canopy bulbs bright and steady on Pixel's clean draw. Then, from some last charge in the base circuit, the calliope woke. Not a full chord. Four bars of whatever it had played last — a minor-key waltz, a name Kyle didn't know, the pipe-organ sound of it climbing into the cold. Then it stopped.

Four bars.

Then the carousel went dark. Not slowly. The lights cut at once. The mechanism wound down over eight seconds and the horses stopped a little off from where they'd started, and it was quiet.

Pixel stood ten feet away, watching. She said nothing.

Kyle looked at the carousel. He marked the job done in his neuretics queue.

Then he added the tip.

The entity's contract format had a reply field. He'd used it before — completion notes, once a question about a follow-on task. He had never added a line item that wasn't in the original contract. There was no field for it. He typed it into the reply as free text:

MORALE: Φ0.5.

He didn't know if it made sense as a line item. He sent it anyway and stood in the quiet, the October light coming through the fence slats, the horses still.

[Beat 102]
He walked back toward the Pivot for lunch. Pixel came as far as Walton, then turned south toward a calibration job she'd mentioned that morning. She didn't say anything about the carousel or the tip.

She said, "Eat something. You're running on cold rice and whatever you burned through that amp draw."

"I'll eat," he said.

"You'll eat cold rice again," she said. "That's not eating. That's maintenance."

He didn't have an answer that wasn't an admission, so he walked north.

Mrs. Chen's stall sat open to the air on Wentworth Passage, where it had stood for twenty-three years — thirty-two square feet, mobile-classified: an awning post, a counter, a single wok. She paid the block's owner a pitch fee, a man named Farida Osei who had tried three times in four years to raise it and been talked out of it every time. Kyle would have paid to watch that negotiation.

The noodle bowl was in front of him before he sat down.

"You look like you've been on the ground," she said.

He had been on the ground. Concrete dust marked his jacket where he'd lain in the crawl space.

"Job," he said.

"Your hands are dirty." Not a complaint. A reading. She set a tea beside the bowl without being asked. The bowl was full today — the extra ounce of broth she added when she thought he needed it, which she never admitted adding and he never admitted taking.

He paid for the bowl, exact, and drank the tea, and ate. He wanted one thing from this hour: to get a reply out of the entity — a confirmation the carousel job had closed clean, the receipt he needed before he'd let himself call it done. He'd sent the query before he left the crawl space. Now he waited on it the way he waited on everything the entity owed him: expecting the format, expecting the fields, expecting nothing he couldn't already predict.

He was halfway through when the reply came in.

The entity's contract format ran in all caps. Forty-seven completed contracts. He knew the format the way he knew Cacophony's weight — by the shape of it in his hands, not by thinking about it. It had fields: CONTRACT NUMBER, STATUS, PAYMENT, NOTES. The notes field was the closest the entity came to a personality. GRATUITY FOR EXPEDIENT RESOLUTION, once. MORALE NOTED, after a hard job on South Clark. EXCELLENT FIELDWORK RE: THE JUNCTION QUESTION, which Kyle had kept and never known what to do with.

He opened the reply.

received. filed under: firsts.

Four words. Lowercase. No field headers. No contract number. No structure.

He read it three times.

Eleven years of formatted mail, every letter kerned the same, every 'e' identical to the last — and the entity had never once sent a freeform line. Every message before this had been a contract artifact: posting, addendum, gratuity, receipt. Kyle hadn't known the entity could send anything that wasn't a filing.

Mrs. Chen watched him from across the counter the way she watched everything — fully, without making a show of it.

"Something strange?" she asked.

"Just a reply," he said.

"From who?"

"Someone I work for."

She refilled the tea. He drank it. He read the message once more.

received. filed under: firsts.

Not a contract. Not a field entry. He thought about the green light going out in the crawl space, the four bars of the waltz, the carousel going dark.

He did not reply.

He finished the bowl, left exact change, and walked out into the West Town afternoon.

[Beat 103]
The woman in the tan coat came back to him halfway down Huron.

He ran the morning again. His neuretics kept a perfect record, exact to the point of nuisance, and he watched it back: the van pulling out of the access lane, the east fence, and there — mid-thirties, average height, tan coat, standing at a slight angle.

The angle was the thing. Not the van. Not him. Not the carousel the way people watch a carousel, chin up, half-smiling at the horses. Her body was set square on the maintenance hatch. The one with the green-striped rim.

She'd been there for the shots, too. He was sure of it, because the shots turned every head in the park and hers hadn't moved.

And when he looked at her, she saw him do it, and she walked. Not fast. Not slow. The pace of someone who wanted it understood that they had somewhere else to be, and that the two facts had nothing to do with each other.

The skin between his shoulder blades tightened before the thought finished. Someone had been watching for the hatch to open.

He didn't know who she was. He kept the image and let it sit — not a conclusion, just a thing that didn't fit yet.

But he wasn't going to walk it off. He turned back toward Huron and the park behind it. He'd go to the hatch himself, get down where she'd been standing, and see what she'd been waiting on.

[Beat 104]
The maintenance hatch told him nothing he hadn't already read from the woman's stance. Green-striped rim, standard grade, a lock that had been picked and reset with the pins slightly canted — professional, patient work. He photographed it, logged the coordinates, and left the park with a name-shaped hole where an answer should be.

Vey's shop was where it always was: down on the Loop's third underlevel, fourteen steps below street grade, behind the door whose CLOSED sign nobody had updated since 2190. The sign beside it read ANTIQUITY & STATIONARY. The second word was, as Casper Vey told anyone who pointed it out, on purpose. He'd once written it down for Kyle on a slip of paper: the past will not move. Then he put the slip in a file and refused to say what the file was for.

The shop smelled of old circuits and dry paper and equipment built before the switch to polymer parts in the 2160s — something metallic, something like resin, a low note of aged solder underneath. The shelves held first-generation neural rigs in their original casings, dead handsets in pieces, early survey drones, pre-collapse server blades, and a run of objects you couldn't identify at a glance, their cards reading only PROVENANCE: CONFIRMED.

Vey was at the back counter, cataloguing. He looked up when Kyle came in and waited.

Kyle set the hatch photo on the counter, face up, and beside it a second item — a paper receipt, physical, from the tea he'd bought that afternoon at Mrs. Chen's stall. Credstick-adjacent, untraceable, the kind of thing Vey's whole trade existed to make sense of.

"Salvage writ," Kyle said. "This morning. Leavitt Carousel Park. I want the funding chain."

Vey didn't touch the photo. He looked at it the way he looked at everything, cataloguing before deciding whether to care. "That would take my contacts in the reclamation registry, a document trace through at least two shell companies, and a fair amount of my time."

"I know."

"You want to know what funded the writ."

"And who set up the program it connects to."

Vey put down his tool. He looked at Kyle over the tops of his glasses — real glasses, not for his eyes, which were easy to fix in 2226, but because they gave him something to look over at people. "You already have a hypothesis."

"I have a woman in a tan coat who watched a hatch instead of a carousel."

"That's an observation. Not a hypothesis." Vey folded his hands. "You could go find her instead. Faster. You're good at finding people who don't want to be found."

"She'd know I was coming."

"And a document trail wouldn't."

"That's the idea."

Vey almost smiled — the closest he came to it, a small adjustment at one corner of his mouth. "You trust paper more than you trust your own reads. That's unusual, for what you do."

"Paper doesn't change its story when I ask it twice."

"Neither do good reads."

"Reads can be wrong and still feel right. That's the problem with them." Kyle nodded at the photo. "Paper's wrong in a way I can check."

Vey studied him a moment longer, then drew the photo toward himself with one finger, unhurried. "You already have a hypothesis," he said again, softer this time, not a question.

"I'd like a document chain that agrees with it or breaks it. Either one's useful."

Vey took the job. Kyle paid standard rate, then set down a second, smaller sum without being asked — the kind of overpayment that wasn't a tip so much as an apology for the traffic he was about to bring into the shop. Vey raised one eyebrow at it.

"Paperwork outlives everyone who signs it," Kyle said, by way of an answer.

"So does a body, given the right storage," Vey said, and logged the payment without further comment.

Kyle left the trace in his hands and walked back up the fourteen steps into the gray afternoon, already running the timeline: how long a shell-company search took, how long the woman in the tan coat could stay ahead of him before the paper caught her shadow from behind. He didn't know which would arrive first — the name, or the next contact from the entity, filed under whatever category it decided this was.

He had the results by evening. He wasn't ready for what they said.

[Beat 105]
He was at the kitchen table again, the same pot from that morning, when the file came through Vey's secure relay. He read it off his neuretics, projected against the wall in the amber light of the one bulb that still worked over the sink.

The salvage writ, CR-4419-W, had been funded through a DominionReach subsidiary called Copper Reclamation West. Real company, real book of municipal copper contracts across three zones. That was the first layer.

Behind Copper Reclamation West sat a budget code. Vey had traced it to a parent program in the West Town district infrastructure accounts.

DISTRICT ACQUISITION, WEST TOWN WEST.

Established 2224. Still running. Budget active, recurring, drawn every quarter.

Stated purpose: INFRASTRUCTURE SURVEY AND ASSET MANAGEMENT, WEST TOWN WEST DISTRICT. Standard language on a standard line, built to look like every other entry on the page and mostly getting away with it.

What Vey had pulled from the detailed records — through a contact in the assessor's office who owed him favors of some unspecified kind — was this: eighteen separate reclamation actions over two years, all inside the same ten-block radius. Every one had targeted physical infrastructure. Copper conduit. Data line access points. Cable terminus housings. Structural anchor points.

Every action along Leavitt. West Town West.

Vey had flagged the pattern on the map. Each action fell within two hundred meters of one corner. Leavitt and Iowa. The carousel park.

Kyle sat with that.

Eighteen actions, closing in a slow spiral, and he'd been reading it the way he read everything — cross-referencing, timestamping, building the shape before trusting it. That was the method. Find the paper, let the paper argue with itself, believe whichever version survived. It had never once failed him. He ran the two years again against the cable's install date and felt the method fail for the first time he could remember: nine years of nothing, then a program that started counting inward, and no version of careful information-gathering was going to slow a thing that had already decided where it was going before he'd noticed it moving.

This morning's action was the nineteenth. The first one to reach the carousel itself.

He went through it again. Cable went in 2215. DISTRICT ACQUISITION started 2224. Nine years between the burial and the first sign anyone was looking for it — if that's what this was. Then two years of patient work, action by action, closing on the source like a hand finding a pulse.

He reached the end of the file and stopped. The last entry wasn't a record. It was live. A twentieth action, timestamped four minutes ago, still writing itself into the district log — CR-4420-W, EXECUTION IMMEDIATE — and under the target coordinates, the string he already knew by heart. Leavitt and Iowa. Not two hundred meters out. The hatch itself.

The relay window went dark. A red flag bloomed where Vey's channel had been.

SOURCE CONNECTION TERMINATED.

He pinged the line. Nothing came back.

Whoever ran the program hadn't just moved on the carousel tonight. They'd felt someone looking through the assessor's records and shut the door on the way out. Nineteenth action aimed at the box. Twentieth already in motion. And the one man who could tell him where it was going had just gone quiet mid-sentence, the way paper wasn't supposed to.

Kyle sat at the table with the dead channel in front of him and understood, in the flat clinical way he understood a rib going or a hand going numb, that he had run out of things to check.

[Beat 106]
Someone had found the entity's thread. Had been following it in for two years. Had gotten close enough this morning that the entity sent contract number 0047.

He held that as a guess, not a fact. Vey's file didn't trace the funding above the district account — either Vey hadn't pushed that far, or the layer above was cleaner than the shell companies below it. He didn't know what DISTRICT ACQUISITION was, or who ran it, or what they'd have done with a signal line in a crawl space if they'd found it before he cut it.

He didn't know if the woman in the tan coat was part of the program. It was possible. That was all he had.

He didn't know what the entity's line had carried. What signal. Why sentimental was the word that had come to him, and not some other one.

He held all of it loosely — the tan-coat woman, the four bars of the waltz, four lowercase words that weren't a filing. Not answers. Just things that were true and didn't yet connect.

Outside the kitchen window, West Town ran its Tuesday evening: a ventilation unit across the alley cycling through its half-hour pattern, the lake smell cutting through everything else once the temperature dropped after dark.

Kyle poured cold rice into the pot, added water, set it on the element.

He looked at the message once more.

received. filed under: firsts.

Eleven years of formatted mail, and one sentence that wasn't a filing. He turned it over and didn't like where it led. He was the maintenance plan, not the map. He cut the cables he was told to cut. He'd fired twice into a junction box and four rounds remained, and the carousel had run four bars of something nobody had named for him and then gone dark, and somewhere in the city a woman in a tan coat had watched the hatch and walked away slow when he looked at her.

Standard rate. Filed under: firsts.

He ate the rice. He let the rest of it sit — not solved, not dropped, just there, the way the cable had sat in the crawl space for eleven years, doing whatever it did, waiting for someone to find it.

But the tan coat he could touch. She'd watched the hatch; she'd know who else was watching. He'd go back to Leavitt tomorrow, before the park opened, and find where she'd stood — and wait for her to come looking again.

The carousel park on Leavitt sat dark and still.

Four rounds remained.

## Chapter 6: Half a Step

[Beat 107]
He knocked at eleven, late even by his standards, and Pixel opened the door without the soldering iron this time — which meant she'd heard the stairs and set the work down before he knocked.

"Ribs," she said. Not a question. She'd seen him favor the left side on the way up.

"Two, probably. The taser found the gap at the lat — the seam the mesh doesn't cross."

She stepped back from the door. He came in and set Silence — the flat-black katana — against the wall by the stool, quiet, the way he set it down anywhere he meant to stay more than a minute. Then he sat where she pointed, no ceremony, and she put her hands on either side of the damage and felt for what the mesh had stopped and what it hadn't. Her hands were cold from the bench. She didn't warn him and she didn't apologize, because that was the understanding between them: these hands, this cold, this room, the work that needed doing.

"Not displaced," she said. "Hairline on the lower one. It'll hurt for a week and then decide it's done." She taped it the way she'd tape any structural problem — the question was whether it held, not whether it hurt.

He looked down at the seam where the mesh stopped, the gap that had let the taser through. "Somebody cheaped out on the coverage?" he asked. It came out flatter than he'd meant; most things did, when he tried to make them light.

Pixel didn't look up from the tape. "No. They traded it for the joint. You can't lay full plate over a lat and still reach with it." She pressed the last edge down with her thumb. "It's not a hole in you."

At the far end of the worktable, Oziel's arm lay in its jig, half its tendons strung — a thing she was building, not fixing. She gave Kyle's ribs the same hands she gave the arm.

When she finished she did not step back.

She stayed where she was, one hand still flat against his side where the tape ended. The room was what it always was at this hour: the lamp on the bench, the smell of flux and something she'd been eating, the soft cycling of the bench coolers between jobs. Nothing happened.

"Close it up," he said, meaning the mesh, meaning the seam — because if she overlaid the joint he'd stop losing skin to gaps like tonight, and she was the only one who could do it. "The lat. Bridge the gap. You've got the jig right there."

Her hand didn't move off his side, but the rest of her went still in a way he knew — the stillness she went into when the answer was no and she was deciding how much of the no to say. "Then you don't reach," she said. "Bridge that seam and you lose the draw off the left. You want to stop taking tasers or you want to keep drawing Silence, but you don't get to want both from the same three inches of you." She finally looked up. "Pick a body. I'll build the one you pick. I'm not building both."

He held her eyes and felt the choice sit there — the seam that hurt against the reach that kept him alive — and he had no answer for it, not tonight, not with two ribs telling him which one he'd already chosen and would keep choosing.

He started to stand. The hand stayed — not pressing, just there, the weight of it between him and standing. His heel came down an inch back. He stayed. She looked at the floor for one beat, and then she was done looking at it.

"Friday," she said, which was when Oziel was coming for the arm.

He was quiet for a breath. "Friday," he said.

She turned back to the bench. He took Silence up from the wall — the weight of it familiar, unchanged — left the door open the width she always left it, and crossed the four steps home through the taser burn's steady report.

[Beat 108]
The taser burn would be worst in the morning. He knew that the way he knew all of it — the shoulder's recovery curve, the rib-tape interval, how long a mesh-seam burn took to go quiet. He ran his thumb over the tape, the hairline under it, the line where the mesh stopped and the decision to stop it there had begun.

The gap was by spec. The engineer who'd laid the mesh in had traded coverage for movement at the lat — a trade Kyle hadn't been asked about. He'd been sixteen. Not a client, not yet — closer to a project on the bench, a variable someone was still solving for, one of the calls made before anyone thought to ask him. The engineer had done clean work. The mesh had stopped two center-mass rounds and a stave follow-through. What it hadn't stopped was exactly what it was built not to stop: the cost of being able to reach.

*She'd called it room, not a hole.* He turned her line over in the dark. He'd spent a long time reading the gap as something done to him. She'd looked at the same gap and called it room. He didn't know which of them was right. He thought he might want to find out, which was closer to a plan than he usually got.

He lay back, the burn keeping its schedule. He thought about her hand flat against his side where the tape ended, and the word "Friday" — the ordinary thing she offered when the other thing came too close — and how the word had come out of him anyway. Not because he knew what it meant. Because not saying it had stopped being something he could do. Then he let it go and slept.

[Beat 109]
The burn woke him at six, as promised. One gun left.

Kyle picked it up.

The NeoCortex had no governor. That was the thing killing him, and it was the only reason the next three seconds were possible. He connected to the detonator port through his neuretics and found the lock on the countdown — a rolling cipher, built to make disarming it in the field impossible. He broke it. Not with finesse. With raw processing power, the way you use a sledgehammer when you can't find the key, running through the cipher faster than the hardware was ever rated to go. It was the wrong direction. That was the point. A man fighting three shotguns runs for the exit. Kyle ran for the high steel, because a stair is a corridor, and a corridor turned three barrels into one.

The stair held for four steps. On the fifth, War Dog put a round through the riser under Kyle's back foot, and the whole flight dropped out from under him at once — steel tearing off its bolts with a shriek that had no business coming out of something that heavy, the landing rushing up gray and fast, no time left to pick where he fell.

He had a problem.

The entity had sent him here to assess a carousel. Instead he'd found an office full of dead names and active files and proof that every breath he'd taken in eleven years had been orchestrated. His hands had stopped shaking.

The rib still screamed. The shoulder still bled. The left arm still hung at an angle that suggested the joint had a grievance. But the hands were steady again, and the mind behind them had moved past the moment of revelation into something colder and more useful.
