She was good at waiting. Kyle watched her a moment longer, then turned from the window and picked up his coat.

"You posted the job," he said. "That means they know you posted the job. We need to move."

"I know," Nadia said. "I was waiting for you to come back."

He pulled the coat on. Checked Cacophony out of habit — four rounds, right. "I didn't go anywhere."

"No," she said. "I know that too."

He held the door for her.

[Beat 305]
The radiator had settled into a sound Kyle had stopped hearing three minutes ago — the pipes ticking, a faint drip somewhere down the hall, Nadia's breathing still working to find its own bottom. He was crouched against the shelving, his back to the cold steel, watching the door they'd come through. She sat with her spine against the next unit, close enough that he could feel her body heat as a plain fact.

He asked because he had the time and because it mattered.

"Why the open board?"

She didn't answer right away. She was the kind of person who treated a silence as a draft she could still revise.

"I couldn't use a secure channel," she said.

"You have contacts."

"I had contacts. Past tense. Anyone I could have reached inside a closed network was either already compromised or watched closely enough that reaching them would've been the same as a signed confession." She turned her head toward him, not quite meeting his eyes, looking at the middle distance the way people do when they're reciting something they worked out alone at three in the morning. "I needed someone outside every network. Someone who wouldn't need it explained. Someone who'd read the phrase and already know what it meant."

Kyle said nothing. The compressor cycled.

"There was no one else who would recognize it," she said. "It's not a real phrase. It was never published. It was never in any training record a person could reach. Seito — the construct — was private architecture. Closed source. The only place that phrase exists is in you. I put it there. I was the one who sourced the teaching aphorisms. I wanted something that would read as real to anyone who hadn't lived it, so I pulled from actual instructors. The phrase itself was real — Yun-Gi Han, 2178, recorded at a practicum in Busan. 'After the choice. Before the cost. That's where you move.' But the context was mine. I wrote the room. I wrote the afternoon. I wrote Seito stopping the drill and saying it to you — the specific you, the student who needed to hear it that way. The phrase was the only key there was. I put it in the posting and waited to see if anyone would recognize it. Whether the program had deployed. Whether the recipient was real. Whether he was still himself enough to read it."

Kyle watched the door.

"So the job was posted to me."

"Yes."

"You just had to trust I was still working boards. Still reading."

"Still yourself enough to recognize it," she said. "Yes."

The compressor finished its cycle. In the quiet after, the cooler felt smaller.

"You could have just called," he said.

She looked at him. "I didn't have your number."

"Nobody does."

The pressure changed. Not a sound yet — a condition, the shift of a fire door opening three floors down, the building's sealed cold-chain corridors registering it as a ghost of moving air. He caught it before his ears did and had it placed between one heartbeat and the next: two bodies, moving with the gait of people who'd cleared a stairwell before.

Kyle was already rising.

"They're here," he said.

[Beat 306]
Kyle heard them at the base of the stairs.

Not footsteps. The building didn't give him footsteps. It gave him weight. The safe house sat on a slab of reinforced concrete, and concrete carries load the way bad news travels — unevenly, but it travels. Six people. Two on the outside landing. Four climbing the stairwell in a stack. He was already moving Nadia before he said a word.

"Desk. Left side."

She moved. No question, no hesitation. He'd seen that in the cooler and again on the bus — she listened with her body first and let her mind catch up. He put her between the desk and the eastern wall. Brick. Load-bearing. Three feet clear of the window's line. Then he crouched beside her and kept his voice low enough to die in the drywall.

"Two on the fire escape. They'll hold the east window until they hear the front door go. Don't move until I tell you. If I say run, you go through the bathroom, out the window, into the courtyard. You don't look back to see what's behind you."

She nodded once. Her eyes tracked the room — not panic, the calm of someone who had already pictured exactly this ending for weeks. He noted it and set it aside. There'd be time to be surprised by her later, or there wouldn't.

He went to his coat on the hook by the door.

Cacophony came free of the holster with a sound he knew the way he knew gravity. He checked the cylinder by feel. Four rounds. He'd spent two inside Northpoint and reloaded one in the corridor. Four was what he had, and four was a number, and a number he could work with.

The stairwell went quiet.

That was the signal. Professionals stop moving right before they move — the last weight on a step, then nothing, then the door.

The door came in on a ram, low and fast.

He didn't wait for it to stop.

The first two rounds went through the upper panel at angles he'd already worked — the door frame, the spacing of a breach team, where the point man's chest had to be at full stride. The shotgun's spread did the rest. The point man dropped into the doorway. The second man caught the edge of the pattern and spun sideways into the frame, still up, still moving, one hand on his weapon.

Kyle was already sliding left.

The fire-escape crew took the east window on the sound of the shots. He'd figured six seconds. They came in four, which told him they were better than the pair at the door, and that fact landed somewhere under his ribs before he'd finished the thought. Glass blew inward. Two shapes, low and fast, spaced like men who had done this together.

Two rounds left.

He put one into the near shooter at seven feet. Center of the chest, nothing fancy. The second was already through the frame with an angle on Nadia, which meant the desk wasn't cover anymore. Kyle fired his last round as he closed — not to hit, just to push the man's aim wide — then got inside the reach of the gun, where a gun is a liability. The scabbard came up before the sword cleared it.

It wasn't clean. He drove the pommel end into the man's throat, blade still sheathed, the angle bad because the man was already lifting an elbow to block. Kyle felt the block land — actually felt it, a jolt he hadn't priced for — and had half a second where the whole shape of the exchange came apart in his hands. He turned the strike down instead of through, ramming the low end of the scabbard up under the ribs. The man folded. Kyle took him by the collar and put him into the wall, and the man stopped being a problem.

Silence came free.

The second man at the door had his weapon up and a ruined shoulder — the shotgun had done enough. Twelve feet, a narrow room, furniture between them. A pistol is slower than a man who already knows where you'll be. Kyle moved before the trigger finger finished deciding, past the furniture line, the overhead cut already committed when the arm came up. Silence answered the arm and then answered him.

The room went quiet except for the building settling.

He stood still for three seconds and counted.

Four in the stack. Two down inside, one on the threshold, one he couldn't place. He went low to the doorframe and checked the stairwell. Nothing. Either the fourth had held outside and was already gone, or he was somewhere in the building Kyle couldn't reach from here. He held for two more seconds.

Nothing moved.

Nadia's voice came from behind the desk, steady. "There's a coat."

He turned. She had his coat over one arm, held out to him — his left arm, the one that needed to be free. She'd taken it off the hook during the fight. He didn't know when. She'd been reading the room the whole time, on her own map, and she'd done the right thing at the right second without being told, and that landed somewhere he didn't have a place for yet.

He took the coat.

"Can you walk?"

"Yes."

"Then we're leaving."

He scanned the room one more time. Not for comfort. For inventory. All four rounds gone. Silence clean. The fourth man still a question. His left shoulder had a new catch in it, the arm that had driven the scabbard paying for the angle. The hit he'd taken in the Northpoint corridor had been grinding on his lower ribs through every exchange and was doing something worse now — two cracked, maybe one broken. It would matter tomorrow. It didn't stop him tonight.

He said nothing about any of it.

The coat went on over all of it.

"The stairs," he said, and she was already moving.

[Beat 307]
The contractors were in the stairwell, the hallway, and the chair where he'd left one of them. He counted them before he counted himself.

Six. All there.

Then he checked his own body, the way a mechanic walks a chassis after a hard run — not hunting for one thing, just finding what had changed. Left side: two ribs cracked, maybe one broken. The shoulder he'd driven the scabbard with had locked up tight, worse now than it had been ten minutes ago, a wrench deep in the joint that biotape wouldn't touch but that he'd pressed on anyway in the dark, in the forty seconds he'd had. His hands were steady. His neuretics ran hot — he could feel the heat at the base of his skull, the small stubborn headache that meant he'd burned past what the read cost him — but the overlay was still up and still readable. He was working.

Nadia stood against the far wall, arms folded, watching him.

"Count's done," he said. "You're not hurt."

"No."

"Northpoint will know the team went dark. They'll wait maybe ten minutes for a check-in, then send a runner to confirm. After that someone senior decides what this becomes." He picked the slate up off the table where she'd set it. "You've got about forty minutes before that call gets made. Be somewhere I don't know about before it does."

She watched him. "You planned this before they came."

He handed her the slate. A sector address in Z4. A transit code that would clear two checkpoints without a flag. A name. "The contact holds for seventy-two hours. Don't go back to wherever you slept last night."

She looked at the slate. Then at him — the same look she'd had in the cooler reading the thermal log, finding something still running that she hadn't expected to.

"You need a doctor," she said.

"I know one."

She didn't push. She wasn't a person who pushed at things already decided.

A silence. Not an uncomfortable one — just the room being what it was now. Someone else's safe house, safe for thirty-nine more minutes.

"The phrase in the posting," she said. "Seito's phrase. I used it because you were the only one who'd know it." She paused. "I didn't know if you'd still be —" She stopped. Started again. "I didn't know if you'd still be yourself?"

"I'm not sure that's the right word."

"I know," she said. "I used it anyway."

She tucked the slate inside her jacket, precise about it, the way she'd been precise about everything he'd watched her do tonight — the bay numbers in the cooler, the way she moved when he told her to move. She had been waiting a long time, he thought, to be moving again.

She went to the door and stopped with her hand on the frame. Without turning she said, "The man they built is the one who came. I don't think they knew that's what they were building."

Then she was gone.

Kyle stood in the room.

He didn't go to the window. She'd earned an exit no one watched.

He went to work. He moved the contractor nearest the door out to the stairwell — not because it would matter in forty minutes, but because tidiness was a habit, and habits don't take the night off. He picked up the casings by count, his neuretics tagging each one as it went in his pocket. He wiped the surfaces he'd touched. He checked the way he'd come in and made sure it still looked like a door no one had used.

The shoulder was bleeding again, slow, through the biotape — a slow leak, nothing urgent. Something to manage on a clock.

He had the doctor's code ready in the overlay. He'd send it two blocks out and moving.

The phrase. It was Seito's, and Seito was a design document, and the phrase had been written into him by people who needed the pieces to fit. He'd known that for four hours now. He turned it over — not for new information, just to set the weight of it down in the right place.

The man they built is the one who came.

He didn't know if she was right. He wasn't sure the question had a right answer. The sword still knew what his hand knew. Whatever the sixty-four had been built to make, it had held. Whatever word she'd reached for and set aside — yourself — it pointed at something still in the room. Still working. Still willing to hold a count.

He thought that was enough.

He picked his jacket up off the floor, thumbed two fresh rounds into Cacophony from the pocket, and left.

[Beat 308]
The stairwell smelled like mildew and mineral water, from a pipe that had been weeping through the wall since before the ferrocement wave. Kyle stopped on the third-floor landing. Not because anything needed it — nothing was coming, he'd checked twice — but because his hands were doing something without him.

The right hand. His sword hand.

It had moved into the first position of the third correction, the grip adjustment Seito had drilled into him across three hundred repetitions on a specific Tuesday he couldn't find now. He had a sense of wooden floors. Slant light. A clear memory of being told his elbow was too high. A less clear memory of the face that told him. And no memory at all of the afternoon it got fixed — because that afternoon never happened. The correction that mattered, he'd worked out himself, two years later, when he noticed the form dragged the cut slightly sideways.

He'd fixed it alone. On a job. After the job. Standing in an alley on the north side with a body cooling behind him and nothing but time.

Seito never saw the change.

Kyle ran the form once on the landing, slow, no urgency. Weight shift, turn at the hip, the drive through the shoulder, elbow where he'd decided it belonged instead of where he'd been told. The form was better now. Cleanly, plainly better. Whoever built the Seito construct had done it from archives — recordings of a thousand real fighters folded into one teacher. Good work. Real work. The skill had arrived in him whole and true. But the archive didn't hold the alley on the north side, or the job before it, or the four hundred times he'd done the grip wrong in the two years after Seito before he caught it himself.

None of that was installed.

He ran the form to the end. His hands came back to rest.

He had a grief with no object. He'd known Seito nine years — which wasn't true in any sense a court would take, and the grief was real anyway, which was maybe the point. The afternoons were invented. The form was his.

There was a second grief under the first. A master, even a made-up one, is someone else's certainty to lean on. Masterless meant no certainty but his own. On the page that sounds like freedom. On a cold landing at four in the morning it felt like a house with the load-bearing walls pulled out. He'd need his own answer soon, about Pixel — whether to send her back from a door he hadn't cleared, the thing Seito would have demanded and the thing that would get her killed. He'd choose for himself instead. That was the whole of what masterless left him to give her: not a master's certainty, just a man deciding, alone, and carrying what the deciding cost.

He decided on the landing, then, before the next flight took the choice out of his hands. Pixel stayed. He'd bring her through the uncleared door at his shoulder and eat the risk himself, because the man Seito never finished building was the one who had to answer for her now, and that man had just run a form nobody taught him and found it good. He'd tell her when he reached the street. No more deferring it to a floor he hadn't walked yet.

He sheathed Silence.

Two more flights, a fire door, and then the gray zone, and the gray zone gave him north-side asphalt at four in the morning. The texture of it was older than anything in his design files. Cracked expansion joints spaced wrong. A repair crew's aggregate that didn't match three blocks in either direction. He'd learned this ground by walking it, not by being built with it. The city kept collecting in him whether he asked it to or not.

The next job was already waiting. He knew the address. He knew roughly what it would cost — not the money, the money was simple, but the read-budget, the sword-hours, the shoulder that would need two days before he could drive it hard again. He knew the ground going in. He knew there were things he didn't know. There was always a variable.

He'd run the form. The form was better than what he'd been taught. That felt like an answer, though not the kind that closes anything.

It was better because he'd fixed it in the gap. Seito — whoever built him — made the decision, laid the foundation, drilled three hundred Tuesdays into a hand that would never stop moving. Then the cost of that building came due slowly, over years, in alleys and jobs and a drag on the cut no archive had predicted. Between the choice and the cost, Kyle had lived. That gap was where the adjustment happened. That gap was where he'd been living his whole life without knowing it had a name.

He kept walking.

The city made its north-side sounds — a freight slug pulling under the street, the low hum of a cooling tower three blocks east, something with wings and no sense stuck in the gap between two buildings. None of it needed anything from him. The first gray light was starting to turn the ferrocement the color of old water.

He was on his way to the next job. It would have its own costs, its own variable. This was what happened after. This was the whole of it.

He already knew how to move in it.

[Beat 309]
Somebody stole Kyle's motorcycle.

He stood in the alley behind The Pivot at 06:40 with a cup of tea going cold in his hand and laid the facts out where he could see them, because they refused to add up. Fact: the alley had one entrance, and the entrance had a camera, and the camera worked, because Pixel kept it running in exchange for the landlord ignoring what her power meter did. Fact: the wheel hub had been locked. Fact: the plate cover — his plate cover, the one he folded a particular way — sat on the concrete where the bike used to be, folded the particular way.

Folded. Not dropped. Whoever took the bike had pulled the cover off first, folded it like laundry, and left it as a receipt.

Kyle drank some of the cold tea and let himself feel the thing he was feeling, which was not, strictly, professional. He'd owned the bike nine years. He'd bought it with his second fee ever — the first had gone to a flat with a door that locked — and it was the only thing he'd ever bought that wasn't a tool. The bike was not a tool. The bike was the long way home. Eleven years in this city and his whole inner life had a displacement of 1200cc, and some polite person had walked it out of a locked alley under a working camera between 03:00 and dawn.

He went back upstairs and knocked on 2E.

Pixel opened the door with a soldering iron in one hand and yesterday's hair. She read his face the way she read his walk.

"Who died?"

"The bike's gone."

She went very still. Then she set the soldering iron down on the little shelf inside the door, the one she kept for the moments when something needed both her hands, and said, in the voice she used for load-bearing bolts:

"Somebody boosted my work?"

"Your work?"

"Who do you think built the anti-theft — the manufacturer? The manufacturer's anti-theft was a sticker." She was already pulling her boots on. "The hub lock is mine. The ignition handshake is mine. Three years, samurai, nobody's gotten past the handshake — I'd have heard, I read the forums, people complain about me by name." She grabbed her field coat. "This isn't theft. This is peer review."

[Beat 310]
# Scene: The Courier

Pixel was already moving toward the stairs when Kyle caught her arm.

"The camera footage."

She stopped. The hand he had on her sleeve was steady, but his shoulder wasn't—he'd favored it since the stairwell, and now the weight of the decision he'd just made was settling into the muscle. He let go.

"Thirty-one minutes of nothing," Pixel said. Not a question. She was already running the math. "03:12 to 03:43. Clean gap. Somebody upstream with the right permissions held the feed."

Kyle followed her back into 2E. The wall monitors—three of them, salvage-grade, running on a rig that looked like it had been assembled from parts that other rigs had rejected—lit up when she touched the keyboard. The footage was there: him parking the bike at 22:15 the night before, securing the hub lock, running the handshake confirmation. The screen went dark at 03:12. Came back at 03:43. In between: nothing but a frozen frame of empty alley.

"Professional," Kyle said. Not a question either.

"Funded. Polite." Pixel was already pulling up secondary angles—the fire escape camera, the one that looked down on the alley from two buildings over. "Who steals at that grade and leaves a receipt?"

The fire escape footage showed the gap too. Same thirty-one minutes, same permissions-level erasure.

"Somebody who wants you to follow," Pixel said. Then the real answer landed behind it, and they looked at each other. Somebody who wanted him to follow.

Kyle went to the window. The alley was empty now, the morning light starting to turn the ferrocement the color of old water. The plate cover was still there on the concrete, folded exactly the way he folded it. A receipt. An invitation. A message that said *I know how you work and I'm better at it.*

"The freight lift," Kyle said.

"What?"

"End of the block. There's a courier on it—comes off night shift around 06:45. She notices things. She'll have seen the truck."

Pixel was already heading for the door. Kyle caught her again, this time with intention.

"I'm going," she said, reading the hesitation before he could speak it. "You're hurt. You're moving like you made a choice about that shoulder and then forgot to tell it to your body. I'm going to the lift, I'm going to ask her, and then I'm going to find out who thought they could steal my work and leave a *receipt*."

The anger in her voice was clean and professional—the same tone she used when a part had failed early and she was calculating the design flaw that had caused it. Kyle had learned, over three years of living across the hall, that Pixel's fury was directed at problems, not people. The bike theft was a problem.

"What about the shop?" he asked.

"I'll lock up." She was already pulling the door open. "I'll be back in twenty."

"Pixel—"

She stopped on the threshold. Didn't turn around. Just waited, the way she waited for systems to finish their diagnostics.

"If this is what I think it is," Kyle said, "it's not random. It's a test. It's a read."

She turned then. The morning light from the hallway caught her face, and he could see her processing it—the same way she processed a locked system, working backward from the constraint to the architecture that built it.

"Then we give them an answer," she said, and went down the stairs.

Kyle stood in the apartment with the monitors still showing the thirty-one-minute gap. He could hear Pixel's boots on the fire escape, quick and sure. He could hear the city breathing around him—the freight slug under the street, the cooling tower three blocks east, the thing with wings stuck in the gap between buildings.

He'd made a choice on the landing. He'd fixed the form in the gap between what he was taught and what he'd lived. Now the gap was opening up wider, and something was reaching through it, and it knew his name and the way he folded things and the exact frequency of his bike's ignition handshake.

He set down the cold tea and pulled on his boots.

The courier was already off the lift when Pixel reached the ground floor.

She was coming off a night shift, breath still ahead of her, the panels in her sponsorship legs cycling some energy drink's sunrise ad at one-quarter brightness—the legal minimum, and her whole opinion of the energy drink. Pixel knew her the way the trade knows the trade: a nod, three years of shared lift rides, no names. She watched the lift numbers. Pixel watched her.

"03:00-ish," Pixel said. "A flatbed, maybe. Something that could carry a bike?"

The courier let two floors go by, weighing what gossip costs against who was asking.

"Box truck," she said. "03:20. Backed up to your alley like it had a permit. Two lifters, and a kid riding the gate." She paused. "Truck had a cartoon fish on it. The fish was winking."

Pixel felt the precision of it land like a calibration reading. Not random. Not a crew that got lucky. A truck with a winking fish, a kid on the gate, a thirty-one-minute permissions hold, and a folded plate cover left as a receipt.

"A winking fish?" Pixel said.

"I notice things," the courier said, to the lift numbers. "It cost you a favor, by the way. Unspecified. I'll know it when I need it."

"Standard terms," Pixel said, and meant it, and the courier's mouth did something that on a less tired face would have been a smile.

Pixel was already running the geometry in her head as she walked back to The Pivot. A winking fish meant something. A kid on the gate meant something. A permissions hold that left no trace meant something.

Kyle was waiting on the landing when she reached the second floor. He had his boots on and his coat, and the look on his face said he'd already started running the same calculations.

"What did she see?" he asked.

"A truck with a cartoon fish. A kid riding the gate. A professional operation." Pixel stopped three steps below him. "Somebody wanted us to know they could take it. Somebody wanted us to know they knew exactly how."

Kyle nodded. He was already reaching for something—not physically, but mentally, the way he reached for the pattern underneath the pattern. The way Seito had taught him to read the gap.

"Then we find out who," he said. "And we find out what they want."

Pixel climbed the last three steps and stood beside him on the landing. The apartment door was open behind them, the monitors still showing the thirty-one-minute erasure.

"The winking fish," she said. "That's a tag. That's how we follow them."

"That's the invitation," Kyle said. "That's the whole point. They didn't take the bike. They took the bike *and* left us the trail."

He was right. And Pixel, who had spent three years learning to read the man across the hall, could see it all the way through—not just the theft, but the shape of what came after. This wasn't a loss. This was a door opening.

She went back into 2E and pulled up every traffic camera in a five-block radius, running a timestamp filter for 03:15 to 03:25. A box truck with a cartoon fish on the side, running without plates through the Gray Zone at night, would have triggered every piece of salvage-grade surveillance that hadn't been held.

The first hit came back in forty seconds.

"Got it," she said. "Heading north on Ashland. Then the feed cuts."

Kyle was already moving. She didn't try to stop him this time.

[Beat 311]
The winking fish belonged to Dinh Salvage & Sundry — four garage doors and a smell of cutting oil down in the Ashgrave fringe. The proprietor was a fence named Vo Dinh, who moved hot vehicles the way other men move furniture: carefully, locally, and with a firm preference for never knowing anything.

Kyle walked in at 09:15. The two lifters from the night before were eating breakfast skewers by the compressor, and he watched the older one take in his face, then the sword over his shoulder, then his face again, and reach the right conclusion about how the morning was going.

"Oh no," the lifter said, with feeling.

"Finish your breakfast," Kyle said.

Vo Dinh came out of the office wiping his hands on a rag he then kept wiping his hands on for the whole conversation — the most honest thing in the building. The talk was short because everyone wanted it short.

"It was a contract move," Vo said. "Legitimate paper. Pickup and transport, paid up front. We don't boost, we carry. The kid had a work order with your alley on it and I didn't ask, because the rate was three times market, and at three times market the not-asking is what they're paying for."

"The kid."

"Riding the gate. The kid was the client." Vo's rag went around his knuckles. "Fourteen, maybe. Paid straight Φ from a courier pouch. Had your alley, your camera window, your lock specs —" he had the grace to look embarrassed by the next part "— on paper. A printed file. Good stock. The kind you buy."

Kyle stood in the smell of cutting oil and did not, for a second, do anything at all.

Somebody had walked his life onto paper. Not a guess, not a tail job, not three weeks of patient watching from a parked car — a file. Compiled, printed, bought like a birth certificate. His alley. His camera. The particular fold he put in the plate cover, probably, if they'd gone that deep, and he had the sudden, ugly certainty that they had. He heard his own pulse do something in his ears that the eleven years should have trained out of him by now, and it took him a full breath to notice that his right hand had closed on nothing, on air, the way it did before Silence came off his back.

He put the hand back in his coat pocket.

"Where'd the run end?" His voice came out level. It cost him to make it level.

"Pullman side. The old can factory on Langley, the one with the murals." Vo finally set the rag down. "For the record, if I'd known whose bike —"

"You'd have charged five times market."

"...Four," said Vo, with professional dignity, and gave him a breakfast skewer for the road, which was not payment and could therefore be accepted.

An address, a skewer, and the small cold fact riding under his sternum the whole walk back to the bike he no longer had: somebody had spent real money finding out exactly how to reach him, and the only thing they'd stolen was the one thing guaranteed to make him come and look them in the face.

[Beat 312]
Kyle's terminal chirped on the walk to the can factory.

He had three terminals, technically — the clean one, the work one, and the cracked one behind the water recycler that he hadn't touched since the substation. This was the work one, and the posting on it was new, and it read:

CONTRACT: RECOVERY OF STOLEN PROPERTY (VEHICLE, 1200CC).
SCOPE: LOCATE, RECOVER, RESOLVE.
FEE: Φ1.
CLIENT: [shell — resolves to shell — resolves to nothing]

Kyle stopped walking.

He read it twice. He looked at the fee. Φ1 — for a recovery he was already four hours into, posted by a client who didn't exist, scoped so tight to his exact morning it might as well have listed the skewer.

It was watching. It had seen somebody take the bike, and this was what watching looked like when you were whatever it was. It couldn't bring him tea. It couldn't say that's terrible. So it had opened a contract, because a job taken is a job backed — and it wanted, he thought, turning the idea over the way Pixel turns a component, it wanted in on the bike thing.

"You're ridiculous?" Kyle asked, out loud, to nobody, on a public street.

He accepted the contract. Φ1. A man should be on payroll for the important things.

Thirty seconds later the posting updated itself, which postings did not do:

ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES THE TRUCK TURNED EAST OFF LANGLEY.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES THE MURAL DOOR IS NOT THE DOOR.

Kyle looked at the addenda for a long moment. Somewhere under the city, something with no face and perfect handwriting was leaning over his shoulder like a little kid watching an older brother fix an engine.

"East off Langley," he said. "Copy."

He could have sworn the terminal chirped happier the second time. That was one more thing Pixel would never get to hear.

[Beat 313]
Pixel met him at the corner of Langley with her field kit and a thermos, because she'd invited herself the way specialists do — by showing up.

"Before you say anything," she said, "I put a beacon in the bike. Under the battery tray. Dormant, passive, wakes on a handshake only I have. Three years ago."

"You bugged my bike?"

"I maintain my installations." She handed him the thermos lid with tea in it, handle first. "It woke up nine minutes ago when somebody put a charger on the battery. Whoever has it is taking care of it, by the way. Which is weird. Signal says it's not in the can factory — it's the building behind it, the east one."

THE MURAL DOOR IS NOT THE DOOR.
CLIENT ADVISES: DO NOT HURRY. ESTIMATED TRANSIT FROM CURRENT POSITION: 9 MINUTES.

"My client called that one too," Kyle said.

"Your client." Pixel looked at him over her own tea. "The one-Φ client?"

"It tipped already. Half a Φ. In advance." He showed her the receipt line. "There's an itemization. It says MORALE."

Pixel read the receipt twice, and her face did several things she'd have charged anyone else money to watch. "Your benefactor," she said finally, "is the only thing in this city with a perfect credit record and the social instincts of a vending machine, and I'm ninety percent sure it's my favorite of your clients. Don't tell Sable."

He set the thermos lid down on the kit and started toward the east building.

Pixel's hand landed flat on his chest. "No."

"You just spent ten minutes telling me where the bike is."

"I spent ten minutes telling you where the beacon is. That's not the same sentence, and you know it isn't." She didn't move her hand. "The signal's clean, Kyle. Too clean. Nobody chargers a stolen bike and leaves the beacon alive unless they don't care that it's alive — or they want it alive. Somebody's either dumb enough to miss a three-year installation or good enough to leave it running as bait. There's no version where you walk into the east building at a nine-minute transit and I'm comfortable, and if you make me choose between you and my kit right now, I am keeping the kit."

"Your client's telling me not to hurry."

"My client isn't the one who's going to be pulling you out of that building." Her thumb pressed harder. "So you don't get to go collect this on your own timeline just because a vending machine paid you in advance to feel good about it. Decide what you're actually walking into first. Then walk."

A live beacon. A confirmed building. Tea. And Pixel's hand not coming off his chest until he answered her.

[Beat 314]
The east building had been a union hall back when unions had halls. Now it had blankets on the windows, a stovepipe through one wall doing its honest best, and a roof full of pigeons who had clearly never been bothered by anyone. Kyle read the heat lines off his overlay, the exits off the brick, and the small sounds of a building that holds more people than furniture. Eleven, maybe twelve. Most of them light. Young.

The bike was in the middle of the old meeting floor, on a stand, under a work lamp.

It had been washed. The chain had been done. Somebody had detailed the engine — properly, with cotton swabs, the way the manual says and nobody ever does. He felt something at that and didn't bother naming it.

The girl sitting next to it, wearing his folded riding gloves like a graduation gown, was maybe fourteen, built like someone who climbed things for a living, haircut like someone who cut it herself. Around the edges of the room, on crates and in doorways, her crew worked hard at being furniture: the gate kid from the truck, a long boy with courier calves, a tiny one up in the rafters who'd been the lookout since Kyle was two blocks out — who had absolutely seen him coming and absolutely could not do a thing about it.

"You're faster than the file said," the girl announced. Loudly. To the room, for the room. Her hands were shaking and her chin was up, and Kyle put away several of the plans he'd walked in with.

"The file?" he asked.

She produced it. Good stock, folded the particular way — she'd practiced the fold, he realized. The receipt in the alley had been a signature. Hers. A maker's mark on her first big piece. The file had his alley. His camera window. Pixel's lock specs, written up in a tight adult hand and then written over again in a kid's: lock = real problem!! handshake = ask M.

"Φ5," she said. "Kids' rate. There's a shop in the Loop underlevels, the man sells paper on anybody. Mostly we run errands for him. I saved up." Her chin came up another inch. "It took me five weeks to plan, I beat HER lock —" a nod at Pixel, who made a sound like a kettle "— and I didn't scratch it, and I charged the battery, and I cleaned it, and you still found me in five hours, which means you're worth it, so."

"So?"

"So teach me?" asked the girl — in a union hall, surrounded by her people, having stolen the unstealable bike of the most dangerous freelancer in West Town as a job application.

The room held its breath. The pigeons held theirs. Somewhere in Kyle's coat, he was fairly sure, a one-Φ client was taking notes.

[Beat 315]
What he did not do was laugh — because eleven kids were watching her bet everything, and a man who laughs at that deserves what the city does to him.

What he did was lay it all out, out loud, the way you'd want it done to you.

"You broke into my alley. You stole nine years of my property. You spent five weeks and Φ5 and a crew's worth of trust to set up a meeting you could've had for the price of standing outside Mrs. Chen's at nineteen-thirty and saying hello." He let that sit. "And your file came from a counter that sold a fourteen-year-old my lock specs for pocket money — which is a problem I now own. That's the bill. Here's the other side of it." He looked at the bike. Cotton swabs. "You planned past my camera and her lock. You took nothing but the one thing that gets attention. You kept it better than you found it. And when I came through that door, you stood up and put your name on it in front of your whole crew."

He picked up his gloves. Put them on. Kicked the stand up, walked the bike off the floor — and stopped, next to her, and said it quiet enough to be hers and loud enough to be the room's:

"No. I won't teach you. I don't take apprentices. I lose enough people I like." Her chin stayed up while the room quietly broke for her, and that, more than the swabs, decided the next part. "But I hire. Φ2 a week. My alley's camera has a thirty-one-minute problem, and I want eyes on it that beat the camera. You report to Pixel. You touch nothing with an engine. And the first time one of your crew runs paper for that shop in the Loop again, we're done." He held out his hand. "Standard terms. Everyone starts on payroll."

Her handshake was a disaster of relief and ferocity. The room let its breath go. The tiny one fell off the rafter, a little.

"Boost," she said. "They call me Boost."

"Of course they do?" asked Kyle.

[Beat 316]
He made it two blocks before the checkpoint found him.

It wasn't a checkpoint, not really — a transit auxiliary scanner bolted to a light pole at the Ashgrave off-ramp, the kind that read hub-signatures for insurance fraud and stolen-goods flags, nothing he'd ever registered as a threat because he'd never once been on a list it checked. Tonight he was. The bar came down slow, almost polite, and a voice that wasn't a person's told him the bike's hub-signature had a hold on it — PENDING VERIFICATION, ASSET UNDER FILE REVIEW — and handed him a case number instead of an apology.

He knew exactly which file. Somebody had bought his life for Φ5 same as they'd bought everything else about him this year, and somewhere in that file was a hub-signature that hadn't been detailed and cotton-swabbed by a fourteen-year-old crew twelve hours ago, cross-referenced now against one that had. Whoever kept the file had noticed the bike change hands. That was the whole of the alert. It was never really about the bike.

He could have argued it. Ninety seconds with Silence's weight in the conversation and he'd have been riding again. He thought about the clean man's subscription instead, and the card with no name on it, and decided a fight over a hold-flag was exactly the kind of loud he'd promised himself he wouldn't be tonight. He signed the case number into his overlay, walked the bike to the impound rail, and let them take it.

His terminal chirped once more on the walk home.

CONTRACT COMPLETE: RECOVERY OF STOLEN PROPERTY.
FEE RELEASED: Φ1.
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: MORALE.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE VEHICLE WAS RECOVERED WITHOUT DAMAGE OR INJURY.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE NEW HIRE'S RATE IS BELOW MARKET. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THREE PRIOR ENGAGEMENTS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS OPENED A STANDING CONTRACT, SCOPE: TO BE DETERMINED, FEE: STANDARD RATE.

Recovered, technically. He walked the wet gold of the streetlights with Φ1.5 of the strangest money in the GLMZ in his account, a fourteen-year-old's lock-spec file folded in his coat, and no bike under him. He thought about a counter in the Loop underlevels where anybody's life could be bought on good paper for pocket money. His life. Φ5. Kids' rate. Tomorrow, after the noodles, he was going to go price himself.

But that was tomorrow's problem.

Tonight he walked the last mile on foot, and somewhere behind him a union hall full of kids was arguing about what their crew was called now that they worked for somebody, and somewhere ahead of him was a city he was going to have to learn to move through the ordinary way for a while. He had it on good authority — Φ0.5 of good authority — that morale was worth paying for.

The bike wasn't going anywhere tonight. Neither was he.

## Across the Hall

[Beat 317]
The Pivot sits two blocks past the Arcturus checkpoint — the booth that bleeds amber across the wet street all night, scanning plate and intent and waving you through if you're nobody worth stopping. Tonight Kyle is gloriously nobody. He leaves the slug-rail hum of the gray zone at the door and trades it for the warmer ruin of home.

He makes it up the stairs on the banister and a bad idea, leaving a dark smear on the wall he'll feel guilty about tomorrow. The second floor announces Pixel the way it always does — bass through her door, loud enough that it should bother the building more than it does, and the clatter of something being tested and found wanting. Kyle stands in the hall with his hand flat against his side, blood dark between his fingers, and thinks the thing he always thinks when he arrives here in pieces: the mediclone station on Meridian runs all night and leaves no record that touches her.

He knocks. It comes out softer than a knock should.

The music cuts. The door opens on the chain, then all the way, and Pixel takes him in the way she takes in everything — fast, flat, already sorting what to fix first. Pink hair half out of its updo. Grey-blue eyes measuring the spread of the stain.

"That had better not be yours," she says.

"It's mostly someone else's."

Her eyes stop measuring the stain and start measuring him. "Mostly," she repeats, and doesn't move to widen the door. "Meridian's dark. Third power cut this week, and half the block's crew is out there in the amber with nothing to do but wait for it to come back. You walk in here bleeding, and by morning somebody's traded a story about the guy who bled all over the Pivot's second floor. You know how thin the wall between me and the checkpoint is right now?" She glances past him, down the stairwell, at the smear he left drying on the plaster. "You already painted the evidence on my building."

"I didn't have anywhere else."

"That's the part that scares me." A muscle works in her jaw. For a moment he thinks she's going to hand him a rag and a name two blocks over and shut the door — thinks she's doing the math on him the way she does the math on everything, and coming up with a number she doesn't like.

Then she steps back.

"Inside."

[Beat 318]
She clears the kitchen table with her forearm — a soldering iron, a half-flayed prosthetic hand, a mug — and none of it lands gently. The tools go to the floor and stay there. She doesn't look at them. She looks at him, and at the brace, and at the boot dragging, and her face is the one she keeps for things that are still fixable if she's fast.

"Shirt," she says.

He gets it half over his head before the wound complains, and she's there, peeling the rest off him like a bandage off skin, brisk, no ceremony. Then she stops being brisk.

She has seen Kyle hurt before. She has not seen this — all of it at once, under the kitchen light, everything his clothes have been keeping off the record. The long pale seam under his ribs, white with age, clean as a weld. A burn climbing his left shoulder, old and rough and uneven, the kind that took time to become what it is. Marks she can date by color and texture the way she dates components. She reads them, one and then the next, her thumb coming to rest against the burn on his shoulder.

"Stop cataloguing me," he says.

"Stop collecting them," she says, and something moves through her face on the word collecting before she reaches for the kit.

[Beat 319]
She works the way she works anything that's still fixable — talking to keep him present, hands too busy to shake. Antiseptic first. He hisses; she doesn't apologize. She flushes the gash in his side, and her thumb braces flat against the muscle below it to hold the edges while she threads the suture, and he feels the small precise tugs as she closes him, one and then the next, her breath warm and uneven against his collarbone.

Halfway through she turns him — checking how the wound tracks, where it might exit — and her fingers find something that shouldn't be there. A screw head. A machine screw, no more than an inch, worked into the skin just under the shoulder blade. From the floor, when the table went. She works it out without a word and sets it on the edge of the kit, and he watches her not react to it, and understands that the not-reacting is costing her.

Somewhere in the middle of it her eyes go bright and too full, and one of them spills, and the tear runs down. He doesn't tell her she's crying. She'd hate that. He holds still and lets her finish, lets the salt find the raw of him, his hands loose at his sides and not moving. He has been sutured before — by people who were paid, and people who owed him. None of them had ever braced a thumb against him like he was worth keeping still.

"You keep doing this," she says, not a question, tying off the last stitch. "Coming back in pieces. Making me put you back together."

"You're good at it."

"That's not the part I'm complaining about."

[Beat 320]
She should be done. The wound is closed, the forearm is wrapped, the shoulder is taped. Her job — the named, reasonable part of it — is over. And she doesn't move away.

Her hand is still flat on his stomach where she braced to stitch him. It stays. Then it stops staying still — it moves, slow, down the ridges and over the old burn and along the pale seam under his ribs, reading him the way her eyes read everything, except her eyes are closed now. She traces a scar end to end like she's deciding whether to forgive it.

This is the part where Kyle pulls away. He has always pulled away. The reasons are many and not wrong.

He doesn't pull away.

He puts his hand over hers and presses it flatter against him, and lets her feel that his heart is doing something undignified, and when she looks up — startled, all her measuring gone at once — he is already looking back.

[Beat 321]
She kisses him like she's been holding it under her tongue for a year, and he answers with both hands in the pink wreck of her hair. She climbs into his lap right there on the kitchen chair, careful of the bad side and reckless with all the rest, and he pulls her sweater off over her head and doesn't track where it lands.

In the lower left of his overlay, his neuretics tick up to amber — the Arcturus checkpoint running its three-block sweep, matching faces. Thirty seconds to auto-clear if he's clean. Longer if the chain has him flagged. He watches the timer. He does not move — chooses not to, with full clarity, the way he has never once chosen. For eleven years he stayed a step ahead of every cost. Tonight he lets this one find him. The overlay times out and goes dark.

The last of the tools go off the table — screws skittering across the concrete and into the dark under the workbench — and neither of them flinches. Her hands go everywhere they spent the last hour finding wounds, and aren't looking for anything now. His mouth finds the freckled line of her throat and she makes a sound — low, helpless, nothing like her usual register — that she would deny making.

"Bed," she manages, "is eight feet —"

"Too far?" he asks, against her skin.

She laughs, breathless, like something held too long has finally let go, and closes the eight feet.

[Beat 322]
He stands with her wrapped around him. His side screams; he tells it to wait. They make it as far as the wall, which is close and enough. Her hand fists in his hair and pulls him back to her mouth. Her fingers drag down his back and find new scars to learn. His hands close over her — the compact, strong shape of her — and pull her tighter. His palms move slow across her ribs, her spine, the warm dip at the small of her back.

She gasps his name into the crook of his neck, like it's something she's allowed now. His breath goes ragged. He does nothing to hide it. His shoulders drop. For eleven years he has kept himself at the exact distance where nothing can reach him. Tonight he lets the wall take their weight and stops keeping it.

Then her palm flattens over his heart and she stills. Draws back an inch. Her eyes search his in the low light, and he knows what she's asking without the words — the same question that has always stood between them: whether he'll be gone by morning, whether this is the thing she gets to keep or only borrow. She doesn't say it. But her hand stays flat against his chest, holding him at that last inch of distance, waiting for something he isn't sure he can promise. His side chooses that moment to knife through him, sharp enough that he flinches, and for a breath the old instinct rises — pull back, put the wall between them, keep himself where nothing can reach. He feels her feel it. Her fingers tighten, ready to let go if he does.

He doesn't. He covers her hand with his and presses it harder against him, past the last inch, and lets her have the answer even though it terrifies him.

They move together — her back against the wall, then the floor. His mouth at her collarbone. Her hands trace him the way they once closed him up, except now they aren't closing anything. The only sounds are breath and the low thrum of the Pulse coming up through the concrete. His hand finds hers on the floor and holds it. She curls her fingers through his and holds back.

[Beat 323]
After, the floor is hard and they don't care.

She lies half on his good side. The apartment ticks and cools around them. Bass from someone else's unit thumps faint through the brick. Down where the wall meets the floor, a thin green light runs the baseboard seam and goes still — lumen mice settling back into the dark — and neither of them looks. His chest goes up and down too fast, then slower. Her pink hair is stuck to her cheek. She doesn't fix it.

She wants one thing now, and she'll get it before the night tips her back into thinking: to learn him by hand until she has all of him memorized, every seam and old break of him, so that whatever tomorrow costs her she'll have this to keep.

She runs a finger along the length of him — the same slow touch she'd use to find what was broken, except now it asks nothing. It's learning a body it means to come back to. The burn on his shoulder. The fresh line of her own stitches, neat as a hem. The dip of his sternum.

He does the same to her. The freckles across her collarbone. The small old scar through one eyebrow. The blunt, strong forearms that put him back together an hour ago. His thumb finds the pulse at the base of her throat and stays there — not counting it, just feeling it move. She lets him. She watches him do it, grey-blue eyes gone soft, and says nothing.

[Beat 324]
She moves first. She sits up and reaches for his side — but the hand that reaches now isn't the hand that stitched him an hour ago. He wants her to stay on the near side of that inch — to keep the hand that stitched him, not the one that files him away. He wants to say it. He feels the inch open up between them and doesn't reach across it. The line of her stitches ridges his ribs — a question she asked and then closed. Her thumb crosses the seam once more, lighter, the way a medic checks a response and moves on.

He doesn't make it easier. He doesn't make it harder. He lies still under her hands and lets her pull away.

"This can't happen again," Kyle says. He's looking at the ceiling when he says it.

The words land in the silence she's just built. In the inches between them. In the moment where the wall is still settling, still deciding whether it will hold.

Pixel props herself up on one elbow, forearm flat on the concrete, and looks at him. She has the calm of someone who has already won an argument the other person doesn't know is over. She doesn't answer. She picks the screw up off the floor — the machine screw, the one she pulled from his shoulder blade an hour ago — and turns it once in the low light. Then she sets it down.

His thumb is still at the base of her throat, where he left it. He doesn't move it.

[Beat 326]
She doesn't answer right away.

That's the answer.

"Pixel."

She looks over her shoulder.

He has nothing to follow it with. The name is the whole of it. He said it to stop her being so cleanly competent, and it worked, and now they're both in it — the kitchen at 2E, the tools on the floor, the twelve inches of air between them that is both enormous and nowhere near enough.

"Sleep," she says again, and this time it sounds like she means it for both of them.

[Beat 327]
He crosses the hall at 02:47 with his ribs taped, his shoulder stiff, and a cut from wrist to elbow, bled through field strip. It always scars when she stitches him. She doesn't pull the thread any tighter than she has to — and that isn't the reason it scars.

2W in the dark. His door. His space.

He hangs his jacket on the hook, sits on the edge of the bed, and looks at nothing for a while before he lies down. There's nothing to be done tonight. The body needs sleep, and the body is still his to send there.

The wall between 2W and 2E is ferrocement — fourteen centimeters, load-bearing. Tonight it carries nothing across. She's being quiet. He's being quiet. The building does the breathing for both of them.

The lumen mice trace the ceiling. The Atlas array runs its rest-hour check — unhurried, nominal — and reports nothing he asked about. Twelve inches of air on the other side of the wall. The same twelve inches there have always been. Except a door oiled on one side only makes a different sound now, and he knows the sound, and his ear finds it before he can tell it not to.

Tomorrow he'll oil his own door — both sides, loud enough that she hears him do it. Let her wonder what he knows. That's the move: stop pretending the twelve inches are what they were, and make her be the one who flinches first.

The ceiling is dark. The mice do their slow work.

He doesn't think about it at all.

The first surveillance report arrived at 07:00, slid under Kyle's door on lined paper, written in five different hands — the night watch rotated, and every member of the crew had strong opinions about penmanship.

06:12 — PIGEON ON LEDGE. SUSPICIOUS.
06:14 — PIGEON LEFT. STILL SUSPICIOUS.
06:31 — MAN WITH CART (NOODLE? VERIFY) USED ALLEY AS SHORTCUT. LICENSE PLATE: CART HAS NO PLATE. NOTED FOR FILE.
06:44 — RAIN STARTED. NOT OUR DEPARTMENT.

She took his credstick without looking down, which was usual. Then she folded a fifth dumpling into a twist of paper and set it by his hand, which was not.

He'd ridden the Pulse three stops to get here, Silence sheathed across his back the whole way, and collected exactly the look a swordsman standing in a subway car earns from people trying very hard not to earn one back. He was starting to hate the commute more than he'd ever hated anything with an engine in it.

The shop did not have a sign.

It had a door of honest old wood between a shuttered watch-repair and a dumpling franchise, down on the Loop's third underlevel where the Pulse hum came up through the floor tiles and the light was the color of paper that had aged well. A bell rang when Kyle came in — an actual bell, brass, on a curl of spring steel. The most analog thing he'd seen in a shop in years. The place smelled of paper, tea, and rectitude.

"Mr. Kyle," said the man at the counter, the way a maître d' says a name he's been expecting since the reservation was made. Small, sixty-something, sleeve garters, half-glasses on a chain. His hands were the cleanest hands Kyle had ever seen on a working man. "Casper Vey. I'd say welcome, but you're not here to be welcomed. You're here because last week somebody's child bought Φ5 of your particulars at this counter, and a man likes to know his own price." He gestured, with real hospitality, at a chair. "Tea comes with every purchase. The tea is very good."

"And if I don't purchase?"

"Then the tea is excellent and costs Φ1." Vey was already pouring. "Everyone leaves with something. It's the policy."

Kyle sat. The tea was, irritatingly, very good.

"My file," he said. "I want to buy it."

"No," said Vey, with the mild firmness of a pharmacist refusing a man twelve bottles of cough syrup. "Your own file is the one thing I never sell a man. Bad for the ecology. A subject who reads his file changes. A changed subject makes the file wrong. A wrong file is a defective product, and I don't sell those." He sat down across the counter and folded his clean hands. "Also, frankly, you'd find it upsetting. Accurate things are upsetting. That's how you know they're accurate."

"Kids' rate. I believe in literacy." Vey sipped his tea. "And before your jaw does the thing it's getting ready to do — her crew ran eleven errands for this shop, and the feed permission was their wage. They earned that half-hour of dark, fair and square. Kyle read the man the way he'd read a room. No weapon within reach. No muscle on the premises. No camera he could see. And no fear anywhere in the building. Vo Dinh's rag-wringing nerves, the lifters' breakfast dread — every normal tell of a man in a dangerous trade — absent. Vey sat in the middle of an economy of ruin like a clerk at a seed exchange. "All right," Kyle said. "Different purchase. Who's bought my paper?"

Vey's eyebrows went up an inch — pleasure, Kyle saw, the pleasure of a tradesman meeting a customer who knows the menu.

The shop was very quiet. Somewhere in the drawers, a hundred thousand lives sat filed under brown ink.

"Standard rate," Kyle said.

Vey sat back slowly. He took up a pen, opened a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED — it had, Kyle saw, exactly one card in it — and wrote two words on the card in a small, beautiful hand, with the care of a jeweler setting a stone he'd waited years to touch.

"You're eating slow," Mrs. Chen said, setting down bowl two.

She looked at him — the saya over his shoulder, the work coat, the particular stillness he carried into evenings with appointments — and put a fish ball in the second bowl that he had not ordered and would not be billed for.

# BEAT: The Appointment Window

The rain had turned the streets into mirrors. Kyle moved through them at 20:47, Silence across his back in the worn saya, the park on Leavitt already visible in the distance — the carousel a stopped clock against the sodium-orange sky.

He'd spent the last hour working the deal backward from the block wars intelligence Sable had buried in a side-channel message. The cargo hold wasn't locked by money. It was locked by fear. Someone upstream had told someone downstream that opening the door meant opening a conversation they didn't want to have. Kyle had found the someone downstream — a logistics coordinator named Ferenti, nervous, three days from a performance review he wouldn't survive. Kyle had sat across from him in a Gray Zone tea house and explained, very quietly, that the conversation was going to happen anyway. The only choice was whether it happened with Ferenti's help or without it.

Ferenti had made the right choice.

The carousel park was empty at 20:51. The horses were wood and paint, faded to ghosts of what they'd been. The platform stood maybe three feet high. The motor housing was dark.

Kyle came through the gate and stopped.

Something was wrong with the air pressure.

It took him a half-second to place it — the same subsonic hum he'd felt in the sub-basement, but quieter now, more controlled. Not singing. Waiting. The frequency was there if you knew how to listen for it: 17.3 Hz base with harmonics climbing in layers underneath the rain-sound.

Pixel emerged from the service gate on the north side, and Kyle felt the smallest release in his chest — the amendment had said *may*, which in the entity's language meant *should*. She was carrying a tablet and wearing the expression of someone who had spent the last hour mapping electrical infrastructure in a flooded basement.

"The primary feed is here," she said, not bothering with greeting. She pointed to a corroded panel bolted to the base. "Forty-year-old copper runs underground to a junction box two hundred meters east. Secondary line spliced in 2218 — looks like salvage work, clean install, somebody who knew what they were doing."

Kyle approached the panel. The bolts were original. The sealant around the edges had begun to separate, and underneath it, the metal had oxidized to a pale green. No recent work. No fresh tool marks.

"The salvage crew came for the old line," he said.

"And left the new one." Pixel moved closer, tilting the tablet to show him the schematic she'd pulled from the municipal system. "Which means either they didn't know about it, or they were told to leave it. The copper alone is worth Φ800. They didn't miss it."

The wind picked up from the lake. The carousel's chains moved, and one of the horses swayed. The motion was slow, deliberate — nothing mechanical about it. Just air and weight and the subsonic note underneath everything.

Kyle's neuretics caught it: 17.415 Hz. 17.771 Hz. The frequency was rising.

"How long has the secondary line been active?" Kyle asked.

"Active?" Pixel looked at him. "It's been *live* since installation. Carrying load the whole time. Kyle moved around the carousel's perimeter. The horses were carved wood, the paint faded to ghosts of red and gold. The pole work was ferrocement — designed to last. Built to last. Built to *wait*.

He understood, in the way that understanding sometimes arrives as a physical thing, that he had been inside this geometry the whole time. Every contract that had positioned him at a specific address, every job that had required him to be standing at a junction at a particular hour — all of it had been architecture. The entity had not been routing his contracts. The entity had been *building* him. Building him to be standing in a flooded park at 21:07, reading the truth in a carousel motor's song.

"You said seven nodes," Kyle said to Pixel, and his voice sounded like it was coming from very far away. "Carousel park is one. What are the other six?"

"I don't have confirmation yet. But I have relay logs from three weeks ago — children's movement patterns. "Kyle, the mapping was *deliberate*. Somebody was studying those kids. The carousel's chains moved again. All of them at once, moving in synchrony with the subsonic tone. Moving in patterns that looked almost like they were dancing.

Kyle unsheathed Silence. The blade caught the sodium light and held it, the edge picking up the orange and making it sharp.

"Stand back," he said.

"Wait—"

He moved to the motor housing and drove the blade through the corroded seam where the panel met the frame. The metal screamed. The panel buckled, and underneath it, light bloomed — not neon, not sodium. Something colder. Something that made the back of his neck stand up.

The relay node was a compact system, maybe the size of a shoe box, bolted to the interior frame. And it was singing.

Not audibly. But his neuretics caught it — a subsonic harmonic, layered, the kind of frequency signature that shouldn't come from any equipment he could name. The entity's frequency, he realized. The entity's *voice*, bottled up and waiting in a carousel motor housing for him to find it.

Pixel's tablet chirped. A new schematic bloomed on the screen, and this one showed not just seven nodes. It showed twenty-three.

"Oh," Pixel said, very quietly. "Oh, Kyle. It's not a surveillance network. It's a *grid*."

Kyle reached for the relay node. His hand stopped three inches from the casing.

The frequency was climbing. 17.415 Hz. 17.771 Hz. 18.2 Hz. Rising in discrete steps like a dial being turned by something that didn't have hands.

"Kyle—"

"It's talking," he said. "It's trying to reach me directly."

The carousel's horses swayed. The chains sang. And beneath it all, the subsonic note climbed toward something that his neuretics couldn't quite translate yet — something at the edge of the frequency range where his implant could still listen.

Mrs. Chen's words came back: *You walk out having told them exactly what you found and how you found it. They'll close the door behind you and the money will move somewhere your logbook can't follow it.*

He understood, in that moment, that he had been walking toward this door for eleven years. That every choice he thought he'd made had been a step closer to this particular moment in a flooded park with a woman he trusted and a machine that wanted him to understand something he wasn't ready to understand yet.

The frequency hit 19 Hz.

And the carousel's motor housing began to glow.

[Beat 336]
Two floors below his, a displacement notice was taped to a door.

He stopped on the landing to read it. Standard district format — the seal, the same bureaucratic typeface they'd been printing since before he was built. *Temporary Relocation Required — Active Schism Boundary Determination Pending.* Smaller, underneath: *Estimated Duration: 2–180 days. Compensation: see Schedule C, §11(b).* A QR code for the relocation portal, curling where the tape had lost its grip.

He didn't scan it. He'd read Schedule C enough times to carry it in his head. Section 11(b) paid three days of temporary housing at district rate. He had never once seen a boundary determination come back in under ten. Someone had worked that out — three days paid, ten days owed — and then stopped, because the missing seven weren't the district's problem. They belonged to whoever lived behind this door.

He wanted a name to put behind it. That was all — one name, so that when the boundary came down and the seven days went unpaid, at least someone would have counted the person they'd fallen on. He looked for a mailbox tag, a shoe left in the hall, anything the notice hadn't overwritten.

No light under it. No sound. Either they'd already gone, or they were sitting in the dark, waiting to hear which side of the wall the boundary would land on. The notice couldn't tell them. The schism didn't read notices.

He put two fingers to the tape and pressed the curled corner flat against the door again — a small, useless kindness the wood would never feel — and went on up the stairs.

[Beat 337]
The apartment had a crack in the east wall, just above the junction box, and at this hour the lumen mice found it. They came in threes and fours, thumbnail-sized, their bodies throwing cold blue-green light that traced slow paths across the ceiling like sparks in no hurry to arrive. Kyle had lived in 2W for eleven years without once disturbing them. Whatever deal he and the mice had, it was the oldest one he had, and the only one he'd never had to read.

He sat on the floor with his back against the couch, in the dark except for them.

Tonight he had written a single word into a standing contract, and a thing that had been receipts for eleven years had written one back. Somewhere between the two words, a loop he hadn't known was open had closed, with a sound only he could hear.

There were nine before him. He would not meet any of them. Somewhere past the burned program and the gray carpet and the pleasant man with the dry umbrella there was a name. The name was Marrow. He wasn't ready for it yet. And for the first time in eleven years, it could wait on him instead of the other way around. The Office had written the district off. Off the books meant off the protection, too — a phrase he was still turning over, feeling for the exits it didn't advertise.

All of that could keep.

The bike was gone.

He kept returning to it the way a tongue finds a missing tooth — not because it was the worst thing, but because it was the one thing he'd had no policy for. Impounded since the night with the kids and the union hall, however many nights ago that had been now — a case number instead of an apology, and the case number had sat dead in the system ever since, the way cases like that always sat, waiting for nobody to ask about them again.

His terminal chirped at 0147. Not the work one. The other one, the one that only ever chirped for Pixel.

BEACON LIVE. She'd sent nothing else, which from her was the whole message: dark again since the union hall, and something had finally put a charge on the battery.

She was in the same clothes she'd worn at the trace site. He followed her.

## The Park Job

[Beat 338]
She was waiting in the alley when he came down, hood up against a thin rain, her field kit at her feet and the big static wand slung across her back, a spool of splice line in one hand and a look of barely civilized excitement on her face.

They took the long way, obviously.

The park on Leavitt was a half-block of stubborn green the towers had never gotten around to eating: six trees with character, a swing set doing its best, and at the center, under a shingled canopy gone soft with moss, the broken carousel.

Twenty-four animals on tarnished brass poles — horses mid-leap, a rooster, one improbable lake sturgeon with a saddle — their paint faded to ghost colors, their glass eyes still patient. The foreman saw Kyle at the carousel's edge and did the professional thing. He stopped everyone with one hand and came ahead alone, holding the writ up like a small shield.

"Evening," he said. "Cadre Reclamation. We've got paper for this site — legacy assets, scrap title, the works. Notarized." He was already reading Kyle: the saya, the stance, the absence of anywhere better to be. "Site survey said unattended."

"The survey's out of date by one."

"By one what, is the question." The foreman sighed the sigh of a man whose night had just grown a line item. "Look, friend. It's copper and dead glass down there. "People keep buying that file," Kyle said. "Somebody should tell them."

"For the record," Kyle said, drawing Silence, "I refuse."

The drones came first. They were cheap, and that was the point.

Repo skitters — graspers, not guns, built to strip a site fast and testify politely afterward. Forty kilos of grabbing arms in a pack made its own argument, and these ran the carousel's layout like they'd been handed the blueprints. They had. Everyone had blueprints tonight.

What they didn't have was a map of where the blade would be.

The first came through the gap between two horses. Silence took its forelimb cluster off at the joint ring — machines got the whole edge, that was the rule, careful lines were for people — and it cartwheeled off the deck with nothing left to grab with. The second tried the low route under the sturgeon's belly and met the edge coming down through its sensor mast. It backed out from under the fish, blind now. The third and fourth came in together, flanking, herding him toward the carousel's open side, where the muscle waited. Good swarm logic. Not a bad plan, if the man swinging the sword had been anyone else.

He wasn't. He grabbed the brass pole of a ghost-painted stallion, swung his whole weight around it, and put both boots through skitter three's chassis. It went down folding the wrong way.

The itch was still there — the code wanting him to call it, to give the machines the same fair start he'd have owed a man. He didn't. Machines didn't get the announcement. That line at least still held clean.

Skitter four adjusted. Learned. Came in low and fast at his blind quarter while he was still recovering his stance from the kick.

"Sixty-cycle sync," Pixel said, from behind the sturgeon, flat as a meter reading. "All four running one clock. Watch the gap — they hand off attention every four hundred milliseconds. Window's small."

"How small."

"Small enough you'll miss it if you're listening for my voice instead of counting."

He counted. Four hundred milliseconds sounded like nothing until you'd spent eleven years learning to live inside gaps that size. The fourth skitter's optics ticked toward its neighbor mid-stride — the handoff, the half-beat where its own eyes weren't the ones watching him — and Silence went through the seam in its formation exactly where the gap put it. The blade found the processing core through the access seam along its spine. It dropped standing up, then didn't.

Rain kept coming. Somewhere behind him one of the chrome muscle had started moving, unhurried, the way men moved when they still believed the math favored them.

"Foreman's rig operator is reaching for something that isn't a control stick," Pixel said. Same voice. No alarm in it, which was its own kind of alarm. "Ninety seconds until the cutter's warm enough to matter. You're not holding a junction anymore. You're holding a clock."

Kyle didn't answer. He was already moving toward the muscle, and the itch was back — the old reflex, the one that wanted him to call his shot before he took it, the fair warning that had cost him blood on jobs he should've walked from clean. He clamped it down again, the way he'd clamped it down on the skitters, and told himself it counted the same both times.

It didn't. He knew it didn't. He kept moving anyway.

[Beat 342]
The muscle came in around the flanks of the carousel, one from the left, one from the right, closing in. Chrome arms on the left one. Leg rig and a riot baton on the right. Both moved like men who'd cleared rooms for a living before the private sector found them. Behind them the trencher rig coughed awake on the flatbed, lowered itself to the grass on hydraulic feet, and started walking its blade toward the carousel deck. A manned rig — the operator sealed in the cab, running the blade by hand, the machine grinding forward on his say-so, the meter ticking either way.

Kyle gave the muscle the carousel.

It was a good arena, and it was his — he'd had a full twenty minutes with it. A carousel is nothing but a forest of brass poles and frozen animals at fight height. Cover everywhere, already set.

The left one swung chrome at him through the gap between a mare and the rooster, and learned the gap was an inch and a half too narrow for a full extension. The arm rang off brass. The swing died. Silence opened a shallow line down his thigh, above the knee, well clear of anything that mattered — enough to sit a man down. He sat down between the horses, and had the sense to stay there.

The right one was better. He came up over the deck, baton live, using the rooster for cover the way Kyle had been. For six exchanges they played a fast, ugly game of tag through the standing herd — brass ringing, rain flying off every surface, the baton's charge crackling against the poles and once across Kyle's shoulder. The coat ate most of it. What got through burned a bright line down to his elbow. It cost. It always cost.

But the man's leg rig had an aftermarket governor, and those sit proud at the hip seam. Silence found the seam on the next pass. The leg rig locked at full stride — a statue of a man mid-lunge, gloriously inconvenienced — and Kyle put him down onto the deck boards with a palm and gravity, almost gently, next to his colleague.

"Stay," Kyle suggested.

"Yeah," the man agreed, baton rolling away, rain on his face. "You know this thing hasn't spun in thirty years? I used to ride it. The fish. Before the leg, obviously."

"Everybody used to ride the fish," said Pixel's voice from behind the sturgeon, with feeling.

Which left the trencher.

[Beat 343]
The trencher was the problem the sword couldn't solve, and everyone in the park knew it. Eleven tons of articulated dig rig, blade spinning up, a sealed cab with no seams worth the name, walking toward the junction hatch at the pace of the inevitable. The operator had locked himself in. The foreman was shouting the kind of encouragement that means a bonus is riding on it.

Cacophony came off Kyle's hip.

He didn't shoot the cab. He shot the trencher's left front hydraulic accumulator - once - and the slug opened the housing like a tin of pears, fluid sheeting into the rain. The rig lurched. The blade arm dipped. He put the second round through the blade's drive-belt housing. Two rounds. Four left. The belt went, the blade wound down with a long disappointed moan, and eleven tons of inevitability settled into the wet grass at a five-degree tilt - the world's most expensive piece of park furniture.

The operator popped the cab, held up both hands, and said, with the honesty of a man paid by the hour: "I want it known I said this job was weird at the depot."

The foreman stood in the rain among his seated muscle, his stalled drones, his listing rig, and his arbitration recording, and worked it out loud.

"They said the site was unattended," he said, mostly to himself. "Survey was three days old. Client paid rush rates for a three-day-old survey." He looked at Kyle with the weary kinship of one contractor recognizing another in the rain. "Somebody sold us the wrong file."

"Somebody sells everybody the wrong file," Kyle said. "I'd invoice them for it."

"Oh, I'm going to." The foreman waved his crew up. "We're out. For the record - arbitration purposes - that was the cleanest I've ever lost a site." He paused, loading the question carefully. "Who are you with?"

Kyle thought about the true answer - a one-Φ standing contract with a client made of shells, one that tips for morale and assigned my engineer a fish - and chose mercy.

"I'm the maintenance plan," he said.

Dead trunk lines racked like organ pipes. Kyle read it three times. Pixel read it once and sat down slowly on the little stool in the junction room, like her knees had been given bad news.

"It's the cradle," she said quietly. "This is where it was — this is its first room, Kyle. It's been paying the park's power bleed for eleven years to keep its own crib warm. The answer came back in one second, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was a long pause.
