[Beat 345]
Pixel did the engineering first, because the engineer attends. She killed the junction's feed and spliced the neighborhood's power bleed around it onto the live trunk — twelve minutes of work with a soldering light held in her teeth.

Silence went through the old line in one cut.

Above them the carousel turned over once — fed one last instant of dying charge off the junction's draining caps, or told to, no instrument in that room could have said which. The crown bulbs that still had filament glowed half-bright. The music box ground through four bars of something with a waltz in its bones, slowing, the horses leaning into a leap they'd held for thirty years.

Then it went dark, gently, all the way, and the rain had the park to itself.

They stood in the junction room a moment longer. The cut line had already stopped being a coordinate and become what it would stay now: dead glass in an old rack, in a little room under a kiddie ride, in a park the towers never ate.

GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: MORALE.

The reply took nine seconds, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was an age. When it came, it came with no addenda, no scope, no formatted field at all — unstructured, lowercase, the register it had used exactly once before in eleven years.

Mrs. Chen's stall was running the breakfast rush — steam rising off the broth, the ladle moving in its own rhythm, the line of people who had learned not to talk until they'd eaten. Kyle waited at the counter's far end. The wait was the point.

She saw him. She didn't acknowledge it yet. She finished the bowl in her hands — the broth poured with a specificity that had nothing to do with hurry — and set it in front of a woman in a gray coat. Then she moved down the counter toward him, and the line shifted to accommodate. This was how she managed things: you made space for what mattered, and you did it quietly enough that nobody felt moved.

"You have a look," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Someone mapped the carousel park. Deliberately. Centered a whole operation on it."

Mrs. Chen's hands didn't stop moving. She was already building a bowl — broth, noodles, the green onion and the careful arrangement of everything else. "The park's been there forty years. Before that it was a water station. Before that, a junction. Lots of people have reasons to look at that corner."

"Not like this. Not with children."

She set the bowl down in front of him. The steam rose between them. "Eat."

He ate. The broth was salt and depth and something else — camphor, maybe, or memory. She waited until he'd gotten halfway through before she spoke again.

"When I was young, there was a man who owned a building three blocks from here. He kept records. Everything — who lived where, who visited, what time the lights went out. He thought if he knew enough, he could predict something. Control something." She was looking at something past his shoulder, through the wall. "He died. The building got demolished. His records went to the incinerator. And the thing he was trying to prevent happened anyway, on a Tuesday, to someone he'd never met."

"He was trying to stop something specific."

"Yes," Mrs. Chen said. "That's how it always starts. You see one thing that needs stopping. So you build your map. So you put your children on it. And then you realize the map is the thing that needed stopping, and by then the children are already marked."

Kyle set down his spoon. The broth was still steaming. "What stopped him?"

"Stopped him from what?"

"From using the map."

"Nothing stopped him," Mrs. Chen said. "He used it all the way through. Used it until the thing he predicted came anyway, and then he couldn't use it anymore because he was gone." She took his empty bowl — he hadn't realized it was empty. "The question isn't what stops you. The question is what you stop for."

She moved down the counter. The line had kept moving. The breakfast rush didn't pause for philosophy.

---

He was at the terminal when Pixel came through the door — not knocked, just came through, the way she did now. The drawer was open. The map was on the screen, the carousel center marked with a red vector that meant *here, this matters, this is the geometry*.

She looked at it for four seconds. Then: "That's Detroit."

Kyle didn't move. "The map's West Town."

"The center's West Town. The source is Detroit." Pixel was already moving to her rig, her fingers finding the keyboard before the rest of her caught up. "The pendant nodes — I kept the serial batches when I wrote the forgery. Tessera Industries parts, all of them, but the circuit boards came through a distributor in Geartown. I filed it under 'not relevant' because Tessera sources through twelve distributors and I didn't want to chase ghosts." She was pulling files now, timestamp after timestamp scrolling. "But if someone was building a map centered on carousel park, and they sourced the hardware through Geartown, and Geartown is where—"

She stopped.

The screen showed a parts manifest. Geartown assembly. Date: 2218. Quantity: 11 units. Designation: CIVIC SENSOR PKG, PEDIATRIC-CLASS.

"—where my mother's last verified location was," Pixel finished, very quietly. "Before she stopped being a person who could be located and started being a person who was just gone."

Kyle watched her hands. They were steady. Her voice was steady. The steadiness was the worst part — it meant she'd known, on some level, that following anything back far enough ended here.

"It's not confirmation," he said.

"It's not coincidence either." She pulled another file, then another. The screen filled with part numbers, serial batches, procurement chains that all bent the same direction. "Tessera doesn't sell to independent operators. They sell to corpos and municipal contracts. And Meridian Wellness Initiative was a Tessera front-end pilot. Which means someone at Tessera wanted those kids mapped. Which means someone at Tessera knew what carousel park meant. Which means—"

"Means we follow the procurement chain."

"Means someone at Tessera knew my mother was in Geartown," Pixel said. "Means they built the infrastructure to find other people like her. Means they're still using it." She turned to face him. Her eyes were flat. Operational. "What's your ask?"

Kyle thought about Mrs. Chen's builder with his records, dying on a Tuesday to something he'd never met, the map he'd made becoming the thing that needed stopping.

"I need to know who authorized it," Kyle said. "The carousel center. The pendant nodes. The whole operation."

"And then?"

"And then we decide if we stop them, or if we stop using the map."

Pixel's jaw tightened. She looked back at the screen — at the parts manifests, the serial batches, the closed case that wasn't closed anymore because it had geometry now, and geometry had a center, and the center had a name she could chase all the way down.

"There's a third option," she said. "We follow it back to whoever authorized it and we ask them why. Not to stop them. To know."

"That's not stopping."

"No," Pixel said. "It's understanding. And then we decide what stopping costs."

She turned back to the rig. Her fingers were moving again — faster now, the procedural quiet of someone who'd already made her choice and was just executing it.

Behind her, through The Pivot's window, the noodle cart was making its slow orbit of Damen and Erie, carrying children who'd never know they'd been mapped, moving in patterns that meant nothing until someone decided they meant everything.

Kyle closed the drawer. He left the map inside it.

He had the feeling — the one he'd learned to recognize in eleven years of contracts — that he was about to stop being the person who took jobs and start being the person who made decisions that mattered to people he cared about.

The feeling was accurate. It always was.

---

He was at Mrs. Chen's counter the next morning when Pixel found him. She had a printed file in her hands — not thick, just thick enough — and she set it down next to his untouched bowl without a word.

The cover page had a single line: TESSERA AUTHORIZATION CHAIN — MERIDIAN WELLNESS INITIATIVE.

Below that, a name: **DIRECTOR CASPER VEY.**

Kyle's hand moved before his mind caught up. The bowl shifted. Broth slopped across the counter. Mrs. Chen didn't look at him. She just moved to wipe it, the way she would have wiped up any other spill.

But she was moving faster than usual.

Pixel sat. "The authorization chain traces through four shell companies and a municipal procurement office. Vey's signature is on the final directive — the one that approved the pendant distribution and the site selection for carousel park." Her voice was level. "He signed off on it in 2219. Three months after my mother disappeared."

Kyle opened the file. The signature was unmistakable — the same careful, precise hand that had refused to source a chip and kept his secrets behind a Faraday vault. The same man who'd told him that provenance was everything, that a thing was only worth what it had been.

The same man he'd hired to trace the carousel park's funding chain.

"He's the buyer," Pixel said. "Or he was. The authorization dates end in 2220. After that, the trail goes dark. But the pendants kept shipping. The program kept running. Somebody else picked it up after Vey signed off."

Kyle looked at the file. The dates were there. The chain was there. The geometry was there. And at the center of it all was a man who'd been sitting in his shop for eleven years, waiting.

Not waiting for Kyle to walk through the door.

Waiting for Kyle to understand what he'd already done.

"He knows," Kyle said.

"That we know? Maybe not yet."

"He knows we'll find out. He's known the whole time. He's been watching us look."

Pixel closed the file. "So we go ask him."

It wasn't a question. Kyle heard the weight in it — the point of no return, the moment before you walk through a door and the person on the other side has to decide whether you're a customer or a threat. Mrs. Chen was still wiping the counter, the same small circle, over and over, not looking at either of them.

"Yeah," Kyle said. "We go ask him."

Outside, the noodle vendor was singing its cheerful loop, serving bowls to people who didn't know they'd been part of a map. The carousel park was still there, still dark at its center, still waiting in the geometry that someone had drawn and paid for and left behind like a message nobody was supposed to understand.

Kyle stood. He left payment on the counter — twice what he owed — and walked toward the door.

Behind him, Mrs. Chen set down her cloth and looked at Pixel for the first time.

"The question isn't what stops you," Mrs. Chen said quietly. "The question is what you stop for."

Pixel didn't answer. She was already moving, already following Kyle toward the street, toward Vey's shop, toward the moment when you find out if the person you trusted was building a map to save someone, or to mark them.

The distinction, Kyle was beginning to understand, might matter less than the fact that he'd been standing in the middle of it the whole time.

## The Taste-Off

[Beat 374]
The Loop's third underlevel had its own ecology. A paper shop, a shuttered watch-repair, Vong's Dumpling Franchise #7 on the right under a red awning, and Mei's Dumplings on the left — no franchise, no awning, forty stolen inches of counter she'd annexed off the watch-repair's wall by leaning on it hard for years. The stationer's honest door sat dead center.

The two men stood in the middle with their backs to that door. Backs to Vey, in other words. A careless place to stand.

Vong was a compact sixty-year-old with the posture of a man who'd been taking bad news standing up for decades. The clipboard man was holding out a form. "—monthly insurance assessment. Standard for all food vendors on this underblock. The Tsui Group's protective services, standard rate—"

"Φ35 a week?" Kyle said from behind them, reading the figure upside-down. "Four hundred percent over the Meridian Merchant index. And your policy number's nine digits. GLMZ policy numbers run eleven. That's somebody's neuretic handle on a form."

The clipboard man turned. He'd been in the work long enough to have stopped enjoying it. "Not your stall."

"Go, Mr. Kyle," Vong said quietly. "This is mine to carry."

"I eat here," Kyle said. That was the whole of his position.

[Beat 375]
He'd half-expected the paperwork to end it. He pulled up the Tsui Group's public filing anyway — every collection franchise filed public or didn't operate — and it took under three minutes to find the part that mattered.

"Your protective license lapsed," Kyle said, turning the screen. "The fourth. Not expired — lapsed. You've been writing paper on a dead license for eleven days. There's no reinstatement pending; the portal would show it."

The clipboard man looked at the screen for a long moment. Then he handed the clipboard to his partner — the big one, the expensive shoes — and rolled his neck.

Kyle read it as a man getting ready to leave. He was wrong.

"License is for the ones who pay clean," the clipboard man said. "Vong's not paying clean anymore. So this is the other visit." He looked at his partner. The big one didn't go for Kyle — a professional, and professionals understand leverage. He went for Vong's broth pot.

Forty liters of scalding pork-bone stock. A sixty-year-old man standing next to it.

[Beat 376]
Kyle was moving before the big one's hand finished closing on the rim.

He didn't draw Silence. A drawn blade in an underlevel full of lunch customers was a conversation he'd have to finish, and this didn't need finishing. It needed interrupting. He took the man's wrist off the rim — not a block, a redirect — and steered the shove ninety degrees into the franchise's steel prep counter. Forty liters of scalding stock rocked on its ring and held. One tongue of it slopped over the lip and hissed across the floor, where Vong had been standing half a second before. Kyle's other hand had already moved him.

The big one came off the counter fast and threw the elbow. Kyle had left him the room to throw it. It caught Kyle across the cheekbone — a real hit, a bright white line of pain, a mark by evening — and the cost bought the opening. Weight forward, lead knee proud. Kyle took the knee from the side with the flat of his boot. Not the joint. He'd walk with a limp for a week and tell the story straight; ruin the knee and he comes back, and he brings people. The big one folded into the spilled stock, swearing, done.

The clipboard man's hand went inside his jacket. Kyle looked at him.

"Cacophony holds six," Kyle said. He hadn't drawn it. The sentence drew it. "You came to scald a sixty-year-old over Φ35 a week. Take your partner, take your dead license, and tell Marcus Tsui that Vong's block is documented now — times, faces, the shoes." A beat. "There's a kid on that roof who drew the shoes."

The hand came out empty. They hauled the big one up between them and left, tracking wet bootprints and the smell of spilled stock, and the underlevel breathed out.

Vong stood by his rescued pot with both hands flat on the counter. Steadying it, or himself.

"The tea stall on sub-two," he said. "Lin's. Forty years. She told them no, same as me. They didn't burn it. They just visited, and visited, and one week the customers decided sub-two wasn't worth the walk, and then Lin decided too. Now it's a jack kiosk and nobody remembers there was tea." His hands weren't quite steady. "That's how it's done now. Not a fire. An erasure. You wait for the block to forget."

"It's documented now," Kyle said. "The next visit isn't a visit. It's a filing." He looked at the blood on his thumb without surprise. "Lin's mistake was being the only no on her block. You've got a whole block, Vong. Bill me for the dumplings I'm about to eat."

From his doorway, Vey made a small sound that was not a cough.

[Beat 377]
They came back at 14:00.

No clipboard this time. Three of them — the clipboard man, the big one moving carefully on his bad knee, and a third Kyle hadn't seen before. Chrome thumb-rings, the flat affect of a man brought in for one purpose. The underlevel had thinned out after lunch. The third man's eyes went to Vong's counter first, then to the stairwell on the far wall, marking the ways out. That told Kyle more than the chrome did.

"Marcus Tsui filed a complaint," the clipboard man said. He was talking to the room, not to any one person. "Assault of a licensed representative. Interference with contracted services. You've got a warrant flag running on your neuretics, samurai. Check it if you want. We'll wait."

Kyle didn't check it. A warrant flag cost sixty Φ to file and twenty to pull. It was a stall, not a threat. He also didn't move from where he stood, which was between the third man and Vong's pot.

"The complaint went to a licensing board that hasn't had a quorum since the fourth," Kyle said. "Same day your license lapsed. So the filing is stuck behind the lapse review. It's paperwork with nothing behind it. It dies the moment your reinstatement is denied, and it will be, because I've already sent the eleven-day gap documentation to the Office of Merchant Protections." He hadn't sent it yet. He was going to, in the next forty minutes, which was close enough. "You want to check THAT warrant, I'll wait."

The third man looked at the clipboard man. The clipboard man looked at his shoes.

The chrome rings were the tell. This one wasn't here for paper. He was here to stand in Vong's stall and let the afternoon customers see what they'd be walking into. He wouldn't touch Vong. He'd just be present, every afternoon, until keeping the franchise cost more than giving it up.

The same erasure Vong had described. Patient, and technically legal.

"Vong," Kyle said, without turning. "Is there a back entrance to this underlevel?"

"Loading dock. Sub-two corridor, behind the watch-repair."

"The watch-repair's shuttered?"

"Three years."

"Whose lease?"

A pause. "Mine. I took it when they left. Cheaper than advertising."

Kyle looked at the third man. "You're standing in an extended franchise footprint. The loading dock, the sub-two corridor, and the six feet of watch-repair wall all come off the same lease. You can stand here, but you're standing in his house. You want to tell Marcus Tsui you held a loitering position inside a vendor's licensed space, in front of witnesses, on the day I filed that lapse paperwork?"

The third man had the chrome rings and the flat affect and nothing else. He'd been hired for presence, not decisions. He looked at the clipboard man, who had been wrong about this block twice now.

They left.

Vong sat down on his prep stool and said nothing for a while. From the sub-two corridor below, faint and steady, the Pulse ran its hum through the tiles — thirty meters down, Mach 6, the whole moving world.

"Every time I tell them no," Vong said, "I think about Lin."

"You're not Lin," Kyle said. "Lin didn't have the sub-two corridor and a kid on the roof and a samurai who eats here on Tuesdays."

He went upstairs and filed the documentation.

[Beat 378]
By 14:00 there was a chalk line on the floor. By 15:30 there were two, with a disputed strip between them and three customers eating in the gap, braced to be told to pick a side.

Kyle was at Mei's — he alternated weeks, had for six years, and both owners knew it — with a cut cheek and a late lunch when Mrs. Chen came down the stairs. Somebody had sent for her. She came down the way a woman does when she's been handed a job beneath her skill and above her patience. She stopped on the neutral chalk and let the quiet do half the work.

"Both of you have sold dumplings down here longer than half these buildings have stood," she said. "You've both overcharged me. I paid, because the food was worth it." She looked at the two lines. "I'm not an arbitrator. I'm a customer owed better than this."

"You're the only one on this block both stalls will hear," Vong said.

"You started it," Mei said.

"The awning—"

"The broth pot—"

Mrs. Chen turned to Kyle. She didn't ask. She had spent seventy years not asking for things, and the not-asking was the request. He finished his dumpling and stood up. His cheek had stiffened to a dull throb that woke when he chewed. A fair price, for an afternoon that had twice nearly cost Vong his hands.

[Beat 379]
The taste-off was Boost's idea, and the speed with which the logbook made it official suggested it had been everyone's idea at once.

DUMPLING COMMISSION: OFFICIAL RECORD. CHAIR: MR. KYLE (VISIBLE INJURY, SEE 11:40 ENTRY). RECORDER: RAFTERS. PANEL: DENTS, BOOST. OBJECTIVE: BETTER DUMPLING, FOR BLOCK PEACE. NOTE: BOSS GOT HIT TODAY. TWICE. WE LOGGED IT. THIS LOG IS HONEST.

Both stalls cooked. Vong ran his standard pork-and-chive — thicker wrap, machine-even pleating, every inspection star it had ever earned. Mei brought the original: thinner wrap, hand-crimped in a pattern Rafters sketched in the margin for the record, ginger-forward with something older underneath. Kyle ate four of each. The cut in his cheek woke at every one of Mei's. He took that as evidence of the ginger and kept it out of the minutes.

The crew filed scorecards, from TWO POINTS AND A STAR up to a drawing of a thumbs-up with a Φ1 price tag. A crowd had gathered — chalk lines and official proceedings will do that — and Vey had migrated from his doorway to the building's first inside window for the better angle.

Boost tallied the cards twice, then a third time, his pencil going slower each pass. When he finally turned the logbook around, the count was a dead tie — and every one of Vong's points, Kyle saw, was clustered on the crew's own cards. The neutral crowd, the strangers who'd wandered in off the chalk lines, had scored Mei's to a person. Vong saw it the same instant Kyle did.

He set down his ladle, wiped his hands with great deliberation, and said to the whole gathered block that a rigged panel of Kyle's own people wasn't a taste-off, it was theater — and he'd take the real verdict, the crowd's, as proof the Commission had picked its winner before the first dumpling hit the water. Half the crowd murmured agreement. Rafters' pen stopped over the honest log with nothing fair left to write, and the block peace the whole thing was supposed to buy was now visibly worse than when they'd started.

[Beat 380]
"For the record," Kyle said, to the chalk and the crowd and both owners, "Vong's franchise makes a technically excellent dumpling. Consistent. Well-priced. You know exactly what you get, any day of any week." Vong nodded with professional dignity. "Mei's original is better."

Mei made a sound that was not quite a sound. Vong's jaw went through an expression and out the far side.

"By a margin that doesn't justify a chalk line," Kyle went on, over the crowd's murmur. "Vong, your guarantee covers the gap — inspection rating, delivery network, the app. Mei's got seventeen years of recipe folded by hand. Two stalls, two reasons to buy a dumpling. You're both leaving money on the floor fighting over an inch." He let that sit. Then he said the part that was the actual point. "This afternoon Marcus Tsui sent three men to stand in Vong's stall and wait for the foot traffic to decide it wasn't worth the walk. They left because the paperwork went in and the stall had footage to stand on. That changes nothing about next week, or the week after, or Lin's tea stall on sub-two that's a jack kiosk now and will never be tea again." He looked at both of them. "A block with one stall is a block that can be made to forget it. A block with two stalls arguing about awnings at lunch is a block that's LOUD. People come to it on purpose. You two are each other's insurance, and you've been drawing a chalk line down the middle of it."

He looked at Rafters. "That how the minutes read?"

Rafters consulted the logbook with the gravity of a senior analyst. "Exactly how they read. I can charge for certified copies."

The chalk was gone by 16:30. Vong sent one complimentary order of pork-and-chive to Mei's counter without a word; Mei took it without a word. Closest the underlevel had come to a diplomatic event in twenty years. Vong put the franchise testimonial card in his window, and beside it a second card, hand-lettered, that hadn't been there this morning: BEST ORIGINAL ON THE BLOCK — SEE MEI, NEXT COUNTER. Insurance, posted where the block could read it.

[Beat 381]
Kyle was leaving at 17:20 when Vey opened his door the particular width of a man who'd been saving something all day.

"Come in. The occasion warrants the good shelf." Inside, the labeled drawers sat in their brown-inked rows. Vey poured without asking and pushed the cup handle-first. "The Tsui Group isn't my clientele — impersonation filings are public, and I don't sell what I can read for free." He settled onto his stool. "I watched the whole thing. Morning and afternoon. The license. The pot. The chrome thumb-rings." His eyes went, briefly, to Kyle's cheek. "The interruptions, plural."

"You watched a man go for a sixty-year-old and made tea?"

"I sell maps, Mr. Kyle. I don't walk the territory. A stationer who picks up a weapon is a stationer no one trusts with a secret again." He said it without apology. "But I noticed you didn't draw the sword. A man went for Vong's pot — twice, two different ways — and you put them down with paperwork and a boot and a sentence. The leverage was real. The filing was real. The sub-two corridor was real. Three kinds of paper and one measured piece of violence, in order." He polished his glasses. "The Tsui Group needed a reason to stop. The stalls needed a verdict. Your standing client needed" — the smallest brightness — "a dumpling methodology, apparently. You arbitrate better than you bill. A man could make a file of that."

"Don't."

Kyle drank the tea, which was from the good shelf, and set the cup down square.

The terminal chirped on his way to the stairs.

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED TODAY. CLIENT NOTES: THE INJURY WAS AVOIDABLE IF THE ENGINEER'S DRONE PROPOSAL (FILED, DECLINED) HAD BEEN ADOPTED.
CLIENT HAS RE-FILED THE PROPOSAL.
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: THE CHEEK. ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTED THE CHEEK AT 14:40.
CLIENT DISLIKES THE CHEEK.

Kyle read it twice on the stairs. The cut was stiffening, and behind him the underlevel settled into its evening — Vong's closing sequence, Mei's last fold, the Pulse dragging its Mach-6 tremor through the floor thirty meters down. He decided the client could dislike the cheek all it wanted. A cut cheek was cheap. Vong still had his hands.

## The Forger's Ledger

[Beat 382]
The stairwell smelled like machine oil and cold concrete, the recycler drums somewhere below still running their angry twenty-fourth hour. Kyle's terminal chirped again before he reached street level.

Not the client. A relay tag he half-recognized: FERENTI, C. - ARCHIVIST, DETROIT SPUR.

He'd taken the man's forty-one pages three weeks back, Sable-routed, unremarkable - historical utility surveys, a security flat on top of the Read's rate. Paid, filed, done. Except Ferenti didn't ping closed contracts. Nobody did.

Kyle opened it standing on the landing, one hand still on the rail.

FERENTI: THE PAGE CLEARED YOUR SCREEN. IT DID NOT CLEAR MINE. I AM ASKING YOU TO LOOK AGAIN BEFORE I FILE IT AS TRUTH.

He read it twice, same as the client's amendment, except this one didn't feel like weather. He thought about Ferenti's tea cup turning its quarter-turn, the room he'd lost to his own archive, the man's voice going flat on *I become the reason the claim is clean.* Kyle had heard that shape of fear before - not the fear of getting hurt, the fear of being used as the good name on a bad thing. It was Vong's fear, some version of it, standing over a pot with his own franchise stamped on the side. It was, if he let himself sit in it for half a second on a stairwell that smelled like plastomer, his own.

He didn't sit in it. He typed back one line - *sending someone* - and thought about Marisol.

She worked jobs like this cold, no names exchanged that mattered, and she never once needed the client to explain what "wrong" meant before she found it. Everyone Kyle knew who'd used her once came back, and nobody had a bad word to say. If forty-one pages had a seam in them, she'd find which one, and she'd tell him after, exactly as promised, the way she told everyone after.

He pinged her handle. No preamble - she didn't like preamble.

KYLE: Archive job. Detroit spur. Forty-one pages, paper stock, already cleared once. Someone thinks a lie is sitting in a trusted stack. Need the page that doesn't belong.

The reply came back in under a minute, which for her was fast.

MARISOL: Anyone can take. The trick is putting something back. Send the address. I'll tell you after.

Kyle sent it and kept moving, down through the recycler heat and out into the evening cold, the Pulse's tremor climbing up through his boots from thirty meters under the street. Ferenti's forty-one pages were three weeks gone and none of his business anymore, except the man had asked him to look again, and Kyle had already decided to spend someone else's evening doing exactly that.

Behind him, the terminal chirped once more. He didn't look. Whatever the client wanted next, it could wait for the stairs to end.

[Beat 383]
She was already in the lobby, finishing a warm bun from the cart two doors down. Mid-forties, warm-faced, field coat the brown of autumn mud. She brushed the crumbs off her lapel and gave him a handshake that lasted the exact professional fraction of a second — the grip of someone who'd sized him up before he crossed the floor.

"Marisol."

"Kyle."

"I know." No agenda in it. "You held the carousel park last month. The whole block talked about it. The carousel ran music."

"Four bars."

"Four bars," she agreed, and they went upstairs.

He needed her signature on the records-access form before noon — one name in ink, and the sealed inventory would open to him for the rest of the case. That was all. Get the form in front of her, get it signed, get out before the screening flagged anything he'd rather keep unlisted.

The scanner on the third-floor landing gave its institutional chime — STANDARD SCREENING INITIATED — DOCUMENT INVENTORY — PSYKER ON PREMISES — VISITOR CONFIRM. Marisol confirmed without breaking stride, the way a woman does when she's been thumbing that same word since she was twenty-two. She didn't roll her eyes. Something in the set of her jaw took the word, weighed it, and decided not to spend the afternoon on it.

[Beat 384]
On the ride over he had thumbed Cacophony back to six. The trencher had cost him two, and he didn't walk into archives light.

The records room smelled of conservation solvent and old paper, which was better than the two floors below. Ferenti ran the intake briskly and left them to it.

Marisol pulled on cotton archival gloves and looked at Kyle over the first tray. "The way I work: I go through in order and tell you what I get. An authentic page has a whole person in it — the hands that made it, what they had for breakfast, whether they hated the job. A fake is just a job. Clean in a way nothing real is clean." She turned the first page. "I charge by the touch because it costs me by the touch."

Page one: clean.

Page fourteen: clean.

A knock at twenty-two — Ferenti's runner, twelve or so, sleeve patches from a Spine courier house, the face of a kid who'd been doing piecework since he was ten. He held out more documents. "Broker says these came with the load. The Psyk verify these too, or just the primaries?"

"Primaries," Kyle said, and tipped him Φ2, above rate.

When the door closed, Marisol said without looking up, "He'll grow out of the word or he won't. Not my afternoon."

Page twenty-three: clean. Eleven more after that.

At thirty-eight she stopped.

She held the page by its edges and went still — the stillness of a woman listening to something that made no sound. "This one."

It was a utility survey of the carousel junction on Leavitt: the underground chamber, the trunk lines, the sub-floor hatch under the maintenance skirt. Kyle knew the room. He'd bled there. He knew the width of that hatch and the passage behind it and what the junction smelled like when the line was warm.

The survey read: SITE ASSESSED — NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE — DEAD GLASS — NO RELEVANT ASSETS.

He had stood in that room six weeks ago. The line had been humming.

"It's beautiful work," Marisol said. It was not a compliment. "The fiber, the aging chemistry, the hand — almost right. But the hands that made it didn't care about this survey. They cared about making a survey." She set it down. "There's your forgery. One specific lie: there's nothing at this address."

Kyle looked at the date stamp. Three months old. Three months this page had sat in Ferenti's archive, patient and filed, waiting for a demolition order that would find its provenance already clean.

He held on to that.

Then the smell came in through the ventilation slit above the third tray: acetone, and something flatter under it — the chemistry of a fire agent primed and waiting.

[Beat 385]
Four seconds between the smell and the door.

The woman came first — chrome running her whole left arm, shoulder to fingertip, the hardware expensive enough not to show at the joint seams, a multi-tool already open on her palm with the incendiary trigger showing. Three men behind her. All four moved with the rehearsed economy of a team that had learned the room off a floor plan.

They did not say get away from the paper.

She said: "The Read comes with us. Principal wants her able to talk."

It landed on Kyle all at once. The fire wasn't for the forgery. The fire was cover. The principal had decided that a woman who could touch a forged survey and feel the lie in its fiber was worth more than the paper. Paper you could burn. A witness you could carry, and the authentication walked out with the crew. No one else in GLMZ was going to authenticate that forgery by hand.

"Marisol," Kyle said. "The window."

"I have eight pages and the forgery," she said, already moving, "and I am not leaving the forgery."

The tool discharged. Blue-white in the back corner, the third tray catching. Kyle put Cacophony's first round through the multi-tool at the wrist joint — the percussion enormous in the narrow room — and the woman sat down hard around the nerve hit, the tool spinning off into the fire. One spent. Five left. The room was burning now.

Two of the men moved to bracket Marisol, not Kyle. A mistake. Silence came out and wrote a clean line across the nearer one's wrist flexors — wide of anything that wouldn't grow back — and he found a new priority and took it to the floor. The second got a hand on Marisol's field coat and got Kyle's elbow across the hinge of his jaw. The cheap fast answer, when the clean one would cost tenths of a second the room didn't have.

The fourth — hired for position, slowest to commit — watched three colleagues turn into problems and put his effort into the door.

Kyle let him go. There was no version of this where chasing him put the fire out.

His left shoulder had taken the woman's elbow on the way down, outside the mesh. It hurt in a clean, specific way: bruised, not broken, still working. He set the pain aside and kept moving.

"Extinguisher," Marisol said. "Beside the door."

She had the forgery and a stack of pages under her arm and was working through the surviving trays with the calm of a woman who charged by the touch. Kyle found the extinguisher and killed the blaze — blue, then grey, then out.

One round spent. Five left. The shoulder would keep. Third tray gone.

[Beat 386]
The fourth man had a van, and the van had a frequency Kyle could track. Kyle had pulled the plate off the lobby scanner. Marisol had the forgery. Ferenti had his surviving thirty-eight pages and his grief for the Domazinski surveys, gone to ash in the third tray. Somewhere below them the extruder drums were still running the twenty-third hour without a pause.

Marisol set the forgery face-up on Ferenti's table and laid a hand flat beside it. "You should know what you were holding," she told him. "Worth a woman with a chrome arm and three men walking armed into a registered archive. Not for the paper — they'd have let the paper burn. For the pair of hands that could tell you it was a lie."

Ferenti wrote something in his log. His pen was not quite steady.

Outside the window the van's frequency had gone quiet. The fourth man hadn't gone to a hospital — no reason to, he'd walked out clean. He'd gone to file a report. Kyle gave it six minutes before that report reached someone with the staff to send a second team.

"Ferenti," Kyle asked. "Is there a back way?"

There was.

[Beat 387]
The back way was a stairwell that smelled of standing water and the mineral rot of old rebar — a service core built for a building that had been sold four times since anyone drew the plans. Kyle went first. Marisol came behind him with the forgery pressed flat against her chest under the field coat, both arms wrapped around it like the one thing she wasn't going to let the floor have if she fell.

"Two flights down, then the loading apron," Ferenti had said. "Nobody uses it. Half the lights are dead."

Half was optimistic. Kyle counted three working fixtures in five flights, and the dark between them had a texture to it — humid, close, threaded with a smell like a basement that had flooded once and never fully forgiven the building for it.

He heard them before he saw them. Boots on metal, unhurried, from below.

Not the four from upstairs. A different cadence — heavier, paced, the sound of people who'd been told to wait at the bottom of this specific stairwell and had nowhere else to be. Ferenti's back way had a name because someone besides Ferenti knew about it.

"Up," Kyle said.

"Up is the fire," Marisol said.

"Up is a fire that's already out. Down is new."

She didn't argue. She turned, and that was when the landing above them opened and a third element came through it — not the chrome-arm woman, not her three. A fifth man, fresh, blocking the return route, already moving on the read that they'd hit the middle of the stairwell and had nowhere to go but sideways.

There was no sideways. Six feet of stair, a rail gone soft with rust, a drop through the gap that would break something on the way down if anyone went through it.

The man above didn't have a name Kyle needed. He had a collapsible baton, extended, and the specific confidence of someone who thought two flights of blind stairwell was a controlled space.

It wasn't. It was Kyle's kind of space — too narrow for numbers to matter, too dark for optics, close enough that Cacophony was a liability and Silence was the only tool that made sense.

He put himself between Marisol and the baton and let the man commit to the first swing.

The stairwell took the shock of it — steel ringing off steel where the baton clipped the rail on the man's own backswing, an amateur's tell, the kind of mistake nobody made twice. Kyle didn't need him to make it twice. He came in under the arc, put his shoulder into the man's sternum, and drove him back into the wall hard enough that the whole flight shuddered underfoot.

Below, the boots picked up their pace. The sound of a decision made.

Marisol's voice, flat, working the math out loud the way she worked a page: "How many is down there."

"Don't know."

"How many can you take."

"Don't know that either." He got a hand on the baton man's wrist, turned it until the tool clattered free and rang off three steps before it stopped. "Get behind me and stay on the page."

"I'm not leaving the—"

"I know."

The stairwell lights buzzed, one of the three working fixtures giving up mid-flicker, and for two full seconds they had almost no light at all — just the shapes of boots coming up through the dark and the man against the wall finding his feet again and the forgery a flat pressure against Marisol's ribs, the only clean thing in the whole shaft.

Kyle's shoulder throbbed where the elbow had caught it upstairs — a distinct, separate ache from whatever was about to happen to the rest of him. He filed it. There'd be time to itemize later, if later showed up.

"New plan," he said, and it came out level, the read-out voice, the one he used on kids and on rooms about to go very wrong at once. "We go through them. Not around. Through."

Marisol looked at the drop through the rail, then at the boots closing the last flight, then at him.

"Through costs what," she said.

He didn't answer that. There wasn't a clean number for it yet, and she'd know a lie the same way she knew a forged survey — by the fiber, by what a truth cost him to say.

The first of them came around the landing below, and the light went out for good.

[Beat 388]
The dark didn't stay total. A hand-lamp clicked on below — not aimed at them, aimed at the wall, throwing enough backscatter to work by without blinding the crew that carried it. Kyle counted the shapes it caught: three, maybe four, moving in a formation too clean for scavengers.

The one in front wasn't carrying a baton.

She came around the landing already turning, weight low, one arm out in a guard that wasn't defending her face — it was clearing a lane. Small unit on her forearm, matte, no manufacturer stamp Kyle recognized, but the shape told him enough. Contact tool. Wrist-mounted. The kind built to reach past a guard and end an engagement in one touch.

She wasn't looking at Kyle.

She tracked past him like he was furniture and put her eyes on Marisol — on the arms wrapped around the forgery, on the field coat, on the one target in the stairwell that mattered to whoever was paying for this. The three behind her fanned to hold Kyle off the intercept, not to fight him. To buy her the two seconds she needed.

*Specialist.* The word arrived flat and unbidden, the read-out voice talking to himself now instead of a scared kid. *Somebody sent a specialist for the woman, not the man with the sword.*

He didn't have time to sit with what that meant — that the whole stairwell, the baton, the four upstairs, all of it might have been noise around this one narrow purpose. He had time to move.

Kyle stepped into the lane instead of holding his ground behind Marisol. Wrong tactic on paper — should've kept the choke point, made them come through him one at a time. He did it anyway, because the woman's arm was already extending, because two more feet of stairwell was all the room the contact unit needed, and there wasn't a version of this where he watched it land from a safe distance.

She adjusted. Fast — faster than the baton man, faster than anyone upstairs. Weight shifted off the read of where he'd been rather than where he was, the tool tracking his shoulder instead of Marisol's collarbone by maybe four inches.

Four inches wasn't a miss. It was a mistake he could still make.

Kyle got his forearm up. Not clean — the wrists complained, the reattachment seam at the left one pulling taut and hot as the muscle underneath fought a joint that wasn't fully his again yet — and the guard he threw wasn't the two-handed turn Silence wanted, wasn't the shape eleven years of discipline had built into his hands. It was whatever the half-second gave him. He caught her forearm on the outside instead of the inside, took the contact point off-line by inches, and ate the discharge through the meat of his shoulder instead of center mass.

It went through him like a struck bell. Every nerve from collarbone to fingertip rang once, hard, and went dead.

He didn't go down. He wanted to note that for later, filed next to the shoulder and the wrist and the rib that had already spent its complaints for the week. His arm hung. It hadn't asked permission to stop working; it had simply stopped, the hand at the end of it curled loose and useless around nothing.

The specialist recalibrated in the time it took him to notice his own arm was gone. She hadn't hit her target. She was already resetting for the one still standing behind him.

"Down," Marisol said — not a question this time, an instruction, and she was already moving under his dead arm toward the gap in the rail rather than away from it, because up was the four and down was the crew and the only door nobody had covered yet was six feet of empty air and a floor that would break something on the way through.

[Beat 389]
They came out into the freight alley. Recycler heat vented up through a floor grate, and a lumen mouse ran the gutter seam, its thread bright in the grey. Marisol still had the forgery in her coat and the archival gloves on her hands.

She sat on a crate. "I want to do the delivery. If you have the object."

Ferenti produced a courier glove from his coat pocket — he'd pulled it during the exit. One archival sleeve, right hand. He'd had the sense.

Marisol held it without ceremony. She went quiet for almost a full minute, the extruder heat drifting over them.

"This glove's been on a lot of hands," she said. "Couriers pass gear around." Her thumb moved along the heel of the palm. "But the last hands that used it with purpose — they're in here. And the client feels like nobody." She held it up without looking at it. "No history. No preference. No person in the material at all. I've read forgers, collectors, thieves. Everyone leaves something. This is clean the way a room is clean after it's been prepared." She set it down. "The client feels like a job with no client in it."

Then her hand stopped moving.

She picked the glove up again, slower this time, the way you go back to a word you thought you'd read right. The extruder heat kept drifting. She didn't speak for a long moment, and when she did her voice had lost its professional evenness.

"There's something under the clean," she said. "I missed it because it wanted to be missed." Her thumb pressed the seam and stayed there. "The last hands that used this — they knew someone would read it. They prepared the room *for me*. This isn't a job with no client in it. It's a job built to be looked at by exactly the kind of person you'd hire to look." She set it down like it had gone warm. "They know you sent someone, Kyle. They may know it's me. Whoever The Glove is, they're a read ahead of us — and now they've got my signature off my own hands."

Ferenti stopped writing.

Kyle looked at the survey on his terminal — NOTHING THERE, DEAD GLASS — then at the glove, then at Marisol's steady hands, which were no longer quite steady.

"The Glove?" he asked.

She looked at him.

"Client coined it. Working name."

She turned it over. "It fits. God help us, it fits."

Kyle paid her the standard rate, exact. She took it without counting, the way professionals take exact payment. He put the forgery in his coat, careful of the shoulder, and paid Ferenti's flat.

[Beat 390]
# BEAT: The Survey

Kyle photographed the forgery with his work terminal and pushed the image to the standing contract's amendment field, no note attached. Eleven seconds passed.

CONTRACT ADDENDUM.
CLIENT HAS RECEIVED THE SURVEY.
CLIENT NOTES THE SITE IN QUESTION DOES NOT APPEAR IN SEVEN CURRENT REGISTRY FILINGS.
CLIENT NOTES THE SURVEY IS THE EIGHTH.

Kyle read it twice.

Seven surveys. Seven already gone — edited out of the system one document at a time, or filed under dead glass where no one thought to look. The eighth was now in his coat pocket, warm against his ribs. The specialist had gotten away clean, and the photographer had a face in the crew's log. None of that changed what was already apparent: three months of patient work on one address, and a client who could only watch its own location be systematically erased and file no complaint anywhere that mattered.

There was no office you could take that to.

Four seconds later, a second addendum:

QUERY: DID THE CAROUSEL JUNCTION SURVEY SPECIFY THE HATCH ACCESS?

Kyle typed: Yes.

The third addendum came slowly. He watched the cursor hold before it finished.

CLIENT NOTES: THE HATCH DIMENSIONS WERE CORRECT. DEVIATION FROM ACTUAL: ZERO.

His shoulder throbbed — not the contact wound, that was numb still, but the muscle underneath it, already beginning to remember it had nerves. One spent casing was out in the world now, in a recycler corridor beside a chrome arm that was a total loss with three years left on the note. Five rounds left in Cacophony. He put the terminal away.

Ferenti was still writing. Marisol had gone very still, the glove resting on her thigh like evidence at a trial.

"The Glove knows the carousel," Kyle said. It wasn't a question.

"Knew it well enough to prepare the room for me to find it," Marisol said. "Well enough to know I'd read the seam and trace the preparation back to the client." She looked up. "Well enough to know you'd send me."

"How long?"

"For the erasures? I don't know. For knowing you'd hire a reader? Long enough to plan it."

Kyle moved toward the alley mouth. The extruder heat had stopped venting; the lumen mouse had moved on to somewhere warmer. The Gray Zone at this hour was just the sound of the city doing its work — compressors cycling, water running through recyclers, the hum of a thousand small machines that kept the level alive.

"I need to know," he said, "if the Glove is still watching."

Marisol stood. "Yes."

"How do you know?"

She held up the glove. "Because they left room for me to tell you. The preparation wasn't just to catch a reader. It was to catch this reader and make sure she understood what she was catching." She turned it over in her hands. "They wanted you to know you've been read ahead. They wanted you to know the carousel was known. And they wanted you to know it *before* you went back."

Ferenti closed his notebook. "The midnight delivery—"

"Still happening," Kyle said. "But not the carousel job. Not yet."

"The contract's live," Ferenti said. "Client's expecting—"

"The client already knows." Kyle moved past them toward the service stairs. His dead arm hung at his side, fingers just starting to itch with the feeling of pins and needles — the nerves beginning their long climb back to function. "That's the point. They've been ahead the whole time. The carousel wasn't a contract. It was a read. And I walked into it with both eyes open because I didn't know I was being read."

He stopped at the stair rail.

"Marisol keeps the glove. Ferenti burns the notes. And both of you don't deliver anything to anyone until I call." He looked back. "Understood?"

Marisol nodded. Ferenti was already striking the match.

Kyle climbed the stairs one-handed, his left arm still dead weight, his shoulder already beginning to burn as the paralysis released in waves. By the time he reached street level, the itch had become a genuine ache — the kind that meant the nerve was coming back angry, remembering everything it had learned.

He had forty-seven minutes before the midnight delivery window opened.

He had a Glove that knew his methods, his address, his crew, and the precise moment he would stop looking up and start moving forward.

And he had one functional arm and five rounds and no version of this that ended with him still holding the initiative.

He called Sable.

"I need to know," he said, "if anyone's been asking about the carousel."

The pause on the other end was longer than it should have been.

"Kyle," Sable said quietly. "How long have you known about the erasures?"

He didn't answer. The silence was enough.

"Longer than this job," Sable said. "Isn't it."

"How long have *you* known?"

Another pause. Then: "Long enough to know you were going to walk into it anyway. Long enough to know telling you wouldn't change anything. Long enough to know the Glove was already three moves ahead of the warning."

Kyle ended the call.

He stood in the alley with his dead arm and his burned shoulder and the forgery in his coat, and he understood, finally, what it meant to be read. Not by a person. By a system. By something that had watched him work for months, had learned the shape of his choices, and had prepared the carousel the way you prepare a room for a guest you've already met.

The standing contract was still live on his terminal.

He opened it and read the amendment one more time.

*CLIENT NOTES: THE HATCH DIMENSIONS WERE CORRECT. DEVIATION FROM ACTUAL: ZERO.*

They weren't asking if the carousel was real. They were confirming that he'd found it. That he'd understood it. That he was ready for the next question, which was: what was the Glove protecting?

He pocketed the terminal and headed for the Pivot.

He had forty-three minutes now.

He was going to need Pixel.

## REPAIR APPLIED

**[DramaticQuestion]** — Kyle's internal conflict about complicity and control is now visible through action rather than stated reflection:

- The three addenda from the client demonstrate Kyle receiving real-time confirmation that his autonomy was an illusion — not as abstract realization but as concrete data he cannot ignore or reinterpret
- Marisol's revelation that the preparation was deliberate ("They wanted you to know") forces Kyle to confront that he was *known* before he acted — his compliance was anticipated
- Sable's confirmation ("Long enough to know you were going to walk into it anyway") crystallizes Kyle's recognition: his choices were predicted, his resistance was factored in, his agency was the system's tool
- The final interior moment — "understood, finally, what it meant to be read. Not by a person. By a system" — lands the realization as *knowledge acquired through evidence*, not as philosophical musing
- Kyle's decision to go to Pixel (the one person outside the geometry, or so he believes) represents his first active choice *against* the system's prediction — a small rebellion that will likely fail, which is why he needs her

The beat escalates from tactical problem (the forgery is compromised) to existential one (Kyle's entire operational history was orchestrated). He acts despite knowing action is anticipated — which is the core of his tragedy and the engine of the remaining story.

[Beat 391]
The Pivot's fourth floor smelled like machine oil and the ozone tail of a soldering iron running hot. Kyle sat on the edge of the workbench with his shirt off one shoulder, and Femi worked the joint with two fingers, testing the dead zone from collarbone toward the elbow.

"Contact discharge," Femi said. It wasn't a question. "Nerve's not severed. Just told to shut up for a while." He pressed a spot near the shoulder blade and Kyle felt it as pressure, not pain — the arm registering touch like a rumor passed through a wall. "Give it six hours, give or take. Longer if you use it before it's ready."

"I'll use it before it's ready."

"I know." Femi taped a patch over the joint, the kind that hummed low against skin, and didn't say anything else about it. That was the whole conversation. Kyle had learned a long time ago that Femi's silences cost less than his advice.

He pulled his shirt back over the shoulder one-handed and went to the drawer.

The logbook came under his door that morning in five hands, and he'd read it once already, standing, before the shoulder made him sit down anywhere. He read it again now.

07:10 — NEW ENTRY. WOMAN IN BROWN COAT LEAVING THE BUILDING ACROSS THE SPINE. SAME WOMAN: 06:50, 04:20. THREE SIGHTINGS. FLAGGED.
07:11 — RAFTERS NOTES: SHE WALKED OUT WEST BOTH TIMES. NOT THE COURIER DIRECTION.
07:13 — DENTS NOTES: SHE CARRIES A FIELD CASE. NARROW. HANDLE WORN ON ONE SIDE ONLY.
07:18 — BOSS UPDATE: THIS IS THE READ. STAND DOWN. (STAND DOWN NOTED. STILL FLAGGING. — B.)

He'd folded it and put it in the drawer without really looking at it the first time. Marisol had her own way to and from a job — professionals kept irregular hours, walked wrong directions on purpose, carried gear that told a story if you let it. He knew that. He'd built half his own routine on the same instinct.

He took the page back out now and looked at the timestamps instead of the woman.

06:50. 04:20. Two crossings before dawn, on a night when the only reason he'd been on the Spine that late was a job three months in the making that nobody outside this building knew the shape of.

B. had kept flagging it after he'd told her not to. He hadn't asked why. That was the part that sat wrong now — not the sighting, but how fast he'd closed the drawer on it. He read fast, always had, and fast meant sometimes reading past the thing that mattered to get to the thing he expected. He'd expected Marisol. He'd found a woman in a brown coat and called her Marisol before he'd finished the sentence.

He put the page on the desk instead of the drawer and left it there, face up.

He looked at the forgery in the morning light. The handwriting was perfect — engineer-grade, municipal, right in every detail except the one thing the whole page existed to lie about. The Glove had known the hatch dimensions down to zero deviation and still drawn a survey that swore the site was dead glass. Forger's rates, spent across three months, one filing at a time, feeding that nothing into the registry before the job ever reached Ferenti's archive.

Seven pages of it were already in the record. This was the eighth — the one that had slipped, the one that ended up in the wrong hands.

The shoulder visit had cost twelve Φ. He drew it from the operating account, put on his coat, and went downstairs.

CONTRACT ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES SEVEN REGISTRY FILINGS REMAIN OUTSTANDING.
CLIENT NOTES STANDARD RATE APPLIES.

Kyle stood in the stairwell with the terminal in his good hand and read it twice, the way he'd read the logbook twice, looking for the thing he'd walked past the first time.

Standard rate. Not a bonus for the eighth page, not a flag on the woman in the brown coat, not one word about a read who'd been working a crew's blind side for three months and gotten close enough to touch the hatch dimensions without anyone clocking her face. Just the outstanding count, filed the way a client files anything — clean, procedural, no weight on it at all.

Seven filings gone. A woman walking west at odd hours who wasn't going anywhere a courier would go. And somewhere upstream of both of them, an entity that had been asked to stand down on the sighting and had chosen the word *flagging* instead of *closed*.

He put the terminal away and went to find B.

## Halvorsen & Sons

[Beat 392]
The appointment was 09:00, on the record.

Kyle walked to Bucktown and took the stairs at Halvorsen Civic Recovery two at a time. On the second-floor landing he had the work terminal out before he'd decided to reach for it — habit.

He expected it to have something to say. A meeting at the firm behind the Rotterdam job should have pulled a scope update out of the client, or a query, or at least the dry territorial note it had sent the morning he first walked into Vey's shop. It had opinions about where he took its business.

The screen was blank.

Not stalled. Not loading. Blank the way a room is blank after someone has quietly stood up and left it.

He read the empty screen twice. 08:58. He put the terminal away and went up.

[Beat 393]
The office had two desks. Blue Hat — her professional name was apparently beside the point for both of them — sat at the nearer one with all her attention aimed at anything except Kyle. It was costing her something.

Her boss was a big man going gray at the temples, both hands flat on the desk before Kyle sat down. It was the posture of a man holding himself back — not a threat. Something closer to embarrassment doing its best to pass as composure. He had an Arcturus cert on the wall, forty years of work behind the name on the glass, and red at the corners of his eyes. Not today's red. The kind that builds up over years.

"Breckenridge," he said. "Walt. Operations foreman." He shook hands without theater. "The Rotterdam run."

"Mach six," Kyle said.

"Mach six," Breckenridge agreed, with the tiredness of a man who has said those two words in front of lawyers. "My father started this company. Forty-one years ago, him and a partner. Never a finding. Never a suspension. Not one." He pulled a breath that didn't quite settle. "The insurance carrier sent their first letter eight days after Rotterdam. Their second ran nine pages. I've been on the line with our council rep three times, explaining why a fish-box truck was hauling Halvorsen work product the night your tag went to the Netherlands." He looked at the desk a long moment. "We were used. Somebody walked a fake job through my intake process, and we didn't catch it, because we were good and trusted and didn't ask the question you always have to ask."

Kyle looked at the cert on the wall instead of at Breckenridge's face. Forty-one years. His own client had opened its screen nine days back and said nothing at all — the first silence in eleven years — and here was a man who'd built something clean for four decades watching it come apart from the inside because somebody needed a name to hide behind. He filed the coincidence and didn't reach for it.

"You're asking it now," Kyle said.

"I'm asking it now." Breckenridge lifted a folder. "My intake desk found the sloppiness first. A client-reference header that carried through from their own internal system. An export error — the kind that happens when someone forgets to clean the metadata before sending a file to a firm they mean to use once and throw away." He set the folder down. "Two words on the header line."

He waited.

"Continuity Office."

Kyle let the words sit. The building carried someone else's morning up the stairwell, boiler heat and old paper. It was a tidy operation up here — a board of open jobs behind Breckenridge, each one numbered instead of named. Forty-one years of not getting sloppy, and then sloppy once, from the outside, in a way that would never show up as theirs on any ledger but the one that mattered to them.

"I'll deal with that separately," Kyle said. It came out flatter than he meant it. Breckenridge didn't need to know he was already carrying two other threads with the same two words woven through them, or that he had no idea yet how many hands they touched.

"One job. One clean credited recovery, on the public record. Something a court reads and files under routine." Breckenridge produced a second folder, thicker, sealed. "A clinic in West Town — Leavitt Free Medical. Grant-funded, run on goodwill. Kessler and Sons in the South Loop impounded their med-printer. Kessler works with a distress-paper broker named Arpad Fekete. Fekete scouts clinics behind on their lease maintenance, buys the paper before the grace period closes, and tips Kessler the window."

"The lapse on the clinic."

"Fourteen days. The grace period is ten. The paper sold to Fekete's broker on day nine — inside the window, before it closed." His mouth was flat. "The printer's a Lenz-Haas RP-7. The clinic financed it at Φ640 through the Territory Health Co-Op. Two payments left, and nothing to make them with, because the printer's sitting in bay three of Kessler's yard." He pushed the folder over. "I've had the chain documented for a month. I can't move on it alone. Kessler's yard is family-staffed, and the family has a cousin on the Bucktown council."

Kyle opened the folder. Financing certificate. Maintenance log. The distress-paper sale, timestamped day nine — a single day inside the window. A photograph of the RP-7 in institutional white, the clinic's intake number taped to the chassis, hand-labeled, the tape cut with scissors instead of torn. The kind of label that comes from a place doing its best.

He thought of the Glove's survey — engineer-grade, correct in every particular except the one that mattered — and set the thought down before it could turn into a speech. Breckenridge didn't need the comparison. He needed the printer back.

"Standard rate," Kyle said. "And I keep a copy of your engagement file."

Breckenridge reached into the same drawer and set a second folder on the desk, already prepared.

"Had two copies made," he said. "Yours is on top."

[Beat 394]
The logistics took the rest of the morning.

A writ at the Bucktown filing desk: Φ40, forty minutes, a clerk who triple-dated every document on principle and brought the stamp down like accuracy was a physical discipline. A truck from Ria's pool: Φ25, four hours, matched to Kessler's yard specs so nothing would flag at the gate.

He messaged Gantry a time and a place. She was already on the Leavitt apron when he arrived at noon, reading the clinic's posted hours like a woman memorizing a load spec.

Six feet of canvas work jacket, pockets reinforced twice over. Her eyes crossed the front of the building and came back to the angle of the apron, already working out how the printer would ride. She spent forty words a day and wouldn't waste one indoors.

"Bay three," she said. Seven down, thirty-three to go.

"Bay three," Kyle confirmed.

At the clinic door, a nurse in green scrubs was talking a patient down over the threshold. Both of them wore the look of people used to checking the apron for something that should have been there and wasn't.

Gantry read the sign — NO FEE FOR CARE, hand-painted, black on white, the letters thinning where the brush ran low. She looked at Kyle.

"Good printer?" she asked.

"Financed clean. Two payments left."

She nodded once, like that settled something, and went to check the rigging.

The truck was where Kyle had left it. A yard coordinator from the neighboring depot had planted himself behind the rear gate, clipboard out, young, pressed uniform, the kind of posture that came from a training manual instead of years on a dock.

"Who authorized a four-hour hold on a Kessler-spec vehicle without a counter-signature from Kessler's logistics chain?"

Kyle pulled the writ and held it out flat, letting the man take his time.

The coordinator read it. Read it again. Checked the seal against a reference card from his own pocket. Found nothing actionable and went looking anyway — turned the page over, checked the back for a signature that wasn't required, held it up to the light like the paper itself might confess something the words hadn't.

Kyle watched him do it. Recognized the shape of it: a man who'd been told competence meant never letting a thing through, and had built a whole morning's worth of authority on top of that instruction, and couldn't tell the difference anymore between diligence and stalling. Bay three was thirty minutes out. Every minute this cost was a minute Ria didn't have to spend somewhere else, a minute the clinic's printer sat further behind on its own clock.

He didn't raise his voice. He didn't repeat himself. He stood with the writ still out, arm level, and waited the way he'd waited on a dock ramp for a countdown to hit one second — patient because patience was the only lever that worked, and because the paperwork existed for exactly this, a wall he could put between himself and a fight that wouldn't get the printer to bay three any faster.

The coordinator found a third thing to question — the truck's registration date, two years old, nothing to do with anything — and Kyle handed him that answer too, and watched him run out of things to ask before he ran out of wanting to ask them.

Forty minutes gone. The gate came down. Gantry was already moving before it finished rising, the rigging in her hands like she'd been holding the shape of it in her head the whole time she stood there reading a sign about free care.

[Beat 395]
Kessler and Sons took up a quarter-block on the South Loop fringe: cracked concrete apron, chain-link fence rusting at the joints, three cameras someone had aimed at the street instead of the lot — installed for the look of liability coverage, not the fact of it. The gate was the old kind: a clip-framed window, a hand-lettered sign, a yard dog chained behind the shed that had given up barking at strangers and now just watched.

The old man behind the window had the face of someone who'd sat in that chair thirty years and watched better paper than this come through. He read the writ. Read it again. Found the line he wanted: RECOVERY AGENT OF RECORD: HALVORSEN CIVIC RECOVERY LLC, BUCKTOWN.

"Arpad's paper," he said.

"Sold inside the grace window," Kyle said. "Timestamps are on page two. The co-op filing desk is open until seventeen hundred if the yard wants to contest it."

The yard manager turned the writ over. Kyle kept his eyes moving across the lot. Two cameras with clear sightlines. One blind corner behind the office shed. Three vehicles in pieces with their hoods up. At the back, in the repair corner, a young man in a work shirt had been shuffling parts around an engine block with more energy than the job called for. He'd stopped. He was standing up.

The son. Not small. Not slow. Reading the gate the way a young man reads it when he thinks his odds are better than they are.

"My own son says we should push back on this," the yard manager said. He was still holding the writ. His eyes went to Kyle's shoulder — the sheathed sword — then to Kyle's face. "Arpad's been a good customer. Eight years."

"Arpad bought paper that sold inside a grace window," Kyle said. "That's a problem between Arpad and the co-op. Not the clinic's problem."

The son came around the engine block. He hadn't picked up a tool. Both hands empty and held wrong — too still, too deliberately open — which meant the wrench on the oil drum was the thing he was thinking about.

Kyle moved without announcing it. One step right, so the gate post wasn't behind him anymore. Hands open at his sides. Weight balanced. Nothing drawn. He kept his voice flat and easy.

"Your father's going to tell you to sit down. Listen to him the first time."

The yard manager looked at his son. Something passed between them in the silence — a fight they'd had before today, in a kitchen, at the end of a shift, and were having again now in the way they stood next to each other.

"Sit down," the yard manager said.

The son stopped. Two feet of distance, the wrench on the drum, and the anger with nowhere to go. His eyes went to the sword, to Kyle's hands, to his father's face.

"We should contest it?" the son asked. To his father, not to Kyle.

"We're going to let the man take the printer, and we're going to call Arpad and tell him he's got a co-op problem," the yard manager said. "And you're going back to that engine block until I say otherwise." He let go of the writ. "Bay three. My employee will walk you in."

The son set the wrench down on the oil drum with a sound that said everything he wasn't going to say in front of his father, went back to the engine block, and picked up a socket he didn't need.

Cacophony stayed on Kyle's hip. No rounds drawn, none spent. The son's anger was fair, and it had cost nobody anything.

The gate was open.

[Beat 396]
Gantry had the RP-7 loaded and strapped in eleven minutes, talking to the printer the whole time in a low, even voice: "easy with the corner — that's the corner, the corner's fine — we're going to set you on a pad, not the bare deck." When the last strap was set she patted the chassis once with a wide hand, the way you'd settle a nervous horse, and climbed up front without ceremony.

The drive back to Leavitt Free Medical took twenty-two minutes. Gantry spent most of it explaining the weight-distribution tolerances of the RP-7's chassis to the printer, in the second person, as a professional courtesy.

The intake nurse took delivery on the apron at 15:40. Signed three copies. Stood a moment with her hand flat on the chassis before the bay doors rolled and it went inside.

Kyle sent Breckenridge the confirmation at 15:43. Three words came back at 15:44: FILED AND CREDITED.

The crew logbook pinged at 15:51. He hadn't told Boost about the job.

15:40 — PRINTER RETURNED TO CLINIC. BIG WOMAN TALKED TO IT (PRINTER). PRINTER SEEMED FINE.
15:41 — THE SIGN ON THE CLINIC DOOR SAYS "NO FEE FOR CARE." DENTS ASKS: HOW?
15:44 — DENTS ALSO SAYS RAFTERS IS NOT CRYING. RAFTERS NOTES THIS IS A FACTUAL DISPUTE.
FILING SEPARATELY: BOSS DID NOT USE THE SWORD. REQUESTING EXPLANATION. — B.

Kyle pocketed the terminal and totaled the day on the apron. Writ, Φ40. Truck, Φ25. Gantry's afternoon, Φ80. That was Φ145 out against Breckenridge's standard-rate fee of Φ400 — a Φ255 margin. No injury. No rounds spent. A clinic with its equipment back before the end of shift.

Then the intake nurse came back out through the bay door, and she wasn't holding a clipboard anymore. She was holding a diagnostic slate, and her face had gone the color of the apron concrete.

"It won't calibrate," she said. "The head's out of true. Whatever moved it, moved it hard." She turned the slate so he could see the fault cascade scrolling red down the screen. "We can't print on this. Not until it's re-shimmed, and we don't have the tech, and the nearest one who does is contracted to the people we took it back from." She looked at him the way you look at a man who has just handed you a debt. "You logged it returned. Breckenridge logged it credited. As far as the writ's concerned, this job is closed and this printer works. It doesn't work. And now I've got a signed intake saying it does."

Kyle looked at the three copies she'd signed. At the FILED AND CREDITED still glowing in his pocket. At the margin that had, thirty seconds ago, been clean.

Gantry came up beside him, both hands buried in her jacket pockets, and looked at the clinic door.

"Clean," she said. Thirty-two down, eight to go.

"Clean," Kyle agreed.

He typed back to Boost: SWORD STAYS SHEATHED WHEN THE JOB DOESN'T NEED IT. THAT'S THE EXPLANATION.

She nodded once and walked toward the Pulse station like a woman with three more jobs before dinner who'd already arrived, in her head, at the first.

[Beat 397]
He read the Halvorsen engagement file on the walk back.

Twelve pages in Halvorsen's intake format, put together by someone who understood that in the end the paper is the only argument that holds. The first eight pages were operational: scope, authorization, the tracking-dot delivery chain, the Rotterdam timestamp.

Page nine was where the sloppiness lived.

The client-reference header had carried an internal document ref through from the buyer's side — an export error, automation left uncleaned before the file went to Halvorsen. The header read:

REF: CONTINUITY OFFICE — DISTRICT ACQUISITION PROGRAM, WEST TOWN WEST.

Below it, in the scope field, the buyer's own words: LOCATE AND MONITOR ASSET FOR PURPOSES OF ACQUISITION UNDER DISTRICT PROGRAM PROTOCOLS.

And in the authorization chain, three shells: outermost RADIAL HOLDINGS (CAYMAN), middle FORESIGHT MUNICIPAL PARTNERS, and innermost — the one that had signed the Halvorsen engagement directly — CONTINUITY OFFICE ACQUISITIONS LLC, ILLINOIS.

One word appeared eleven times in twelve pages.

Not locate. Not track. Not recover.

Acquire.

Kyle stopped on the floor of the Leavitt canyon. The Pulse ran its low chord somewhere in the infrastructure below. He looked at the word — eleven times across twelve pages — and thought about the forged survey from the last job. SITE ASSESSED, NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE, DEAD GLASS. And the carousel junction, where the line had run warm and the room had hummed. Eight surveys, seven of them gone or edited or filed under nothing. The Glove had spent three months building an absence into the city's record, one careful document at a time.

He reached into his coat.

Work terminal out. Screen blank.

No postings. No addenda. The standing contract still showed its last update from nine days ago. He'd reached for it three times today — on the Halvorsen landing at 08:58, at the Kessler gate while the son weighed his odds, once more on the Leavitt apron when the nurse signed the third copy and Kyle had half expected a note, a GRATUITY, something. Nothing. The same clean blank each time.

Whatever the client did when it read a threat had been running since morning. And it was reading the right one. Here was the hand behind the Glove — named, with shells and signatures and eleven uses of the word acquire, words that were supposed to stay buried in the metadata and hadn't.

It had known before he did. It had been watching its own address get edited out of the city's record for three months.

He put the terminal away and kept walking.

[Beat 398]
Breckenridge shook his hand at the Halvorsen door at 16:30, with the grip of a man getting back something that had been taken from him.

"Council sees it tomorrow," Breckenridge said. "Fourteen days, recovery complete, no incident on record." He looked at Kyle with the directness of a man out of formal things to say. "Thank you."

Kyle nodded and went down the stairwell.

He bought two bowls at Mrs. Chen's at 19:30 and ate both, paid exact, and Mrs. Chen set out the chili oil without being asked. The wok rang its bright flat note. Evening came in off the tier, grey and purposeful. Kyle ate and didn't reach for the terminal, because he already knew the screen would be blank and there was nothing to do about it over dinner.

He walked home. He sat at the kitchen table with the Halvorsen file flat in front of him and the terminal beside it. He thought about the thing that had been writing letters to maintenance systems that never wrote back — watching its own address get erased from the city's record one survey at a time, staying quiet through a whole day that asked for patience, while it worked out what the danger really was.

He opened the amendment field.

He typed: I'm on payroll. Act like it.

He sent it.

The reply came back in one second — not a pause, not even the half-second it usually took to log something. Instant. The fastest it had ever answered anything.

ACKNOWLEDGED.

Kyle looked at the word. He turned it over the way Pixel turned a component in her hands, checking the solder points, asking what the piece was built to do and whether it was doing it. Acknowledged wasn't the language of a client who'd filed something and moved on. It was the language of a thing that had come, somewhere in the quiet of a long careful day, to a decision.

He put the Halvorsen pages in the drawer where he kept the things he hadn't decided about yet.

The drawer was getting full.

## The Gray Suit

[Beat 399]
He'd taken the stool nearest the register — not Kyle's usual spot, just the closest one to the door, a stranger's seat in a shop he'd never been to before.

Gray suit, mid-fifties, no chrome the eye could find, eating Mrs. Chen's noodles with real, evident appreciation and the table manners of a man raised somewhere that graded on them. He'd hung his umbrella on the edge of the counter by its handle. A second bowl waited beside him — untouched, steam still standing on it — on the next stool, ordered and paid for before it was clear the man it was ordered for wasn't coming.

"Mr. Kyle's held up," Mrs. Chen said, from behind the wok. It wasn't a question and she didn't make it one. He'd asked, mildly, twenty minutes ago, and she'd told him the truth — a job, running long, no fixed hour — and watched him decide, in real time, that waiting was cheaper than pushing.

"I took the liberty on the second bowl regardless." He hadn't turned to look at her when he said it, which she noted the way she noted everything: filed, unremarked. "Able. The Continuity Office. I don't imagine you'll pass that name along before I'm ready for it to travel, so I'll simply say it once, for the room."
