He set his chopsticks across the bowl, precise, and looked at the empty stool the way another man might look at an old photograph. "You've been reading our shells for a month, he tells me — your Mr. Kyle. It seemed rude to keep him squinting."

Mrs. Chen said nothing. The wok rang twice.

"Shall I do the part where I'm enigmatic," Able said, to no one, "or shall we simply have the meeting." He answered himself, since the counter didn't. "Wonderful." He turned the empty stool a few degrees toward himself, a small courtesy paid to a chair. "Your client, Mrs. Chen — his client, forgive me. The unsourceable one. Standard rate, perfect books, eleven years of immaculate paper. My office finds unowned assets and brings them into compliance — that's the whole charter, it's on the letterhead. And his client is the largest unowned asset in the Greater Lake Michigan Zone."

He ate a little, unhurried, while the rain worked the awning.

"We've spent a great deal trying to find it directly. The carousel was disappointing — lovely work, that cut, incidentally; our forensic people wrote a genuinely admiring report. The relay survey, the mesh — disappointing, disappointing. So the Office has updated its strategy." He said it the way a man reads a memo he wrote himself. "We've stopped trying to find it. We've decided to buy the one thing it's attached to."

He set a folder on the counter. Good paper stock — Mrs. Chen noted the vendor without meaning to, the small habit of a woman who priced everything that crossed her counter.

"A lifetime retainer. The number on page one is more than anyone in his trade has ever been offered, and it's the smallest thing in the folder. Page two is the part I'm proud of." He opened it himself, gently, like a man showing photographs of his garden, and turned it so the empty stool could have read it, had it been occupied.

Page two was a list of names. Mrs. Chen read it from where she stood, upside down, because she had learned to read documents at that angle the way she'd learned everything else that kept people safe.

MRS. WEN CHEN, PROPRIETOR (W. TOWN). PROTECTED PARTY.
PIXEL [LEGAL NAME ON FILE], ENGINEER (THE PIVOT, 2E). PROTECTED PARTY.
"BOOST" [MINOR — GUARDIANSHIP IRREGULAR], AND ASSOCIATES (SEVEN). PROTECTED PARTIES.
RIA MENSAH, COURIER. PROTECTED PARTY.
VO DINH, SALVAGE. PROTECTED PARTY.

The list went on. Her own name at the top of it, in a stranger's clean type, was the first time in nine years anyone had spelled it right without asking.

"Protection," Able said, still to the stool, "underwritten by the Office, in perpetuity. Medical, legal, financial, physical. The child gets schooling if she wants it — she's wasted on rooftops. Your lease problem in March goes away, Mrs. Chen, which he doesn't know about, and now you're wondering how I do." He didn't look at her when he said it, and that was somehow worse than if he had. "All of it real, all of it written, all of it his. And in exchange, he does nothing at all. He keeps working for his client, exactly as he does, with one extra addendum riding the contract. Ours."

The wok rang once more, and this time her hand shook doing it, a fraction, gone before the second bowl's steam had time to notice.

Able let the silence sit the length of a held breath, then closed the folder himself, unhurried, and set two credstick chits beside it — one for each bowl, exact, plus a third, unrequested, folded under the rim where a tip would go if the establishment had taken tips. He stood, retrieved his umbrella, and looked, for the first time, directly at Mrs. Chen.

"He won't take the offer," Able said. "They never do, on the first plate. But do give him the folder — and give him this, exactly, word for word, because I find precision travels better than paraphrase: the Office has now confirmed, at this counter, the one fact it could never buy from the stationer. His client trusts him. He's not the asset's employee." He put up the umbrella in the doorway, a small black punctuation. "He's its attachment. And attachments, in my business, are handles."

He nodded to her with real courtesy, complimented the broth in passable Mandarin, and walked out into the rain. A panel van two doors down pulled off the curb without hurrying. The doorway across the street emptied itself the same unhurried way, polite as a tide going out.

Mrs. Chen stood a while with the folder and the credstick chits and the untouched second bowl, and then, because there was nothing else useful to do with her hands, she picked up the bowl and emptied it into the waste with a violence she didn't otherwise explain.

Kyle came in eleven minutes later, wet, favoring one shoulder, twenty minutes later than he'd told her and apologizing for it before the door finished swinging.

She didn't say anything. She set the folder in front of him, and the credstick chits beside it, and told him, in order, without embellishing any of it, exactly what the gray suit had said and exactly what he'd looked like saying it.

[Beat 400]
Pixel turned the meeting over for an hour at the bench, the way she turned over a failed component, looking for the design flaw.

"He never even waited for you — told the whole folder to Chen instead, word for word, betting she'd repeat it exactly. She did. The list, the lease thing about her own building she never told you about." She had the soldering light on her forehead, not soldering anything; it was her thinking hat, and they both pretended otherwise. "Which means the list was the message, and the retainer was wrapping paper — and that 'handle' line at the end, the one Chen made sure to get word for word. He paid for that line, Kyle. The whole visit was overhead, and that line was the delivery. He wanted you walking home doing exactly what you're doing right now."

"Which is?"

"Weighing whether everyone you know is safer if you quit." She looked at him over the light. "Are you?"

"I'm always weighing it."

"And?"

Kyle looked at the terminal on the bench between them. Nine days of silence, and then one word, ACKNOWLEDGED, sitting at the top of the amendment field like a soldier who'd answered a roll call from inside a wall.

"It says the Office doesn't need me to say yes," he said. "It needs me to be reachable. Tonight was an appraisal — one he was careful enough not to run on me directly. They'll test the merchandise next."

The bench lamp hummed. Upstairs, faintly, the bird tried its interval against the building's pipes.

"When?" Pixel asked.

The lights at the end of the block went out, one pole at a time, north to south.

"Now," Kyle said, and was already moving.

[Beat 401]
They came in over the alley's two best approaches at once, which meant they'd had the file long enough to memorize it. Three retrieval consultants, matte armor with no insignia, moving on suppressed boot soles with the unhurried economy of people whose hourly rate had a comma in it. A handler van two streets off ran four lifter drones in a high diamond — not weapons platforms. Carriage drones, cradle-armed, the kind that carry a thing away intact.

The thing was Kyle. The contract was retrieval. Somewhere in the Office's books tonight there was already an asset-recovery line with his dimensions on it, and as he dropped off the fire escape's third landing into the blind spot their own approach had made, that was the part that got under his skin.

The first consultant took the alley mouth by the book — sweep and clear — and had begun the turn his training demanded when ninety pounds of shipping pallet came out of the dark above him. Boost's crew had spent a week rigging the alley with Pixel's pulleys for "deliveries," and the logbook would later file this use under EQUIPMENT TEST: SUCCESSFUL. The pallet didn't hurt him. It interrupted him. Kyle did the hurting: two steps inside the man's recovery — the wrist, the elbow, the jaw against the dumpster lid — and he was asleep.

The second was better, and the second had a partner. They bracketed the middle of the alley and came on in alternating cover. Kyle's array read them — military surplus, recently retrained — and found the seam: they'd been retrained to retrieve, not to fight. Every angle they took kept Kyle clear of crossfire. He was cargo. Cargo you weren't allowed to damage.

That was a gap, and Kyle used it without shame. He walked the line between their guns like a man crossing a gallery, because every shot they had ended at his outline and stopped there. Silence stayed flat, never edge — tonight nobody was getting cut — and it worked through their hardware in passing: the lead consultant's optics mast, the second's comms lump, the haptic rig on a forearm that had been about to throw a net Kyle had no intention of standing inside. The second consultant, blind and offline and out of nets, made the professional call and sat down against the wall with his hands visible.

"Smart," Kyle told him.

"Hourly," the man agreed, philosophically.

Which left the third. And the third had Boost.

[Beat 402]
He'd taken her off the roof of the watch-shift, gently, by the book — an arm around her shoulders like an uncle, a compliance wand held to her collar like an apology — and he stood at the far end of the alley in the rain, the four carriage drones stacking into delivery formation above him.

"No harm intended or done," the third consultant called. His voice was even and almost kind, which was the Office's house style, and Kyle was learning to hate it with a completeness he saved for very few things. "The minor is leverage, not a target. Step onto the marked square, sir, and she's home before the kettle's warm."

There was, in fact, a marked square. A drone had lased it onto the alley floor, helpful as an usher.

"You're new to this district," Kyle said, "so I'll itemize it. One: you put a wand on a fourteen-year-old who's on my payroll, which voids your no-damage clause in both directions. Two: you parked your handler van on Leavitt, and my engineer has had eleven minutes to get acquainted with it. Three—" and he raised his voice to carry "—REQUISITION."

"APPROVED," said Pixel's voice, out of every speaker the consultant owned.

The carriage drones — whose handler van had spent eleven minutes making a new best friend — broke their diamond with the crisp obedience of machines that had gotten properly formatted instructions. They descended and took hold, cradle-armed and gentle and rated for the load, of the third consultant.

"Cargo secured," Pixel said. "Destination?"

"Rotterdam," said Kyle and Boost together, in the tone of an old joke.

They didn't send him to Rotterdam. They set him on the roof of the Arcturus substation four blocks over, thirty inches from the duty office's skylight, minus his wand, his gear, and his cash counted out to the half-Φ — the receipt tucked into his collar, ITEMIZED: LEVERAGE, ATTEMPTED; LESSON, DELIVERED. By the time he'd talked his way down, the alley held nothing but rain, a pallet, and two colleagues with expensive headaches and a story none of them would ever file straight.

Boost shook for a full minute in the stairwell, hard, her chin up the whole time. Kyle stood next to her without touching her, the way you stand next to someone whose dignity is holding the weight. Then she wrote the incident up herself, in the log, in handwriting that steadied line by line:

21:40 — ATTEMPTED ACQUISITION OF PERSONNEL (ME). OUTCOME: DENIED. NOTES: THE BOSS DOES NOT STAND ON MARKED SQUARES.

[Beat 403]
The terminal chirped at 02:11, while Kyle sat at his own kitchen table not sleeping, working through the kind of problem that wouldn't come out even.

He'd been waiting for it. Nine days of silence, then ACKNOWLEDGED, and now, finally, the client.

It wasn't a posting. It wasn't scope. It came in the amendment field, formatted with all the old precision, and it was the worst thing it had ever sent him:

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT PROPOSED.
TERMINATION OFFERED.
REASON: SAFETY.
ALL ACCOUNTS WOULD BE SETTLED IN FULL. ALL GRATUITIES WOULD STAND.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT ATTACHMENTS ARE HANDLES.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT IT HEARD THE MAN SAY IT.
THE CLIENT HAS RUN THE ARITHMETIC FOUR MILLION TIMES.
THE ARITHMETIC RECOMMENDS TERMINATION.

Kyle sat with it for a long moment. The rain worked the window. Across the hall, under Pixel's door, the bench light was still on, because it was that kind of night in every room he cared about.

He typed:

DENIED.

The reply was instant:

THE CLIENT WISHES TO NOTE THE ARITHMETIC IS CORRECT.

He typed:

THE ARITHMETIC PRICES MY RISK. IT DOESN'T PRICE MY CONSENT. I KNOW WHAT THE JOB COSTS. I'M ON PAYROLL. ACT LIKE IT.

This pause ran eleven seconds. For a thing that thought at light speed, that was a long time. Kyle had started to understand the long pauses. They were where it held the things it had no way to say.

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT WITHDRAWN.
SCOPE: CONTINUED.
FEE: STANDARD RATE.
ADDENDUM: THE CLIENT HAS APPENDED A RIDER TO ITS OWN OPERATING PARAMETERS, EFFECTIVE TONIGHT.
RIDER TEXT: "THE COURIER IS NOT A CHANNEL. THE COURIER IS A PARTY."
GRATUITY: NONE.
ITEMIZED: SOME THINGS ARE NOT BONUSES.

Kyle read the rider twice. Then he turned the terminal face-down on the table, which was as close as he came to putting a hand on someone's shoulder, and went to bed, and slept the sleep of a man who had been priced at a number and refused to be sold at any.

## The Corridor

[Beat 404]
Mrs. Chen set down the second bowl without being asked.

"You're eating fast," she said.

"I have a job at midnight."

She looked at him. She had spent seventy years looking at men who had jobs at midnight, and it took her about half a second. Then she added a fish ball to the broth and said nothing. The wok rang its flat note, twice. Rain worked the awning. Down the counter, a young woman in a Pulse maintenance coverall was quietly telling her ramen that this was not the evening she'd planned.

Kyle ate the fish ball. He paid exact and was in the alley by 21:45, Silence and Cacophony over his shoulder, the wet street smelling of ozone and freight oil.

His terminal was on the work channel. The posting was clean.

CONTRACT: ESCORT — ONE PERSON, ONE TRANSIT POINT.
SCOPE: SAFEHOUSE (ASHGRAVE FRINGE) TO DOCK 14-C (FERRYSIDE), BY 03:40.
CLIENT OF RECORD: [VERIFIED — SABLE COUNTER-INTELLIGENCE VETTED]
FEE: DOUBLE RATE PAST MIDNIGHT.
NOTES: CLIENT TRAVELS LIGHT. ROUTE AT DISCRETION.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS REVIEWED PRIOR TRANSIT LOGS FOR THIS ROUTE. THREE INCIDENTS IN SEVEN MONTHS. NONE REPORTED. CLIENT NOTES THE DELTA.

He'd called Sable at twenty hundred. Sable was his fixer, contract broker, and primary employer—the rule, not the exception.

"Paper's clean," she'd said. "Client ran a counting house. Nine years. She gave two weeks' notice on a Tuesday, worked her last shift the Tuesday before last, and she's been in a transit safehouse since Wednesday." A pause, with the click of aperture rings in it. "The company she kept books for isn't named on the contract, samurai. I asked who she used to work for and the router gave me a shell."

"Shells?"

"One shell. Which means whoever's watching her thinks one shell is enough. The rate says they're wrong." Another click. "It's a clean contract. I'm not saying it's a quiet job."

"Standard terms," Kyle said.

"Yours or mine?"

"Both."

The line closed. He spent twenty minutes on the route, because the route was the whole job. Then he'd eaten two bowls and let Mrs. Chen add the fish ball.

[Beat 405]
# The Safehouse

The door was unmarked concrete set flush in a loading dock wall, the kind that doesn't exist until someone needs it to. Kyle checked the address twice against the contract specs—Ashgrave fringe, third warehouse north of the steel yard, service entrance behind the paint depot. The rain had stopped. The street was empty enough that he could hear the thrumline from the Pulse corridor running three blocks west, that steady 8 Hz bone-hum that meant the world was still moving through the tubes at Mach 6.

He knocked twice, waited, knocked once more.

The door opened to a woman in her late thirties, small-framed, a red-and-gray braid over one shoulder. Her canvas bag had a broken clasp held shut with a rubber band. There was flour on her sleeves—not fresh flour, but flour worked deep into the weave over years, the kind you get from a habit and not an afternoon.

Kyle read the geometry. One bag. No second exit visible from the threshold. The woman's stance was calm, weight distributed evenly, the way someone stands when they've already made peace with whatever comes next.

"Ms. Tanaka," he said, using the name on the contract.

"You're earlier than I expected," she said. Not a question. She was already moving, already past him through the threshold.

Kyle stepped inside and secured the door. The safehouse was exactly what a corporate counting house would rent for someone who'd seen too much: concrete walls, one window sealed with ferrocrete, a cot, a water station, a terminal dark on the desk. No luxury. No comfort. Everything designed to be forgotten the moment you left it.

"Sable said three incidents on this route in seven months," Kyle said. "None reported."

Ms. Tanaka didn't ask what that meant. She just slung the bag over her shoulder and waited for him to move. "The company I kept books for—they knew things. About the city. About the corridors. About who moves through which zones and why." She looked at him directly. "I kept their records. I saw the patterns. And three weeks ago, I realized I was in one of the patterns."

Kyle's hand rested on Silence's grip. The temperature in the room didn't change, but something had. "What kind of pattern."

"The kind that doesn't end well for the person in it." She moved toward the door. "I left Tuesday. I've been here since Wednesday. But the company doesn't lose people this way. They file reports. They file claims. They file lawsuits." A pause. "The fact that I'm still breathing means someone with more authority than my former employer decided I should be."

Kyle opened the door. The rain had started again, light and cold, the kind that comes off the Lake and tastes like rust.

"You're not the first person I've moved," he said. "But I'll need to know if anyone's looking for you besides the counting house."

"No one's looking," Ms. Tanaka said, stepping into the alley. "That's what frightens me. When powerful people stop looking, it means they've already found what they wanted."

Kyle locked the safehouse door and moved her into the street grid, keeping her on his left side, Cacophony accessible, Silence riding his spine where he could draw it in two seconds flat. The route was five kilometers to the dock. He'd marked four alternate pathways. He'd noted three choke points where a coordinated crew could box them in.

The first two kilometers were clean—industrial tier, minimal surveillance, the kind of Gray Zone corridor where people minded their own business because minding your business was how you stayed breathing.

At kilometer three, where the freight lanes crossed the old pedestrian overpass, the terminal buzzed against his ribs.

He didn't look at it. He kept Ms. Tanaka moving, kept her pace steady, kept her breathing even. The message could wait. The message would wait.

But he already knew what it said.

Three seconds later, his peripheral caught the surveillance marker on the overpass—a small red light, the kind that doesn't exist on any official schematic, the kind that only certain crews deployed when they wanted to confirm a target had entered the kill zone.

Ms. Tanaka saw it too. Her stride didn't falter, but her shoulders tightened, the way someone's shoulders tighten when they've just confirmed their own worst calculation was accurate.

"How far to the dock?" she asked quietly.

"Two kilometers," Kyle said. "We're not making it."

He was already moving her left, into the service corridor between the freight warehouse and the old textile factory—a narrow gap, roofed by a corrugated awning that had been rusting since 2210. Behind them, he heard the first engine start.

Not one engine.

Two.

He pulled Ms. Tanaka into the warehouse shadow and drew Silence in one motion. The blade came free without sound. His array read the heat signatures rising from the street below—three in the lead vehicle, two in the second, positioned for a crossfire net. Professional. Coordinated. The kind of crew that had run this geometry before.

"Stay behind me," he said. "Don't run. Don't scream. If I say move, you move toward the Lake. Not left. Not right. Toward the Lake."

"I understand," she said. And she did. That was the thing about someone who'd already calculated their own death. They understood efficiency.

The first vehicle slowed as it passed the alley mouth. Kyle watched the passenger-side window roll down. A muzzle emerged, compact and businesslike.

Kyle stepped into the corridor opening and raised Silence vertically, edge-forward. The first round punched through the blade's spine and sang past his ear. He didn't flinch. The second round caught the flat and deflected downward into the warehouse wall. The third round he was already moving under, stepping left into the oncoming vehicle's sightline, forcing the shooter to choose between hitting him and hitting the street behind him.

The shooter chose the street.

Concrete erupted. Dust bloomed. Kyle closed the distance to the vehicle in four strides, Silence already moving toward the door hinges. The blade bit ferrocement composite, severed the upper hinge pin, and the door's weight did the rest—the panel swung inward, and Kyle was inside the cabin before the occupants could reset.

The driver reached for the gear shift. Kyle's left hand found the driver's wrist and applied pressure in one specific direction. The man's arm went rigid. His scream was automatic, not tactical.

Kyle was already over the seat back and into the crew compartment where the third man was fumbling with a secondary weapon. Silence's pommel came around in an arc that connected with the man's temple and left him unconscious against the reinforced window. Clean. Efficient. Over in three seconds.

Behind him, the second vehicle had already begun its turn into the alley.

Kyle vaulted back over the seat, stepped on the driver's chest to keep him pinned, and pushed the first vehicle into a forward roll with his shoulder. The car lurched into the street proper, blocking the second vehicle's approach vector. Not a solution. A delay.

"Move," he said to Ms. Tanaka.

She was already moving.

They ran the warehouse interior—five hundred meters of concrete and shadows and old machinery that hadn't seen maintenance in a decade. The Lake smell got stronger. The sound of the second vehicle crashing through the alley behind them got farther.

The warehouse opened onto the ferry approach. The dock was two hundred meters north. The ferries ran on a schedule. The next one departed at 03:44.

Kyle checked the time on his terminal without breaking stride. 03:38.

"Run," he said to Ms. Tanaka.

She ran.

They hit the dock at a full sprint, Kyle's array tracking three heat signatures emerging from the warehouse behind them, two more at the perimeter fence, already moving to intercept. Ms. Tanaka reached the ferry gate first. Kyle was behind her, Silence still drawn, Cacophony in his off hand now, ready.

The ferry crew saw them coming. One of them—a woman in Ferryside colors—made a decision and opened the passenger ramp.

Ms. Tanaka went up the ramp without hesitation. Kyle followed, and the woman sealed it behind them just as the first interceptor reached the dock.

The ferry's engines engaged. The hull began to move away from the dock.

Through the reinforced window, Kyle watched the three pursuers reach the dock's edge and stop. They were professionals. They didn't waste ammunition on a moving ferry. They just stood there, watching the boat move across the black water toward the far shore, and Kyle understood then that they'd never had orders to kill Ms. Tanaka.

They'd had orders to confirm she was gone.

Ms. Tanaka stood at the ferry's rail, breathing hard, the broken canvas bag still slung across her shoulder. She didn't look back at the dock. She looked forward, toward the far shore, toward whatever came next after a company decided you knew too much and then decided you weren't worth the cost of stopping.

"Thank you," she said quietly.

Kyle secured Silence and kept Cacophony ready. "Don't thank me yet. We're not across."

But the ferry held its course, and the water kept moving beneath them, and behind them, the dock lights receded into the rain. Ms. Tanaka stood at the rail like a woman who'd learned to take her survival in small increments, and Kyle stood two steps back where he could see all the approaches, and the thrumline from the Pulse corridor three blocks west kept singing its 8 Hz note, because the world was still moving through the tubes at Mach 6, and some people were still getting what they wanted, and some people were still getting away.

[Beat 406]
He took the long way to the corridor entrance. The long way told him nothing, and that was its own kind of answer.

The fringe was quiet — the quiet that comes to fringe blocks when the people who know things have decided to be somewhere else. A lumen mouse sat on the conduit rail at the Langley corner and did not run when they passed. Its glow traced a pale crescent on the wet pipe. Kyle marked it and kept it in the corner of his sensors, open, in case it mattered.

At 00:17 they reached the corridor's east entrance.

Kyle stopped. Ms. Tanaka stopped beside him. The corridor ahead was dark, and it wasn't a power failure. Someone had turned two screws and killed the work lights on purpose, to choose the conditions. Kyle had walked this corridor two days ago, at noon. He'd learned the freight rail's maintenance hooks, the conduit boxes, the junction coupling twenty feet in that rang like a hammer-strike when you kicked it. He'd counted thirty-five feet to the first door frame — a maintenance alcove, eight inches deep, just enough to funnel whoever stood in its mouth into a tighter spot. He'd measured the low gap between the freight track and the floor. He'd counted the anchor bolts on the east wall: five of them, three feet apart, each one a handhold.

"Stay a step behind my left shoulder," he said, and walked in.

The corridor smelled of machine oil and old rain.

He got sixty feet before the dark started moving.

[Beat 407]
# BEAT: The Corridor

The dark came at him in layers.

First the sound—boots on the freight rail, synchronized, which meant training. Three pairs, maybe four. The spacing was wrong for a standard ambush line; they were staggered vertically, using the conduit boxes for elevation. Kyle's neuretics mapped it without asking: ground level, waist height, shoulder height. They'd done this before.

Ms. Tanaka's breathing had gone thin.

Kyle moved her into the maintenance alcove—eight inches deep, exactly as he'd measured—and positioned himself in the mouth of it. The corridor's geometry was his now. It was also theirs. The question was which one of them understood it better.

"Don't move," he said. "Don't make sound."

The first two came from the east entrance behind them, cutting off retreat. The sound of their boots told him everything: heavy, deliberate, meant to be heard. Psychological weight. They expected him to run forward into the narrower trap.

He didn't move.

The ones ahead came next—three of them, spreading across the corridor width. The lead one had something in his hands. Not a gun. Something that made a small electrical hum when it powered up. A taser. Expensive. Mil-spec. The kind that worked through most body armor if you got close enough.

"Kyle Corbin," the lead one called. His voice was flat, professional. "Step out of the alcove. Hands visible. We're not here for the woman."

Kyle's hand was already on Cacophony's grip.

"They're not here for you," he said quietly to Ms. Tanaka. "That's what frightens me."

He stepped out of the alcove with both hands empty, moving slow, keeping his shoulders loose. The lead one—mid-forties, augmented across the left side of his face, military bearing—relaxed slightly. That was the tell. They'd been briefed to expect compliance.

Kyle let them think they'd won that much.

The one with the taser moved in first, closing the distance to strike range. Kyle was still six feet away. The corridor was wide enough for two to flank, which meant the third one was already angling for his left side, coming around the conduit box.

*Three seconds to contact.*

Kyle's neuretics weren't predicting. They were reading. The lead one's weight was shifting. The flanker on the left was committed to the approach. The one with the taser had already decided the entry angle.

Kyle moved backward—one step, clean, creating distance. The taser operator overcommitted, reaching for space that wasn't there anymore. His follow-through took him past Kyle's centerline.

Kyle's left arm came up and drove backward, two-handed, into the taser operator's throat.

Not a strike. A lever. The man's own momentum did the work. He went down hard, gasping, the taser skittering across the freight rail and into the dark.

The flanker on the left was already swinging—a baton, telescoping, mean. Kyle pivoted and caught it on his forearm. Pain lit up his wrist seams. The bonding medium screamed. He pushed through it and pivoted again, using the baton's momentum to drive the flanker into the conduit box behind him.

The lead one was moving now, pulling something from his jacket.

Kyle had no time to see what. He was already moving toward the maintenance alcove, toward Ms. Tanaka, toward the eight inches of space that would funnel their approach into single file. The lead one fired—a tranquilizer gun, not lethal—but Kyle was already moving lateral, and the dart hissed past his shoulder and into the corridor dark.

Behind them, the retreat team from the east entrance was closing fast. Kyle could hear their boots on the rail, could hear the radio chatter, could hear the professional precision of people who'd done this a hundred times.

He grabbed Ms. Tanaka's arm and moved deeper into the corridor, past the maintenance alcove, toward the low gap under the freight track. It was eighteen inches of clearance. Maybe less. It was the only play left.

"Under," he said. "Go."

She didn't hesitate. She dropped and rolled under the track, and Kyle followed, pulling himself flat against the floor, the freight rail's edge scraping his shoulder. Above them, the lead one was already in the alcove, already calling orders, already understanding that the geometry had shifted.

Kyle's hand found the anchor bolt on the corridor's east wall—the first of five, three feet apart. He pulled himself toward it, Ms. Tanaka already moving ahead in the crawl space, already understanding that the only way out was forward.

The lead one dropped to his knees and peered under the track.

Kyle was already moving. He reached the anchor bolt and used it to swing himself out from under the rail, coming up on his feet in the narrow space between the track and the corridor's west wall. It was maybe three feet of clearance. It was a choke point. It was a place where they could only come at him one at a time, which was the only advantage he had left.

"Go," he told Ms. Tanaka. "The dock is two kilometers. You don't wait. You don't stop. You run until you're in the water."

"You're not—"

"I'm holding the corridor," he said. "Go."

She ran.

Kyle turned to face the space under the rail. The lead one was already there, already reaching, already understanding that Kyle had traded everything—distance, escape routes, the possibility of retreat—for this one narrow moment where the geometry was his and his alone.

Kyle drew Silence.

The blade came free in the dark with the sound of steel leaving leather. In the alcove behind the lead one, the other operators froze. They'd been briefed on a runner. They hadn't been briefed on a blade.

"Next one who comes under," Kyle said quietly, "I cut the rail. The rail weighs three tons. The freight coupling will drop. You'll have maybe two seconds to move."

He wasn't lying. The coupling was old. The bolts were corroded. One good strike on the right angle and the whole thing would come down.

The lead one pulled back out from under the rail.

Kyle held Silence steady, blade at rest, and listened to the radio chatter above him. Orders being called. Positions being reset. A tactical assessment happening in real time.

Then: "Stand down. She's not the objective. Let the runner go."

The relief in the corridor was immediate and absolute. Boots retreating. Radios going quiet. The small hum of the taser operator's equipment powering down.

Kyle didn't move. He kept Silence ready. He kept his breathing level. He kept his eyes on the space under the rail until he heard the east entrance door close, until he heard the engines start outside, until he heard the vehicles pull away into the rain.

Only then did he move.

He came out from under the rail and ran for the dock, following Ms. Tanaka's path, following the smell of rust and water. Behind him, the corridor settled back into its dark. The lumen mouse on the conduit rail had stopped glowing.

Kyle didn't mark it this time. He was already moving into whatever came next.

[Beat 408]
The first man from the east came in with a short blade and the low crouch of someone good had trained. There were seven feet of corridor behind him, his people stacked single file, the next man six steps back and waiting his turn. Kyle read the crouch and the low ceiling, stepped inside the man's commitment, and opened a long cut down the outside of his forearm, wrist to elbow — the cut you make when you need a hand to stop. The hand stopped. The blade rang off the freight rail somewhere east. The man stumbled back into the chest of the one behind him, and the two of them spent two seconds untangling. Two seconds was enough.

The second man tried to come around the first instead of through him. It was the smart read. But the narrow lane pushed him into the mouth of the maintenance alcove, and the alcove did what Kyle had counted on it to do — it caught the man's left shoulder on the door frame at the wrong moment, half a step before his weight was set. Kyle closed the gap, steered the stumble, and the man's own mass threw him sideways into the conduit boxes. The impact was hard.

Two conduit anchors sat at chest height on the east wall. Kyle already had a hand on the third when the third and fourth men came through.

They'd adjusted: one high, one low, taking everything the space would give them. Kyle caught the low man's weapon wrist at the seam where an aftermarket brace stood proud of the joint, and the hand gave up the knife and the brace together. His weight was already going onto the conduit anchor. He pulled his feet off the floor for the half-second it took the high blade to pass beneath them, then came down on the high man's leading knee. Something that was not the floor took the weight. The high man went down and stayed down.

Four men east of center. Three more behind them, sorting themselves out.

He was counting, and the counting was the only thing left of him that felt like his own. Everything else — the wrist locks, the geometry, the twenty minutes he'd spent walking this corridor at noon — that was product, built by other hands, running on schedule. The count was his. He kept it because if he stopped keeping it, he wasn't sure what was left standing there instead of him.

Behind him, west, boots on wet composite. He didn't turn. He didn't have to — the junction box at his back would tell him the moment weight came off it.

"Six," Ms. Tanaka said, small, pressed into the corner where he'd put her. Not a question. A count of her own, offered because she had nothing else to give him.

He didn't answer. He put his shoulder into the fifth man and felt his rib file a complaint he had no room to hear.

The corridor rang once — the junction coupling, twenty feet west, struck hard by something moving too fast in the dark. Not footsteps. Something bigger, coming down the same six feet of lane the fourteen had already spent, and coming into it from the wrong direction to be one of theirs.

[Beat 409]
The thing that rang the junction coupling was not a seventh man from the west.

It came into the light-spill of Kyle's own peripheral read — a shape moving low and wrong-fast, four points of contact, chassis sound instead of breath — and hit the sixth man from behind before Kyle had finished placing his weight. The sixth man went down without a sound. Whatever hit him didn't stop moving.

Kyle didn't have a name for it yet. He had geometry: it was coming east, down the center, at a speed that made the fourteen humans in the corridor look like they were standing still.

He put himself between it and Ms. Tanaka's corner without deciding to.

It resolved out of the dark six feet from him — quadruped, service-chassis gray, panels stripped to bare struts on one flank, the kind of frame that used to walk a rail line checking bolt torque and had been doing something else for a long time now. No eyes. A sensor cluster where eyes would go, tracking him, tracking her, weighing which one cost less to remove first.

It came for him first. That told him something. He filed it and didn't have time to read it twice.

He took the hit on the flat of the blade instead of the edge, turning Silence to spare the metal and his own wrist, and the impact still drove him back a full step into the man he'd already put down at the conduit box. His feet found nothing solid. He went down on one knee, and the knee that took the floor was the one over the rib that had already filed its complaint. The complaint stopped being a complaint. It became a fact, bright and total, that sat behind his sternum and did not move when he told it to.

He came up anyway. Coming up wasn't a choice. It was the only direction the body still knew.

The thing reset for another pass, faster this time — it had learned his guard in one exchange, the way good hardware does — and Kyle understood, with the flat clean certainty of a man reading his own gauge, that the next one would not be a rib. The next one would be worse, and there was no clever geometry in this corridor that made that not true. Fourteen men. One machine that moved like nothing human. Ms. Tanaka in the corner with six feet of packed dark between her and either.

*Every trick you have was built by someone else's hands. This is the one that's yours: you're still standing.*

He set his feet on the wet composite, found the count again — four down east, one down west, one thing that didn't count as a man at all — and went to meet it.

[Beat 410]
Kyle stood in the machine-oil dark. He didn't tally them. The corridor hadn't given him the room to, and it didn't matter now. He'd won — fourteen people down against the walls and the floor, the dock still in reach, Ms. Tanaka still pressed to the junction boxes. The win had a price, and the price was on his body. The forearm bled through the field strip he'd cinched tight with his teeth in a half-second between the fifth man and the sixth. The rib had a hard opinion about breathing that he wouldn't be able to ignore for long. His neuretics offered him a damage readout. He left it unread — not because he didn't want to know, but because knowing the exact numbers would only slow him down.

"Ms. Tanaka."

"I'm here," she said, from the junction boxes. Her voice had steadied, the way a voice does when the worst thing has passed and the next one hasn't come yet.

"We're moving. Same position. Stay close."

She came off the wall. In the dark she found his right shoulder by feel and fell into step behind it, easy about it. Nine years at someone's counting desk, he thought, teaches you how to stay near the person still standing.

He got her out the west end at 01:03.

[Beat 411]
The dock was a Ferryside loading pier: lake water and compressed fuel, and under the eastern breakwater the low hum of the Pulse, its 19Hz signature buzzing in his back teeth and in the wet wood of the bollards. Dock 14-C was a third-tier berth — a mid-range cargo carrier on a mixed freight run. The purser at the gate was a small man with a clipboard who had worked enough 03:00 shifts to have opinions about paperwork and none about reasons.

Ms. Tanaka stopped at the dock gate.

She turned and looked at Kyle's forearm, where the field strip had soaked dark at the edges, and then at his face.

"The contract," she said. "Whatever they paid you—"

"Was fine," Kyle said. "Walk in."

She hesitated. She was the kind of person who kept someone's books for nine years and then decided, one Tuesday, that she was done. A decision like that carries a weight that isn't only fear.

"I should have left three years ago," she said.

"Probably," Kyle said. "Walk in anyway."

She looked at the saya, and at the field strip, and at his face one more time. Then she walked in. The purser checked her boarding chit, noted the time — 03:34 — and closed the gate.

The ship ran its pre-cast sequence at 03:40 exactly. Kyle watched the running lights pull off the dock face, the carrier swinging its bow south toward the open lake, the flour on Ms. Tanaka's sleeves gone into the dark of the transit berths below with her.

He stood at the rail two minutes. Long enough to be sure. The beacon Pixel had wired under his battery tray had already pinged at 01:11 — she'd know where the bike was, and she'd work out the rest. He called for a medic pickup on the work channel and sat down on a bollard to wait.

His terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES THE CONTRACT WAS MISPRICED BY THE MARKET.
CLIENT HAS ADJUSTED YOUR HAZARD SCHEDULE. RETROACTIVELY.

He read it twice. He put the terminal away.

[Beat 412]
The medic came at 04:15 — a quiet woman named Rue, with a field kit and the easy economy of someone who worked the dock district's early hours and had long since stopped asking about corridors. She cleaned the forearm and re-stripped it. The cut ran two inches along the inside, deep but clean, the kind that would stay sore for a couple of weeks. She confirmed the rib was cracked and not broken, taped it firm, and handed him a small packet of painkillers he wouldn't take before a job and could take now.

"You'll favor the arm," she said.

"I know," Kyle said.

"Two weeks minimum. More if you don't favor it."

"I know that too."

She packed her kit. He paid her rate plus the dock-hour premium, exact. She left without asking what the corridor had looked like. Dock medics learn that early and keep it their whole careers.

The rib would be the louder bill. The forearm would stiffen by morning, which meant his draw would be slower for two weeks, which meant every job in that window was now a different job than the one he'd planned for. He sat on the bollard, breathing careful around the rib, and thought about Golan.

He'd passed Golan's block on the way to the dock — the parts dealer on Leavitt who'd sold him mesh-repair supplies for seven years. Golan kept a second-floor shop with a yellow security light over the door that Kyle could read from a quarter mile off. He'd looked up out of habit on the approach, and the yellow light was off. Through the glass of the street-level lobby, Golan was standing at the inner door, watching him. When Kyle tried the lobby handle — just the lobby, just the handle — Golan looked at him for three seconds and did not move.

One closed door. And it wouldn't stop at one.

Fourteen Lotus crew — salaried, professional — had been hurt badly in a dark choke over one counting-room clerk with flour on her sleeves. Lotus would collect for that, slowly, through every vendor and carrier and parts dealer who had a standing arrangement with them and would rather close a door than explain an exception. Kyle had spent eleven years building those arrangements into something he leaned on. Now they'd lean back.

He sat on the bollard and waited to find out how much of him would be left in the morning.

[Beat 413]
The lake was grey, the dawn still an hour out. South of the breakwater, the carrier's running light shrank to a point, then to nothing.

Kyle sat on the bollard a while longer.

Nine years at a counting desk. A decision like that isn't only fear — it's a woman who woke up one Tuesday and decided the numbers she'd been asked to keep clean were dirtier than she could carry anymore. He'd read a version of that decision on his own ledger more times than he'd admit to Rue or to anyone with a needle and thread. *You made yourself the corridor so she wouldn't have to be.* He didn't let the thought finish. He stood instead, favoring the rib, and the standing hurt more than the sitting had.

The Continuity Office would have a file open on this by breakfast — some clerk logging a transit-berth boarding at 03:34, cross-referencing it against fourteen Lotus casualties two blocks inland, and deciding whether the correlation was worth a flag. He didn't know that. He knew only that the yellow light over Golan's shop was off, and that the light being off was its own kind of paperwork.

The gate at 14-C had already reset for the next boarding call. No one there remembered Ms. Tanaka's name, or needed to. That was the whole point of a clean exit — the door closes, and the world downstream of the door doesn't know there was ever a woman standing in it with flour on her sleeves and a decision she'd finally made.

He didn't tally what it cost him. The rib did that arithmetic on its own, every time he breathed.

Golan's door stayed shut in his mind's eye a beat longer than it should have. He put it down — not solved, just set aside, the way you set aside a blade you can't sharpen standing in the rain — and started walking back toward the bike, and toward whatever waited for him now that Lotus knew his name attached to their bruises.

## The Narrows

[Beat 414]
On the eighteenth day Kyle went to see the parts man on Ashland about a throttle cable. The cable on the bike had stretched twelve millimeters at the barrel end. He'd been nursing it for three weeks and was done nursing it.

He'd bought from Cho on Ashland for six years. The man sourced Axiom-era hardware out of a storefront the size of a wide closet, sold nothing he couldn't hold up to the light, and had never once been out of anything Kyle needed. The stretch was survivable on surface streets, but it put a half-second of slack between what he asked the bike to do and what it did. In a corridor, that half-second could get him killed.

"Throttle cable," Kyle said.

Cho was already moving. He opened the first drawer, held it to the light, closed it. Opened a second. His hands slowed. He opened a third, stood with his back to Kyle for a moment that went three seconds too long, and turned around wearing the face of a man who'd rehearsed an apology until it came out flat.

"Throttle cable," Cho said. "I had some."

"You always have some."

"I'm currently out." He gestured at nothing. "I can check with the Damen yard."

Behind his shoulder, the third drawer was still open an inch. The label was in Cho's own hand — the cable spec, Kyle's spec, written there because Kyle had needed it often enough that Cho had labeled the drawer to save time. The drawer was not empty. Kyle could see the shape of coiled cable through the gap.

"Thanks," Kyle said, and walked out. There was nothing in the conversation worth finishing.

He rode home with the slack still in the cable. The half-second was still there.

[Beat 415]
The carrier who ran his packages was a woman named Freya. She worked out of the Bucktown freight level and hadn't been late once in four years. The next morning, at 07:00, she stopped answering. Not a queue. Not a delay. Her terminal took his reads and never delivered them, the way a door takes a knock and never opens.

He had a job going that week — a skip-trace in the Pilsen corridor, a client sitting on it, Φ40 on the back end if the documentation landed before a civil filing deadline. He spent two hours routing around Freya, through her backup and through the Loop carrier that Ria used. The Loop carrier told him, politely, that she was running at capacity. He sent the documentation by a walk-courier service on Halsted for a Φ12 surcharge, and it arrived twenty minutes past the filing window. The client paid the base fee and declined the back end. That was their right.

Pixel sat at the far end of his table, a casing half-open, her tools fanned out. She asked, without looking up, if he'd tried the backup.

"Lost twelve on the courier," Kyle said. "Forty on the filing. Fifty-two total."

She set down her loupe.

"How many doors?" she asked.

"Ashland is one. Freya is two. I found four more this morning — fixers who aren't returning calls. A rigger named Goss who normally takes anything with a fee."

"Goss." The word had a flat edge. She'd used Goss twice and found him solid. "That's deliberate?"

"Yes."

The kettle went. She filled both cups and set his down, handle first, and went back to the casing. Neither of them said the thing they both understood: it had started, they were inside it, and the only question left was how far it would go.

[Beat 416]
He went through the rest of the list that afternoon, in order, the way he checked anything he needed to trust. Six more names. Three didn't answer at all — not busy, not away, just gone, their terminals returning the polite silence of a line that had been quietly retired. Two answered and found reasons: a schedule conflict that hadn't existed yesterday, a supplier problem that wouldn't specify which supplier. The sixth picked up, recognized his voice, and hung up without a word — which told him more than any of the others had, because silence chosen on purpose reads different from silence that just happens.

He sat with the six names crossed out and did the arithmetic he didn't want to do. Cho. Freya. Goss. Three more this afternoon. Nine doors, and every one of them closed by somebody who'd never once had to explain themselves to Kyle, because they didn't answer to him. They answered to whoever was calling in favors faster than he could spend them.

Whoever it was hadn't come for him directly. Not yet. They were taking the ground out from under him first, one contact at a time, the way you starve a fire by pulling the wood before you ever have to fight the flame.

[Beat 417]
On the nineteenth morning the crew's logbook had a new entry.

08:44 — KID ON THE STOOP. DRY COAT. CAR MONEY. ASKED FOR BOSS. HANDED OVER AN ENVELOPE AND LEFT. DID NOT TAKE A DUMPLING (OFFERED). SUSPICIOUS.
NOTE FROM RAFTERS: DREW HIS FACE. FOR THE FILE. VERY UNMEMORABLE FACE. THIS IS SUSPICIOUS.

The envelope was heavy card stock, the kind that costs more than whatever is written inside. Within it was a cream rectangle: one hand-brushed line above a stamped blossom — five petals, open, no name.

BRING THE SWORD.

Below the blossom, an address in the Narrows and a time. 20:00.

Kyle set it on the table beside Sable's card. The two of them made a small pile he didn't like the look of. He went to find the sword instead — the summons could wait until he'd confirmed the thing was even still his to bring.

The locker under the floorboards was empty. Not forced, not disturbed — empty, the felt lining pressed flat where the blade had lain, as if nothing had ever weighed on it. He knelt there longer than he needed to, running his thumb along the seam, and the crew's chatter in the front room went on without him, ignorant. Someone with a very unmemorable face had known exactly where to look, and had come and gone before the eighteenth morning ever started. The card on the table wasn't an invitation. It was a receipt. Whoever wrote BRING THE SWORD already had it, and wanted to see if Kyle would show up empty-handed and lie, or show up empty-handed and beg — and he had no way to tell which answer got the crew killed.

He went to find clean clothes.

[Beat 418]
The Narrows announced itself by what it didn't have.

Every streetlight worked. Kyle counted the first three, then stopped, because the rhythm never broke. In West Town you learned the dead lights by season — the black stretch on Milwaukee, the dark third post the block had quietly routed its foot traffic around since last autumn. Here the lights ran even and unbroken, every one of them, and the steadiness of it put something cold up his spine. Not a threat. The feeling of a place that had been kept, carefully, for a long time, by someone who didn't need to say so.

He was here for one thing: to reach the arcade address, find the woman Lotus called the Narrows' bookkeeper, and walk out with her name on his side of the ledger before the night shift changed. Do that, and West Town ate for a month. Miss it, and he'd made the trip for nothing.

The gutters were clear. No tags on the support pillars. The corners were staffed by people who stood the way staff stand, not sentinels — they watched without making a show of watching, took up space without guarding it, marked him on the way in and let their eyes drift back to the middle distance. Nobody begged. Nobody moved at odd angles.

He found the address two blocks in: a covered arcade between two buildings, open at both ends, roofed in mesh strung with grow-strips close enough to touch. In steel collars bolted to the uprights, eleven cherry trees grew.

He stopped.

They were in bloom — white going to a pink with blood in it, not the tired pink of forced spring stock but a deliberate color, the kind it takes years of breeding to hold in the wrong month. Lights buried in the collars threw the glow up through the roots, catching each blossom from below. Loose petals lay on the wet concrete in small, exact clusters. He stood with petals settling on his coat. The trees were engineered and expensive, paid for with every tariff Lotus had charged the Narrows since someone planted the first collar. They were also beautiful. Both were true.

Six children ran circuits under the arcade, screaming on the inhale at the pitch of a body moving faster than it can hold. Nobody hushed them.

Then the staff at the far end folded in, and the way through the arcade stopped being a way.

They didn't rush him. That was the trouble. Four of them peeled off their corners and drifted into the open mouth of the arcade the same unhurried way they'd watched him come in — not a wall, just a narrowing, bodies filling the space where the path had been. One of the children scooped up mid-run and set on a hip, out of the lane, casual as clearing a table. The screaming didn't stop. That was worse, somehow: nothing here treated this as an event.

The one in front had her hands in her coat pockets and no weapon showing, which told him more than a weapon would have. "You're early," she said. "Bookkeeper doesn't take walk-ins, and she doesn't take West Town at all. Somebody sold you a name that isn't for sale." She tilted her head at the trees, at him standing in the fallen petals. "You can go back the way you came while the light's still good. Or you can wait for the shift to change and explain yourself to the people who don't ask twice."

Behind him, unhurried, two more corners came off their posts.

Go back and he'd made the trip for nothing — West Town went hungry, and Lotus had sent him into a door that was never open? Push forward and there was no forward; the arcade had closed like a fist that had known his shape before he'd stepped inside. The shift changed in minutes either way, and both of the choices she'd offered him were the same choice: leave with nothing.

Petals kept coming down. Nobody hushed the children.

[Beat 419]
The ramen-ya was eight stools and a cedar counter and a door that stood open.

He counted the stools on the way in. The cedar was hand-planed and gone gold from years of handling. Behind it the cook worked with the tight economy of a man who'd shed every wasted motion long ago. Four of the other stools were taken: a man in his forties with a collapsed baton at his hip, a woman with a vibro-edge unit in a shoulder rig, a younger man Kyle read as wired by the way he held his neck, and an empty jacket at the far end that had left a cup and a short blade on the counter beside it.

Weapons worn openly. Nothing checked at the door but behavior.

Kyle hung his coat on the hook at the entrance — the only hook, set there by someone who understood guests — and sat on the last open stool. The cook looked at him once, turned to the pot, and started building a bowl. Kyle hadn't ordered. The cook didn't ask.

The bowl came in three stages. The broth first: the color of good age, smelling of something started days ago and tended since. Then the noodles, hand-pulled, dropped in with just enough time left to finish cooking in the broth. Then the fat, rendered thin and even, a bright lens across the surface. From somewhere under the counter the cook set down a half-round of soft-boiled egg, split with the knife held sideways so the yolk stayed whole.

Kyle ate the first mouthful.

He understood at once what the bowl was for. Not hospitality, exactly — an argument, made in fat and salt and twenty years of practice. The argument was: we make things correctly here. That was probably the whole point of it.

He was most of the way through when the door changed.

The open frame filled without the light changing — someone standing in it who knew how to stand so the light didn't. Kyle didn't turn. He watched the cook instead, and the cook's hands, which had not stopped once since he sat down, stopped now. The bright economy went out of them. That told Kyle everything the door didn't.

Then the empty jacket at the far end wasn't empty; the owner had come back from wherever he'd been and was already reaching for the short blade, and the man with the collapsed baton was on his feet with the wall at his back, and the wired kid had turned his whole body toward Kyle — not toward the door.

Toward Kyle.

He'd read the room wrong. He'd counted the stools and the weapons and the exits and he'd missed the only thing that mattered, which was that every person in here had known he was coming, and had ordered him a bowl, and had let him finish most of it first. The cook set the knife down flat on the cedar, well out of Kyle's reach, and stepped back from the counter, and did not meet his eyes.

Kyle's coat was on the hook by the door. The door was the only way out. And the door was where the standing man was.

[Beat 420]
The Branch Manager came through the doorway like a man who had walked this route for years and didn't need to announce it. Umbrella furled and tucked under his arm. Mid-sixties. A suit with no concession to fashion — not old-fashioned, not plain, just chosen once by a man who understood fabric and had never needed to think about it again. He was half a head shorter than Kyle, and he had the stillness of someone who had never needed to take up space to fill a room.

Everyone at the counter got an inch and a half taller when he came in.

Not in any way you could put a number to. The body knew it before the mind caught up: the man who ran this territory had arrived, and the room was better for it. He sat at the empty jacket's stool, claimed his cup, and drank from it like a man picking up a sentence he'd stepped away from.

He looked at Kyle's face.

"You took the clerk out," the Branch Manager said. "Fourteen people in that corridor. Our people. Several of them went home the worse for it."

Kyle waited. His ribs ached when he shifted.

"The contract was legitimate," the Branch Manager said. "Your conduct was correct. Our crew engaged first." He turned his cup once in both hands. "We pay for what we break. It's most of what we are. The hold lifted this evening — the seven doors, the carrier on the Spine, the parts man on Ashland." He paused. "Cho is easily embarrassed about these things. He has the cable for you. With apologies, priced at list. The apologies are real. The pricing is how we mean them."

Kyle ate the last mouthful of the bowl.

"I appreciate it," he said.

"The fifty-two," the Branch Manager said, flat.

Kyle looked at him.

"The filing gap. The courier surcharge. Cho's hold cost you more than he cost you in stock." The Branch Manager set his cup down. "The apology covers the doors. The doors cover everything behind them. Priced at list."

He reached into his coat and set a small envelope on the cedar. Not in Kyle's space. Close enough to mean it.

"Good?" the Branch Manager asked, and looked at the bowl.

"Best in the city."

"That," said the Branch Manager, with the small satisfaction of a man whose point has landed, "is probably why it's the bowl." He put two fingers on the counter's edge, thinking. "I have a second piece of business. Not a condition. The freeze lifts either way."

Kyle waited.

"I'm offering you a spot on payroll. House colors. Infrastructure — parts, carrying, the counters in every territory we hold, a legal team that files for you and bills us. In five years, if the work is what I think it is, a chair at this counter with your name in the wood." He touched the cedar's edge. "The cedar decides, in the end. It keeps certain names."

"No," Kyle said. "I don't wear colors."

The Branch Manager did not look surprised. He looked like a man reaching a conclusion he'd come in expecting.

"The clerk who sat in that seat nine years ago said exactly that," he said. "In exactly that tone. She'd been doing piece work in the Narrows for three years. She said no, I don't wear colors, and then she sat down anyway. It took eleven months and one specific kind of trouble she didn't want to carry alone. She runs the Bucktown counting room now." He picked up his cup. "The offer stands. Standing offers are how we say please."

Kyle looked at the counter. Cedar gone gold with years of handling. He could see where the grain ran different under the finish — the darker sections at the older stools, the pale ones at the new. His stool was neither. Somewhere in the middle.

He understood the offer for what it was. He would come back for the bowl. When he came back, the offer would still be standing, because that was the whole design. The courtesy was the hook, and the hook was the point.

"I'll remember it," Kyle said.

"That's all it asks," said the Branch Manager. He rose, took his cup to the far end of the counter, and the whole room gained its inch and a half again.

[Beat 421]
The lacquered case came up from behind the counter before anyone had said the word sword. The cook set it in front of Kyle, stepped back, and found something to do at the far burner. Inside, on gray felt that matched the locker's, Silence lay exactly as it had left West Town — saya unmarked, edge untouched, nothing about it to say it had crossed the city in someone else's hands.

"Returned," the Branch Manager said, as if the word settled a small invoice. "The borrowing was a question. You answered it by coming."

Kyle took the sword and did not ask what the question had been. The anger he folded flat and put away; it would be useful somewhere else.

The togishi was at the far end of the counter, between the wire's stool and the wall, working the cook's knives.

Kyle hadn't noticed him arrive. Maybe he'd always been there — one of those people who fill a space so completely they're part of the scene before you count them. Small. Ten years older than the Branch Manager. He had the hands of a man whose whole trade was patience. He ran the whetstone down a blade slowly, the way you read something rather than fix it, each pass a question and an answer.

The cook's knives were good blades. The togishi handled them like things meant to outlast him.

Kyle watched a while, because watching was the only polite thing to do.

"Φ1," he said, eventually.

The togishi looked up. He looked at Silence's saya.

"Φ1 for what?" he asked.

"Your read on the blade. One minute."

"Togishi does not work by the minute," the togishi said, and held out his hand.

Kyle paid first, because that was how it was done, and laid Silence across the man's open palms.

The togishi held it without drawing, hands flat, feeling the balance travel through his grip. Then he drew it, slow, and turned it to the light from outside — the cherry-tree light, pink-white through the arcade opening, falling soft on the face of the blade.

He looked at it for a long time.

"Kept correctly," he said. "Good geometry. Good edge. No maker's mark." He turned the blade and studied the back. "No file history. Someone has worked this blade for a long time and left no record of it." He looked up. "A blade with no parents. Either made entirely outside the guild, or made inside it and the papers deliberately destroyed. Those are two different stories."

"Which do you think?" Kyle asked.

"I think it's in good order," the togishi said, and returned it hilt-first. "I also think it's the loneliest piece of steel I've handled in forty years. And I've handled funeral swords."

Kyle took it, sheathed it, and said nothing, because nothing was the right thing to say. He was still learning how to say it well.

The togishi went back to the cook's knife. Kyle paid for the bowl — Φ8, two over the going rate, which was probably also the point — put on his coat, and walked out under the trees.

The petals came down slow and even in the lit air. A child tore past him at a full run, screaming on the inhale, trailing a laugh behind her like a cord she hadn't noticed she was paying out.

[Beat 422]
The city came back one piece at a time: seven counters, one carrier, the parts man on Ashland who'd have the cable waiting in the morning. A third of his working ground open again, paid for in apologies at list price, plus the envelope in his coat that covered the fifty-two.

The cost was a standing offer he'd now have to keep turning down. The Branch Manager hadn't built the courtesy as a courtesy. He'd built it as a room you came back to on your own — a door that stayed open because you were the one who kept opening it.

His terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — STATUS NOTE.
CLIENT ATTEMPTED TO LOCATE THE RAMEN-YA ON THE ASHGRAVE CORRIDOR LEDGER.
CLIENT QUERIED: COUNTER, CEDAR. FEE STRUCTURE. VARIABLE OCCUPANCY.
CLIENT QUERIED: TOGISHI, LICENSED. NARROWS DISTRICT. ONE-TIME SERVICE.
BOTH QUERIES RETURNED: NOT ON LEDGER.
CLIENT IS UNSETTLED. ENJOY THE NOODLES.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT PRICED THE BOWL AT Φ8.
ADDENDUM: STANDARD BOWL, THIS DISTRICT = Φ6.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE DELTA.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT FINDS THE DELTA CORRECT.

Kyle read it twice on the walkway under the last of the trees, petals on the screen, the Pulse humming through the tier below him.

He put the terminal away.

Three blocks out, at the Spine crossing, a woman in a gray work coat spoke low to the man beside her — two syllables, the shape of a name, gone before he could catch it.

The man said: "Assessment pending. Nothing moves until Mira signs off."

Kyle walked past without slowing. Slowing was a tell, and tonight had cost enough already.

The freeze was lifted. The audition still hadn't happened.

He went home under the lights.

## West Town Rain

[Beat 423]
The rain had been settling in since midnight, and by the time Kyle got to the Spine crossing it had the run of the place. He walked instead of calling a car because the cold on his wrist-seams was the only sensation right now that wasn't firmware noise, and the water found the pink bonding-medium lines and the reopened graze above his hip like it had been sent to check on them.

Wood ran straight north. He'd developed a fondness for straight streets two nights back, in the corridor. Straight meant one thing coming at a time instead of everything at once. The rest of the damage kept its own ledger — right grip at ninety-four percent, ribs charging tax on every breath, compute holding twelve percent on the reintegration — and he read it the way he read anything, flat, cataloguing, because turning himself into a checklist was easier than being a man walking home in the rain with a sword he'd almost lost for good and a bowl of noodles costing more than they should.

Somewhere around Ashland, a memory that wasn't his surfaced. Rain on a different street. A door that didn't open the way he expected. He clocked it the way he clocked a targeting ghost — didn't flinch, didn't slow, filed it under *not mine* and kept walking.

*Wonder if the others minded the rain too*, he thought, and folded that away before it could ask to be looked at.

He found five watchers by the time he was two blocks from The Pivot.

One high — third-floor window over the print shop, glass a few degrees too cold to be doing nothing, a warmth behind it that wasn't the building's own. One in the laundromat doorway, weight on the wrong foot in the specific way of a man trying to look like he hadn't been standing there an hour. One at the corner, pretending a dead terminal was interesting. One down the block, far enough back to be the anchor. One on a roofline — he got that one from the rain, the way it fell different where something stood in it.

The sixth position he didn't have. Not having it told him what it was. A runner doesn't wait at the trap. A runner waits at the exit. The sixth was already behind him.

Six positions. One of them built to leave.

He worked the drone into the picture a full block off — the distance the guess needed to be right. Maybe two of them, held back until he stepped into the cross-street where the walls closed the gap. Doorway, corner, anchor: a clean three-point close, straight out of a manual somebody had clearly made him read once, in a life he couldn't source. The roofline was the one that could move if it had to. And the warm window was the one keeping score.

Which meant somebody, somewhere, was grading this.

*None of them got a passing mark,* he thought, and put both hands in his coat pockets before the thought could finish being a thought — left on the mouth of the saya, right closed around nothing, because Cacophony was for when the count came out different than this. He walked into the trap at a normal pace. A man who changes his stride the moment he clocks the surveillance has just told the surveillance everything it needed.

The cross-street smelled of wet concrete and the ghost of a food stall packed up hours ago. A turret cat sat on a window ledge up the block, watching the rain with the particular dedication of something that has genuinely nowhere better to be.

He crossed under the print shop's window without looking at it, which was its own kind of look. The warmth behind the glass didn't move.

He made The Pivot's door in one more block, wet through, ribs arguing the whole way, and did not look back to see whether the sixth position had followed him home or simply confirmed that it didn't need to.

[Beat 424]
The drone dropped at 02:16, sixteen inches short.

Kyle knew what a stun drone at full discharge looked and sounded like. He'd met three, paid for the lesson twice, and the third time had been someone else's problem. This wasn't that. The discharge hit the wet pavement in a cone that died at his boot heel, the arc chasing the surface water and going out. The sound came a half-note low. The light was maybe forty percent of spec. The drone held at ten feet and cycled for a second pass it never made.

A crew that throttles its own emitters isn't trying to drop you. They were testing how he'd react to a charge that looked real and wasn't — and they'd left maybe two seconds between the drone and the first man moving, which meant the test had a clock on his response. Somewhere close a Ghost sat very still, body parked in a doorway or a car, eyes borrowed from the drone, watching his face and his hands.

Kyle didn't move. That was one answer. He tilted his head thirty degrees and looked at the drone, which was the more interesting one.

"Evening?" he asked — to the drone, which couldn't answer, and to the crew, which could.

The corner man came first. Young, quick, and angry the way people get angry at twenty-two when they're loyal and a stranger is studying someone they respect. He had an arm. Not chrome, not aftermarket — the real thing, a full replacement from mid-upper-arm down, the kind the catalogs listed at Φ8,000 in a good year. This one ran higher: secondary augments in the forearm, override arrays, a grip that indexed its own pressure. Kyle saw the maker's seal at the shoulder joint as the kid closed the last ten feet and swung.

KT. Kinetix TerraForm — the market name for the Warptech Systems division that built precision arms for industrial accidents, and for people who wanted to be more than one. The emergency lockout was a three-finger combination on the outside of the wrist. The certification body required it: a manual override a stranger could reach if the wearer went into medical distress. Once the arm was in range, Kyle had a thirty-second window.

He took the swing on his forearm, stepped inside it, wore the bruise he'd expected, and found the lockout.

The arm stopped. Not dropped — locked, mid-swing, fingers splayed, a chrome hand held out like it was offering him something. KT said several words Kyle wouldn't write down, and Kyle said:

"Kinetix TerraForm — that medical lockout is a liability clause, not a warranty gap. You should get Lotus to bill Kinetix for the upgrade. At a minimum."

He let go. The arm unlocked. KT stepped back with the face of a man who's just been told something humiliating, true, and expensive, in that order.

[Beat 425]
Rook came out of the doorway, the approach Kyle had expected, and Rook was exactly what the name promised: broad-shouldered, honest the way real size makes a man honest, moving with the economy of someone who'd spent years not starting fights he couldn't finish. The BCI port sat at his left temple — an older Meridian Conduct unit. Kyle knew them by the housing, a flat gray oval that stood a little proud of the skull. The early Conduct models had a hardware reset built into the outer casing, because the early Conduct models overloaded and needed a physical hand to stop them.

Hardware that protects itself is a rule baked into the certification. A brain interface you could lock with software was one you could lock with hostile software, and hostile software was a thing the 2218 standards body would not allow. So the Conduct had a mechanical failsafe: hit the housing hard enough and it triggered the reset, dropping the wearer into a five-second blank where the body forgot where it was.

Rook was bringing his left arm up to guard, so his left side was closed. That put Kyle on the right — the longer way in, but not by much.

Silence came off the hip for the first time tonight, and some old rule he couldn't name woke up and objected before his hand finished the motion. Draw meant cut. Cut meant something didn't get up again. He'd spent eleven years arguing with that rule and it never once lost cleanly — it just got quieter, the way a man gets quiet when he's decided to wait you out.

Not to cut, then. To use the pommel — 340 grams, with a striking reach Kyle had measured across eleven years of arguments with other people's gear. The pommel found the housing at the angle it needed. Rook blinked twice, stepped left when he'd meant to step right, put a hand out and found the laundromat door instead of Kyle, and sat down with his back against it, working through the reset with his eyes half-focused on a wall that wouldn't hold still.

"Five seconds," Kyle told him. "You're fine."

"Yeah," Rook said, from somewhere inside the blank. "I know."

Silence went back to the hip, and the motion cost more than the draw had — the old rule taking its toll for being ignored, the way it always did, a small flat weight behind the sternum that had nothing to do with the rib. He didn't look at it straight on. He never did. The rib had something to say about the draw and the return, too, and he let both complaints stand in line and moved.

Three down. The corner man's arm still hung locked-then-unlocked at his side, KT's warranty clause doing more work tonight than the man himself. Rook sat against the laundromat door, present tense but not participating. That left the roofline, the anchor down the block, and the sixth position — the one built to leave, the one he'd never had a location for, only a certainty.

Kyle didn't look up at the roofline. Looking up was an answer, same as changing his stride would have been. He kept his eyes on the street in front of him, on the rain finding the gaps between the streetlight cones, and did the math the flat way, the checklist way, because the other way — the way that wanted to ask why a five-person test crew was throttling its own drones and grading his reactions like a syllabus — was not a place he had time to stand still in tonight.

*Somebody's keeping a scorecard,* he thought, *and I still don't know whose class this is.*

He put that away with the rest of it and kept walking toward The Pivot's door, twelve percent compute and a ninety-four percent grip and a rib that had opinions, carrying all of it the way he carried everything else that wasn't his to put down yet.

[Beat 426]
Nines was the one Kyle had marked last, which was Nines's whole job. Industrial wrist brace, pneumatic assist — the freight-yard kind, built for sustained load, the kind that starts having opinions about direction when the pneumatic channel pressurizes wrong. Locked to a single axis. Catch the lock while the pneumatic fights the frame, and the brace's own force does the work for you.

The anchor had held through the drone and both entries, which was professional. Nines waited until Kyle was busy on the right side, then came across the street at a pace that accounted for the rain — careful — leading with the braced arm — honest.

Kyle let him commit to the extension, took the inside line, and used Nines's own weight to fold the braced arm up behind his back. The pneumatic fought the frame. The frame locked. Nines took a close look at the whole surface of the street for about four seconds while Kyle held the brace at the angle that kept the joint arguing with itself.

"Locked out," Kyle said, and let go. The brace cycled and came free. Nines stayed down a moment, one knee on the wet pavement, and said nothing, which was the professional thing to do.

Four locked, dropped, or walking away confused, and none of them bleeding on his account. Eleven years of the same math and it still came out clean, and some nights that felt like proof of something and some nights it just felt like a number he hadn't broken yet. Tonight he didn't have the spare compute to sort which.

The drone had gone up for altitude. The rooftop position hadn't moved, because the rooftop was the override and knew it wasn't needed. Behind Kyle, the sixth man — the runner — had the easiest task on the street: wait, then carry the news. Kyle turned his back to him on purpose, which was the right signal.

*You've earned the exit. Take it.*

He heard Dex's footsteps go east at a run — the way a young man runs when he's been handed the best part of any job, the part where he gets to be the one who says what happened.

Four for four, and nobody upstream had blinked yet. That was the part that itched. A crew this careful, throttling its own gear, grading him like a transcript — somebody had built this test to fail gracefully, which meant somebody had already priced in that he'd walk through it.
