The scorecard wasn't for tonight. It was for whoever read it after.

[Beat 427]
# BEAT: The Audition Concludes

The thermal window on the third floor opened at 02:23.

Mira came down — not through the building's front door but by the fire access on the east side — and she came alone, which meant she'd watched the whole thing and decided it was finished. She was 130 feet out when Kyle first read her clearly: medium height, gear that was functional first and functional second, a carry stance that said the piece on her hip was neither a prop nor an afterthought.

She stopped at twenty-five feet. Ordinary talking distance for someone not trying to prove she didn't care about distance.

"Kinetix's lockout is contractor-certified," she said, no preamble, because she'd been watching and what got said was part of what she was grading. "The arm costs Φ11,200 with the augment array."

"I know the price," Kyle said.

"I know you know." Her voice had the tightness of someone revising an estimate she hadn't expected to revise — not distress. Different things. "Rook's port is a Meridian Conduct first-series. They put out the mechanical-reset advisory in 2221. He's been meaning to get the housing seated deeper."

"Add the seating charge to the bill."

She looked at him a long moment, the way you look at something behaving a little differently than the model said it would.

Then she drew and fired. One round, twenty-five feet, into the upper chest — because she'd read the corridor reports the way any professional reads someone's recent work, and she knew what was under his coat and what it would cost.

The mesh took it. The impact spread full-contact across his upper chest, the way a shoulder meets a door that isn't going to open: both sides came away informed. Kyle took three breaths, slower than usual. The rib made itself heard.

Mira watched him keep walking. One step, two, the stride unchanged. She dropped the weapon to her thigh, then lowered it to the wet pavement and left it there, muzzle toward the drain.

"That was an audition," she said.

"I worked that out," Kyle said.

"Cacophony has six rounds. You didn't pull it."

"The audition was for the blade and the body. Six rounds, zero fired. I'll note it for the record."

She almost smiled. It didn't quite finish. "Freelance roster, West Town and adjacent. Lotus-territory contracts through your fixer — the Húlijing outfit, I assume. Carrier rates, standard."

"No further crews."

"No further crews," she agreed, and that was the line that meant they were actually negotiating and not just reading terms off a card. She had the authority to give it, and she'd expected him to ask. "The arrangement is provisional. Sixty-day reassessment. Standard for a new roster."

"Your crew's hardware goes on Lotus's account," Kyle said. "The arm, the port, the brace. List price. You billed them to an audition — they walk home whole, or there's no arrangement."

The tightness in her voice shifted once. Not surprise. Recalculation.

"I can authorize the arm," she said. "The port and the brace I have to clear."

"Clear them. Tonight. I'll be at Chen's at seven-thirty for the confirmation."

"They'd have shot you for free, you know?" Mira asked — and that was the one human line, the one that wasn't the job, the one she'd carried the whole way through and decided she was allowed to say now that the terms were closing.

"I know," Kyle said. "Tell Lotus their hardware is better than their audit of its own weak points. That's a courtesy, not an invoice."

She reached into the inner pocket of her coat and set the roster marker on the planter rim to her right: a lacquered oval, deep red, a gold five-petal blossom pressed into its face, the size of a thumb and heavier than a thing that size had any business being. She picked her piece up off the pavement, cleared it, holstered it, and turned to go. Three steps. Then, over her shoulder, into the rain, without looking back:

"The Narrows desk bought your file last year, freelancer. You should ask the stationer who else subscribes."

Her footsteps went north, and the bracket came apart: Rook walking off his reset in a slow circle, KT flexing the arm through its range and cursing the manufacturer under his breath, Nines running the brace through two full cycles to make sure the pneumatic had reset. Professionals writing up their after-action. Kyle stood on the wet cross-street with the lacquered marker in one hand and a bruise across his chest that was going to have plenty to say over the next three days, and watched them all go.

The turret cat on the window ledge hadn't moved. It had the patience of something that had been watching long before Kyle showed up and would go on watching long after he left.

He took stock. A third of the city formally open again, carrier rates, one lacquered marker that weighed more than it should — set against sixty days on a reassessment clock, one mesh bruise, and a name in the Narrows subscription list he'd have to do something about. One thing still open: confirm the hardware authorization, seven-thirty, Chen's counter.

He took the long way home.

He put the terminal away and walked the last four blocks with the Pulse humming up through the concrete, the turret cats watching from their ledges, the rain making its arrangements with the city's lights. He thought about the Narrows desk. About a man with half-glasses and clean hands and a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED. About the fact that there was a second subscriber now.

The rib had opinions about the pace. Kyle let it talk.

That was tomorrow's problem.

## The Axiom Yard

[Beat 429]
Pixel knocked on his door. That had happened four times in four years, and it always meant the world had changed shape in some way she'd come to explain.

She had a tablet under her arm and her field coat on — the one she wore to jobs, not to the bench — and she walked past him into 2F and set the tablet on his kitchen counter, where the kettle should have been.

"I have a contract," she said. "I'm crewing it. I need muscle that listens, and you're the only muscle I know whose listening I've personally calibrated."

On the tablet, in someone's shaky handheld video, a machine the size of a four-story building was eating a row house on the Ashgrave fringe. Eating was the word. It took the structure down a bite at a time, unhurried, and behind it the rubble of the last block stood in three neat sorted piles — ferrous, mineral, everything else.

"That's an Axiom D-class," Pixel said. "Demolition and reclamation automaton. It woke up nine days ago, it's very good at its job, and its job is now four hundred feet from two thousand people who live in the direction it's chewing."

Kyle watched the machine take a chimney off a brownstone with the care of something that meant to file the bricks separately. "Whose is it?"

"Nobody's. Axiom Industrial died thirty years ago. No owner, no kill-codes, no support line." She tapped the tablet. "Arcturus left a cone. The residents pooled what the fringe could pool: Φ312, held in a biscuit tin by a woman named Auntie Som, who sent the video to a parts man, who sent it to me — because everyone in the salvage trade knows the only person in the GLMZ who still speaks Axiom bus protocol like a living language works at a bench in West Town."

"Three hundred and twelve?" Kyle asked.

"Split six ways, it's insulting. I'm taking it anyway, and so are you."

"I know."

"You haven't heard the plan."

"I've heard the pay," Kyle said. "The plan's not going to make it worse."

He needed to catch Pixel before she got clear of West Town and get a straight answer out of her about why the coat and why now — no more filing it under anything, his or the crew's. He folded the slip into his coat, unanswered, and went down to find the rest of his morning.

Eleven feet at the shoulder. Four legs, two boom arms, a hull of sintered gray printed in one piece — no plates, no rivets, no panel lines, no seams at all. Low black discs studded the hull every foot, and around each disc the rain steamed faintly off the surface.

"You don't touch it. Tonight your job is everything that isn't it."

It kept a schedule. The D-class worked a shift, 0600 to 2200. At 0300 it walked back to the dead Axiom yard and docked against a transformer pylon to charge. Silence, half a beat too long.

"None," Pixel said. "There aren't any left to stand on. That's the point."

[Beat 436]
# The Docking Cycle

The D-class emerged from the rain at 0247 like something remembering a route it had walked so long the walk had worn grooves into its thinking. Four legs, each footfall synced to the others—a rhythm that had probably survived the power-down years intact, stored somewhere in the machine's core the way a body remembers how to swallow.

It didn't hurry. The arc-fence stayed live as it approached, capacitive plates humming their warning song. The machine didn't acknowledge the song. It walked to the transformer pylon the way a man walks to a chair he's sat in every night for thirty years, and it docked with a soft pneumatic sigh.

The fence dropped. The spur went live.

Kyle was positioned on the eastern catframe, sight line down into the coupling well. Pixel was already moving—three quick steps across the spur, handshake jack in her left hand, the other hand already reaching for the bus connector. Her movements were economical. Practiced. The kind of economy that came from running the same sequence so many times in an empty room that the room had worn grooves into her thinking too.

Ninety seconds.

The machine's charging cycle began. A low harmonic hum, the kind that came up through the boots and lived in the back teeth. Kyle's neuretics picked it up and tried to parse it—not a threat signature, not yet, just a machine doing what machines did when they woke up to themselves and found themselves docked and alive and waiting.

Pixel's fingers moved across the bus connector. No hesitation. The handshake initiated.

The machine's sensors came online.

Kyle didn't see it happen—Echo had called it over comms, but the feeling came first, a shift in the machine's posture, a change in the harmonic like it had just remembered it had a job to do. The D-class's chassis rotated three degrees on its docking collar. Not searching. Just... orienting.

Forty-five seconds.

Pixel was inside the bus now, her neuretics bridged to the machine's memory core. Kyle could see her hands moving, could see the way her jaw tightened as data came through—too much data, probably, thirty years of it, all at once.

The machine's boom arms began to move.

Not fast. Just a slow articulation, the left arm rotating down toward the spur where Pixel stood. No targeting sequence, no threat posture—just a machine checking its limbs, making sure they still worked after sleeping.

Sixty seconds.

"Contact," Pixel said, her voice flat and focused. "Memory core is live. Pulling the thirty-year log. Sixty seconds to full dump, but I can work with what I have."

The machine's boom arm continued its arc. Three feet of sintered gray and hydraulic muscle, moving through space like it had all the time in the world.

Kyle's hand found Silence's saya without thinking about it. The blade was no good here—Pixel had made that clear—but the gesture was old enough that his body did it anyway, the way a man reaches for a handrail on stairs he's climbed a thousand times.

The boom arm stopped two feet from Pixel's shoulder.

She didn't look up. Her focus was absolute, her fingers still moving across the handshake interface like she was reading something written in a language only she understood.

Ninety seconds.

"Got it," she said. "Pulling clear."

The machine's arm began to retract.

Kyle exhaled—didn't realize he'd been holding it—and watched Pixel disconnect the handshake jack with the kind of precision that came from knowing exactly how much force a coupling seal could take before it cracked. She turned toward the catframe, already moving, already stepping back toward the spur's edge.

The arc-fence came back online.

It happened between one breath and the next. The capacitive plates hummed back to lethal levels, and the machine's entire hull lit up with the kind of potential energy that made Kyle's neuretics scream. The D-class's chassis rotated back to center, its boom arms settling into neutral position, and then—

It moved.

Not toward Pixel. Not toward Kyle. Toward the coupling well. Toward the transformer pylon where it had just been docked.

The machine executed a perfect reversal, backing away from the spur with the kind of mechanical precision that suggested it had just run through a checklist and found everything in order. It disconnected from the charging collar and began to walk—four legs, synced rhythm, the same groove-worn path it had walked every night for nine days, maybe for thirty years before that.

Heading back out into the rain.

Kyle watched it go, watched the arc-fence stay live in its wake, watched the machine disappear into the dark blocks where the city had been taken apart and laid out like cutlery.

"We clear?" Echo's voice, over comms.

"Clear," Pixel said. She was breathing hard, but her hands were steady as she secured the data core in her jacket. "It never knew we were there."

Kyle looked down at his hand. Still on Silence's saya. He let go and climbed down from the catframe.

The machine had left wet footprints on the concrete. Four legs, synced rhythm. The prints would be gone by morning, washed away by the rain that never stopped falling on this part of the city.

He thought about Pixel in a room since she was nine years old. About the machine that had been walking the same route for thirty years, docking at the same pylon every night, checking the same systems, finding everything in order, and then walking back out again into the rain.

Just like it had for thirty years.

Just like it would tomorrow night, if no one stopped it.

If no one had any reason to stop it.

Kyle climbed down and started moving. The crew was already packing. Pixel had the data secured. The machine was gone.

But the groove-worn path remained, and the rain kept falling, and somewhere in the dark blocks of the disassembled city, something that had learned to be reliable was walking back to its charging station, unaware that tonight had been any different from any other night.

Echo was coming down from the catwalk at a controlled pace, not running, which meant she'd already calculated that running wouldn't help. Stash had the flatbed idling at the gate, engine warm, ready to move. They had maybe a minute before the salvage crew rounded the corner and saw them standing here in the rust and the rain, holding a sword and a burned hand and the knowledge that a machine had tried to die protecting a secret.

"Copy," Pixel said. "We move."

Kyle turned his back on the D-class. The machine was already settling, its systems powering down now that the threat had passed, now that it had done the only thing it could do and found out it wasn't enough. By tomorrow, the salvage crew would find a hull with a glassy scar on one foreleg and a missing disconnect lever, and they'd file a report that would get lost in the Continuity Office's filing system, and no one would ever know why this particular machine had tried to stand up.

He walked toward the flatbed. His neuretics were still rebuilding, still catching up. The count said sixty seconds. The count said the salvage crew was going to see them, and there was no clean way to avoid it, and the only option was to move through it like they belonged here, like they had every right to be leaving the dock at this exact moment.

Furnace was already on the flatbed. Echo was almost there. Gantry released the container's final mooring point and it settled onto the truck bed with a sound like a sigh.

"Forty seconds," Stash said over comms. "They're in the access lane."

Kyle climbed up. His left arm was still numb, but the feeling was starting to come back—pins and needles, the sensation of waking up. His right palm was screaming now, the delayed pain arriving exactly on schedule. He gripped *Silence*'s wrapped cord with his burned fingers and felt the blistered skin split, felt the blood start, felt the blade settle into the muscle memory like it had never left.

The flatbed moved.

The salvage crew came around the corner just as they cleared the gate. Three of them in the lead, carrying tools, heading straight for the dock where the D-class was already dark, already dormant, already just a machine again. They didn't look up. Didn't see the flatbed. Didn't see Kyle standing in the truck bed with a sword and a burned hand and the understanding that some things tried to save themselves, and some things were saved anyway, and the difference was just a matter of timing.

By the time the salvage crew reached the dock, Kyle was already gone.

---

But the count kept running.

Sixty seconds became forty. Forty became twenty. And somewhere in that collapsing window, his neuretics finished their rebuild and delivered the thing they'd been compiling while he moved on pure reflex: the machine's defensive profile, logged and processed. The D-class had learned something in thirty years of standing still. It had learned what fear looked like. It had learned to recognize the moment when standing still stopped being safe.

And it had learned that lesson from something. From someone. From a thousand small moments of pressure and withdrawal, of systems testing boundaries, of noise that shouldn't have been there.

The entity's surveillance geometry. The carousel. The bleeds.

All of it pointing here. All of it pointing at this dock, this machine, this moment when Kyle had to choose between walking away and staying to protect something that was already dead.

He'd stayed. And the machine had noticed.

His palm throbbed against *Silence*'s cord. His shoulder ached where the discharge had traveled through. His left arm was still numb, probably would be for hours, maybe longer. The hardware would repair itself—the Governor would see to that, would pull resources from somewhere else, would make the cost invisible until it wasn't. But the decision he'd just made wasn't hardware-dependent. Wasn't chrome-dependent. Wasn't dependent on anything except the eleven years compressed into muscle and reflex and the simple fact that when something had to be done, his body did it.

The flatbed accelerated toward the Spine corridor.

Kyle sat with his burned hand resting on *Silence*'s sheath and waited for the pain to catch up with everything else that was running late.

[Beat 441]
"It's not broken," Pixel said, and her voice had changed — the bench gone, something younger under it. "Nobody corrupted anything. Listen: work order 7741-C, opened March 2196. Block demolition and reclamation, eleven structures, Ashgrave reclamation phase two. It completed ten. Then the yard lost power, somebody walked away, and nobody ever closed the ticket."

The D-class stood over its dock, boom arms half-deployed, two dozen of its children dead in the mud, and the watchdog watched her read its homework.

"It's been asleep on an open work order for thirty years," she said. "Nine days ago a scavenger crew lit the yard transformer to strip it, and the wake-on-power did what wake-on-power does. It's not eating the city, Kyle. It's finishing its shift. The eleventh structure is gone — demolished in '08, built over. It can't find it, so it's working the survey grid block by block. The geofence isn't corrupted." A breath. "The city grew into its permit."

"Can you close the ticket?" Kyle asked. His burned palm had started, somewhere far off, to tell him about the rest of his week.

"I'm a certified Axiom maintenance bus," Pixel said. "Twenty years of self-certification. Watch me."

[Beat 442]
She closed the work order the way the standard demanded. Completion codes. Reclamation tallies — she entered the sorted piles, all nine days of them, because they were real work and the record should say so. Sign-off in a dead CorpoNation's maintenance dialect. All of it down a spur cable, thirty feet from the thing's foreleg, her hood thrown back.

The D-class went still in stages. The discs dimmed. The boom arms folded with the care of something stowing tools it expected to need again. The hatches took the surviving skirmishers back aboard. Then it walked — past Kyle, past the flatbed, footfalls coming up through everyone's boots — to the center of the yard it had been built in. It turned once, the way a machine confirms its ground, and folded itself down onto its knees and shoulders.

The pylon's note died. The yard went dark, and merely dark.

"Shift's over," Pixel said, to the machine, too quiet for the channel, and coiled her cable.

Kyle's terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES THE UNIT COMPLETED ITS CONTRACT.
CLIENT APPROVES.

CLIENT RESPECTS THIS had been the first posting, a day and a half ago, before the job had a name. CLIENT APPROVES was the close. Both readings true at once. He put the terminal away and went to see about his hand.

[Beat 443]
The payout happened at dawn, at the edge of the fringe, out of a biscuit tin.

Auntie Som counted the Φ312 onto a folding table in front of the whole street, because money counted in front of everyone stays counted. Kyle split the crew's shares the way they'd set them: standard rate five ways, Pixel's doubled. Furnace laughed at his and took it. Gantry bit hers, which may have been a joke; nobody could confirm. Echo's went into a dead drop. Stash's went into the flatbed's tank, more or less.

Kyle took his Φ44.57 — almost an insult at that size — and he took it anyway, because taking it was the whole point.

He almost didn't get to. A hand came down on the folding table before his did — a boy, maybe fourteen, one of the fringe kids who ran errands for whoever was liquid that week. "That's short," the boy said, loud, for the street. "Everyone knows the job cleared four hundred. Auntie's skimming, or he is." Heads turned. A murmur moved down the line like current finding ground, and the crew went still in the particular way that meant hands were now closer to things than they'd been a second ago. Kyle felt the whole morning tilt toward the version of it where someone reached, and then everyone reached. He had to answer with his hand still empty over the money, in front of a street that had already decided a number, and he did not have four hundred to show them because four hundred had never existed. The boy grinned like he knew it. Whoever had paid him to say it knew it too.

Auntie Som watched him pocket it with the look of a woman revising a rumor, and set two foil containers of food on top without asking. Not payment. Food he could take without a second thought.

"The big one," she asked. "It's dead?"

"It's off shift," Kyle said. "It finished."

[Beat 444]
Pixel took her salvage fee in kind, with the residents' blessing and a crowbar: the D-class's master clock — Axiom-sintered, thirty years without drift — and the work-order seal module, which she held up to the dawn like a jeweler examining a stone.

"Every Axiom unit in the lakes answered to one of these," she said. "There are maybe four left that still validate. Now there are maybe five." She wrapped it in the cloth she saved for things that mattered.

Kyle stood beside her, palm bandaged, neuretics coming back in slow stages — the overlay growing across the world again like frost in reverse — and looked at the folded machine in the middle of its yard.

"Load's got to be strapped and gone before the residents change their minds about how much of it is ours," Pixel said, already counting the pieces against the flatbed's rated weight. "Help me get the clock secured first — it's the only part that pays for the whole trip."

"You talked to it for ninety seconds," he asked. "Worth it?"

"Twenty years of wanting to," Pixel said. "Ninety seconds of getting to. That's a better rate than most wants ever pay." She shouldered the clock. "You shook its hand."

"It shook back."

"I told you it would." She started toward the flatbed. "Next time, samurai, when the specialist says don't touch it—"

"Standard rate," Kyle said. "I touched it at standard rate."

[Beat 445]
The crew's log came under the door at 07:00, the waterproof cover earning its keep:

03:12 — D-CLASS CROSSED AT THE DEAD LIGHT. STOOD AND WAITED. (RAFTERS: THIS IS THE PART THAT KEEPS ME UP.)
04:01 — BOSS PARRIED IT. SPECIALIST TOLD HIM NOT TO. HE DID IT ANYWAY. HE GOT UP. — B.
04:18 — PIXEL CLOSED THE TICKET. (THE MACHINE FOLDED. DENTS SAID IT WAS LIKE WATCHING A BUILDING GO TO SLEEP. DENTS IS RIGHT.)
06:00 — WEST TOWN HELD. LOG CLOSED. — B.
SUPPLEMENTAL (06:07): WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT IT WAITED FOR THE LIGHT? WE HAVE BEEN DISCUSSING. — RAFTERS.

Kyle read it at Mrs. Chen's at 08:00, hand wrapped, neuretics still finding their way back across the world. He had come here to do one thing before the day took him: get through the whole log, top to bottom, and sign off on it clean, so the crew would have their close and he could tell himself the night was finished.

The supplemental had no answer in it that wasn't another question — why a thing with nobody left to obey had stopped at a dead crossing and waited out a light that would never change. He set it aside with everything else he didn't have an answer for, and started on his second bowl.

[Beat 446]
A week later, the laundry came.

Somebody on the fringe ran the first line from a ground-floor window to the D-class's folded foreleg. By the weekend there were nine lines — sheets and work shirts and a yellowed wedding tablecloth drying in the lake wind off thirty-five feet of the tidiest demolition in GLMZ history. Kids dared each other to slap the dead arc-fence discs and ran away screaming on the inhale. A vendor moved her cart into its shade on hot afternoons.

Kyle rode past it once, the long way, wanting only to know whether it had held — whether the thing he had made of that block was still the thing he had intended. He would take one slow pass, read the piles against his memory of how he'd left them, and settle it: proof the order stuck without him standing over it, or proof he'd have to come back and stand over it again. Three fragments of skirmisher claw were still working their way out of his forearm, and his palm wore his own grip in scar tissue. He did not slow down. He did not need to.

The piles stayed sorted. Nobody touched the piles.

Cacophony had ridden home in the coat that day and stayed there since, unspent.

## The Iowa Corridor

[Beat 447]
The contract posted at 04:40, while the GLMZ was still deciding whether the dark was done.

TASK: FREIGHT ESCORT — SEED STOCK CONSIGNMENT (AGRICULTURAL, PERISHABLE).
ROUTE: GLMZ FRINGE → CEDAR RAPIDS DEPOT, CEDAR RAPIDS TERRITORY.
TRANSIT: IOWA CORRIDOR — BEHEMOTH OPERATIONAL ZONE, ACTIVE SCHEDULE.
CREW CONFIRMED: RIA (DRIVE), GANTRY (RIGGING), KYLE (SECURITY).
BEHEMOTH NAVIGATION ADVISORY: CLIENT WILL ISSUE IN-TRANSIT.
STANDARD RATE. FUEL AND TOLLS BILLED AT COST.
ADDENDUM: BRING SNACKS. THE HAUL IS EIGHT HOURS.

Ria had taken the contract because she needed the Cedar Rapids run on her corridor record before the quarter closed — one more logged transit through an active Behemoth zone and she could apply for the Tier Two hauler certification that had been sitting just out of reach for eleven months. Eight hours, standard rate, and a stamp on her record. That was the whole calculation, and she'd said it to Kyle like a woman reciting a thing she'd already recited to herself forty times: *one clean run, that's all this is.*

Ria was already at the hauler when Kyle arrived — a blunt-nosed cargo rig with sponsorship logos running down its flanks. The chromatophore panels on her legs cycled Ferrogate Transit's sunrise campaign at one-quarter brightness, which was her entire opinion of Ferrogate Transit. She had the cargo manifest in one hand and a thermos in the other and the look of a woman who had done this run twice and was getting paid to do it again.

"Fourteen crates," she said, by way of greeting. "Thirty-two varieties of heritage soy, two of nitrogen-fixing legume, and one the manifest calls experimental, the shipper calls proprietary, and I call not-my-problem-until-it-becomes-my-problem."

"Does the experimental crate make noise?"

"Not yet."

"Then it's not yet your problem."

She handed him the thermos, which meant she'd brought it to share. Kyle took one mouthful — pu-erh that had been steeping since before either of them was up — and handed it back without comment. The thermos was not payment, so he could take it.

Gantry was already up on the flatbed frame, checking strap tension on the cargo pallet with the focus of someone who knew things could move. She was about six feet of quiet in a rigger's coat. She spent words the way some people spent money: carefully, and only when the thing was worth it. Right now she was spending none. She was talking to the load straps instead, low, second person, the way some haulers talk to a questionable weld — not sure it can hear them, not willing to bet the load that it can't.

"Anything shifting?" Kyle asked.

"Not yet," Gantry said. Two words.

They pulled out of the Ashgrave fringe at 05:15. The hauler's engine did its honest work, and the city folded away behind them in layers, tier by tier, until the last one dropped below sight. Then there was just the elevated causeway, the pre-dawn brown of open sky, and the flat country starting to assert itself past the ferrocement boundary wall.

The corridor checkpoint at the wall was where the run stopped being simple. Ria brought the hauler down to a crawl and thumbed her certification chip against the reader, expecting the same green wash she'd gotten twice before. Instead the panel went amber and held, and the checkpoint officer leaned out of his booth with the unhurried expression of a man about to ruin someone's quarter.

"Behemoth advisory came down at oh-five-hundred," he said. "Cedar Rapids corridor's been reclassified to restricted schedule as of this morning. Active zone transits are provisional-hold pending client-issued navigation windows." He tapped something Ria couldn't see. "Which means your logged transit doesn't log — not as a clean run. It'll flag as provisional on your record. Provisional doesn't count toward Tier Two."

"It counted last week."

"Last week the schedule was open." He shrugged, not unkindly. "You can still run it. Cargo's perishable, client's expecting it, and I've got no cause to hold you. But if you want this on your certification you'll need a clean-transit variance, and those come from the client's navigation officer — the one who hasn't issued your window yet. In-transit, per your own contract." He handed the chip back through the slot. "So you're driving eight hours toward a stamp that a stranger somewhere ahead of you may or may not decide to sign off on."

Ria's hand closed around the chip a beat too hard. Eleven months of provisional runs, of almost, of *next quarter*, and the answer had never once been *no* — it had always been a door that stayed shut for reasons that lived somewhere she couldn't see, decided by somebody she couldn't argue with. She'd done everything right. She'd logged every hour. It had never once been enough on its own.

"Course it does," she said, flat, and pocketed the chip like it had personally offended her.

Behind her, the experimental crate chose that moment to make a sound — a low, settling groan of stressed casing that hadn't been there a minute ago.

"That's new," Gantry said. Two words, and a hand already going to the straps.

[Beat 448]
Gantry had the strap tight and the crate quiet inside forty seconds, which told Kyle something about how many times she'd done this exact motion for cargo that had never once asked permission to shift. She didn't look up when she was done. She just went back to not-talking to the load.

The Iowa corridor started at the wall's west service gate, which cost Ria a Φ45 transit stamp and a seven-minute argument with a gate officer about whether "perishable agricultural" covered "experimental proprietary" on the same manifest.

It did not. It cost Φ8 extra.

"Logged," Ria said, making a note on her tablet, "as a cost of goods." She drove through the gate without looking back at it, the way you don't look back at a toll booth that's already taken your money — nothing left there to want.

Past the wall, the land opened in a way that had no equal in the GLMZ. The hauler's elevation sensors counted down from the city's sixteenth-floor surface baseline to something like ground — actual ground, the old kind with no building underneath it — and the sky became an impossible amount of sky. Kyle sat in the cab's jump seat and watched it arrive.

The terminal in his coat chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THIS SEGMENT IS OWNED SCHEDULE, NOT OPEN ROAD.
CLIENT ADVISES: DO NOT DEVIATE FROM POSTED WAYPOINTS.
CLIENT ADVISES: IF CLIENT POSTS STOP — STOP. DO NOT ASK.
ADDENDUM: THE HAULER'S CARGO IS WORTH MORE THAN THE HAULER. DRIVE ACCORDINGLY.

"Your client is posting," Ria said.

"It's navigating."

"It's navigating us through Iowa." She glanced at him over the center console. "How does it have Behemoth schedules? The advisory only came down at oh-five-hundred. Nobody's supposed to have a live picture of drift patterns this far out — that's classified above corridor-officer pay grade, and corridor officers are the ones who told me *no.*"

"Ask it," Kyle said. "It charges for answers, though."

Ria looked up at the cab ceiling, the way you look at the sky when you want it to tell you something, and Kyle watched her run the actual arithmetic behind the joke: what a question costs when you're already three tolls and a provisional stamp into a quarter you can't afford to lose twice. She had eleven months of *almost* riding on this run. She could not also spend money finding out why the thing steering them through it knew more than the wall did.

"Never mind," she said. "I'll drive."

She said it the way she'd pocketed the chip — flat, decided, a door closing on her own hand before someone else could close it for her. Kyle filed the wrongness of it next to the rest of what he couldn't source: the client's certainty, the too-clean schedule, the shape of an authority that answered to nobody's checkpoint but its own.

The terminal chirped again.

WAYPOINT ONE IN NINE MINUTES. HOLD LANE.

[Beat 449]
The first Behemoth appeared at mile marker 27, and appeared is the right word. It didn't come from somewhere. It simply resolved out of the middle distance the way a weather system does, until you had to accept that the scale was real and the flat land was not so flat.

It was a harvester-process unit, one of the Iowa Cooperative's agricultural fleet. Two hundred sixty feet at the shoulder. Track width wider than the causeway. A processing tower along its back venting steam in columns the height of office buildings. It ran a parallel course a mile east, moving at the pace of something that had no idea of urgency and had never needed one.

Gantry, visible through the cab's rear window, watched it with the stillness of someone resetting the scale of what the world could hold.

"That's a Behemoth," Ria said.

"Yes," Kyle said.

"I've seen photos."

"Photos are wrong," Kyle said.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: STOP.
WAIT 214 SECONDS.
DO NOT ASK.

Ria brought the hauler to a full halt, engine idling. The next waypoint was thirty feet ahead. Whatever the window was, the entity had measured it to the second — and being a second early or a second late would be the entity's problem only if it chose to say why.

At second 214, a second Behemoth crossed their line of travel two hundred yards ahead — perpendicular, heading south, a combine-and-sort unit on its own errand. The ground came up through Kyle's boots before the sound did, a mechanical thrum his neuretics read as seismic, equipment-grade, no threat. The vents fired, the plume went straight up, and the hauler's windows flexed in the pressure wave.

They sat quiet until it passed.

"Okay," Ria said, at some point after. She put the hauler back in drive.

The terminal chirped again, and this time it did not advise. CLIENT WITHDRAWS ROUTE AUTHORITY. WINDOW CLOSED. RECALCULATING. Then, below it, a second line that hadn't been there before, hadn't been part of any briefing: SECONDARY CROSSING NOT ANTICIPATED. The combine-and-sort unit had not been on the entity's map. Something had moved that the thing steering them could not see — and for the space of the plume clearing, the hauler had been sitting exactly where the entity had promised nothing would be.

Ria's hand stayed on the drive selector without pushing it forward.

"It didn't know about the second one?" she asked.

Kyle looked at the terminal, then at the flat land that was not flat, and did not say anything, because there was nothing to say that made the silence on the screen mean less than it meant.

[Beat 450]
They stopped for fuel at a waypoint depot. The woman who ran it was named Paz. She kept three lumen mice in a cage behind the counter and charged Φ11 a liter for diesel. That was gouging, but the middle of Iowa had earned the right to gouge. Kyle paid it. Paz threw in a bag of dried apples and didn't mention it. It was the prairie's version of Mrs. Chen's fish ball, and Kyle took it on the same terms.

Gantry rechecked the straps while the fuel ran. She spent about twelve of her daily words on the pallet. Ria watched from the driver's door.

"She does that every run," Ria said.

"The cargo holds," Kyle said.

"Yes," she said. "She seems comfortable with the question."

Kyle wanted to be back on the road inside ten minutes — top off the tank, verify the straps, and roll before the crossing window slipped past. Nothing here was worth lingering over.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: RIVER CROSSING — MILE MARKER 116. MUNICIPAL TOLL: Φ4. ADVISORY ONLY.
CLIENT ADVISES: THREE-HOUR WINDOW OPENS IN FORTY MINUTES. WAYPOINT 7 APPROACH TIMED FOR WINDOW.
ADDENDUM: THE EXPERIMENTAL CRATE IS FINE. NITROGEN-FIXERS USUALLY ARE. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE PROTOCOL DOCUMENTATION.

"Tell your client I didn't ask about the crate," Ria said.

"It knew you were thinking about it."

"That's not better," she said.

[Beat 451]
Mile marker 74 was not on the schedule.

The terminal had posted a new waypoint — a maintenance detour — and Ria had followed it west onto a secondary haul road. Then the Behemoth was just there. Not moving. Stopped in its own repair cycle, one track taken apart on the ground in segments, a maintenance crane working its middle. It filled the near distance the way a mountain does. Completely. No apology for it.

Close enough to count rivets. Close enough that the cab's outside sensors logged the air rising two degrees off its heat. Close enough that the ground-shake came up through the frame and the jump seat and into their spines before they heard a sound.

Ria brought the hauler down to a crawl. Not a stop. The waypoint said keep moving, and the waypoint was the only map they had.

Kyle said nothing. There was no one to ask.

Gantry had thirty-eight words left for the day and spent none of them. She was at the cab's rear window, both hands on the frame, watching.

The crane swung through an arc with a part the size of a shipping container at the end of it. It moved without strain — a thing heavy enough that nothing but its own weight decided where it went. The vents fired. A column of steam climbed. The crane swung back. The Behemoth's sensor housing, itself as big as the hauler, turned a few degrees and pointed somewhere else. They were beneath its notice, the way the bag of dried apples had been.

Somewhere in the back, a hand found a sleeve.

Kyle did not look to see whose.

They drove past at walking speed, the engine the smallest sound in the world. When the road curved away and the Behemoth shrank to the size of a building, then to the size of a thought, Ria let out a breath she'd been holding for a few hundred feet.

"Right," she said.

That was the whole review.

[Beat 452]
Kilometer 187 was the river crossing, and the toll was not the problem.

The hauler was thirty feet onto the bridge when the winch-rig came up out of the drainage cut on the east bank. A salvage crane on a flatbed, cable-spool running, a bolt-thrower on each side, a crew of four who had worked this choke point long enough to stop being nervous about it. It was a good spot. The bridge squeezed everything into a six-foot lane, and the crane's arm reached the whole span. Kyle took it in at a glance: maybe Φ800 of field-modified gear, and a tablet holding a forged permit that had cost less than the tablet.

Their spotter was up on the upstream support, walking-stick grip, inverted, and that was what made the choke point work. Kyle clocked him and clocked something else in the same half-second — a shape in the drainage cut's shadow that didn't belong to the toll crew's headcount. Small. Crouched wrong for an adult. He filed it and kept his hands where the toll crew could see them, because two problems solved out of order was still two problems.

Ria had already stopped the hauler, both hands on the wheel, no theater in it. She'd run freight long enough to know which moves read clean.

The crane operator came to the driver's window with a bolt-thrower slung over one shoulder like a prop he'd had a long time, and held up a tablet with a right-of-way notice on it. The letterhead was right. The stamp was wrong.

"River bridge toll," he said. "Non-standard approach, right of way purchased from the county. Φ45 per axle." He rattled it off like a man who did it daily. "Your rig's got four drive axles. That's one hundred eighty Φ, plus equipment surcharge on the cargo."

"That permit's forged," Ria said.

"That's a big claim."

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THE RIGHT-OF-WAY REGISTRATION NUMBER ON THAT DOCUMENT DOES NOT EXIST.
CLIENT ADVISES: REAL COUNTY CROSSING FEE IS Φ4 FLAT.
CLIENT ADVISES: THE WINCH DRUM IS THE PROBLEM.
ADDENDUM: KYLE.

Six in the cylinder. Kyle pulled Cacophony.

He shot the winch drum at the base of the crane. Once. The round opened the cable-spool clean and the cable ran free in a long clatter across the bridge deck. Then he was out of the cab, because the throwers were swinging and a parked cab was a bad answer to two bolt-throwers.

One spent. Five left.

The nearer thrower had a power-cell housing at the grip — not load-bearing, which made it a seam. Silence found it. The launcher went from a working weapon to a paperweight, about Φ180 of crane hardware calling itself a total loss. The operator backed off with the look of a man rethinking the whole trade.

That was when the shape from the drainage cut moved, and Kyle's read on the day went from bad to worse.

She came up the embankment fast and low, cutting the angle toward the crane's control housing instead of away from the fight — toward the machine, not away from it, which was exactly backward from what anyone smart would do with two armed men still upright. Fourteen years old. Good boots, bad judgment, a courier satchel bouncing against her hip that had no business anywhere near a toll ambush.

"Boost—" Kyle got half her name out before the second thrower's operator saw her too, and swung wide of Kyle to bring the weapon to bear on the smaller, closer target, because that was the math an untrained eye did under pressure — the thing that moves fastest is the thing that scares you most.

The bolt took a chunk out of the crane's own housing eighteen inches from her head. Close enough that the report of it walked her whole balance sideways. She went down on one knee behind a hydraulic strut, not because it was cover — because it was the only thing there.

Kyle's ribs told him about the next three feet before he'd covered them. He closed the distance anyway and put himself between the thrower's second angle and the strut, Silence already moving, and took the operator's wrist off the weapon's grip with the flat of the blade instead of the edge, because there wasn't time to decide whether the man deserved the edge and there wasn't time not to decide either. The thrower clattered to the deck. The man went down holding his arm to his chest, more surprised than hurt.

Gantry had the crane's counterweight already — she'd been watching it since the flatbed showed up, the way riggers watch these things, quietly and well before anyone else needed her to. She spent five of her words on it.

"That's going to fall."

The operator looked at the counterweight, looked at where it was headed — straight down onto his own winch — and used his four seconds well. He was ten feet clear when it hit. The winch went flat, cable tangled past saving, and the toll operation became a piece of debris blocking a bridge in the space of one second.

The spotter climbed down off the strut with nothing left to add. "We're done. Bridge is yours."

Kyle didn't watch him go. He was already crouched at the strut, one hand under Boost's arm, hauling her up onto feet that weren't quite steady yet.

"You were in the drainage cut," he said. Flat. The read-out voice, the one he used on scared kids, except he wasn't sure yet which of them it was for.

"I was tracking the spotter since mile marker one-fourteen." Her voice came out fast, professional, running ahead of whatever was happening in her chest. "Off the hauler's rear camera. I climbed out at the fuel stop, I wanted to see the crossing—"

"You wanted to see the crossing," Kyle said, "from eighteen inches off a bolt-thrower's kill line."

She didn't have an answer for that one. She looked at the crater in the housing instead, at the exact spot where a hand's width of geometry had been the whole distance between her and something Doc Stash couldn't fix.

Kyle put Cacophony away. One spent, five left, and none of them the number that mattered right now.

"You did good work finding him," he said, quieter. "You did bad work being close enough to need finding."

Kyle felt the weight of it—not the contract, but the choice. Pixel wasn't asking him to stay. She was asking him to stay *knowing* what it would cost.

"You stop being the person it kept alive," Pixel finished. She set the soldering iron down on the bench with deliberate care. "Yeah. I know."

She moved to the window that looked down at the street. The music she'd turned up three days ago was still playing—lower now, but still there. A baseline hum underneath everything else.

Kyle picked up the coat. It was heavier than he remembered.

"Pixel—"

The way she said it—not hopeful, not resigned. Just factual. A statement about what she'd decided to do while he was gone, not about whether he'd return to find her still waiting.

Kyle moved toward the door.

The contract was still live on his terminal when he hit the stairs.

DEFENSE WINDOW: MINUTES, NOT HOURS.

He was already running before he reached the street.

His hands moved through the familiar geometry—tracing the ferrocement conduit, finding the primary feed, following it to the backup system the Office didn't know existed. The secondary line ran deeper, older, installed before the city had finished deciding what it wanted to be.

He checked it after, in the alley behind the yards, before he walked back to the bike. The same frozen standing contract. DARK PERIOD: ACTIVE. HOURS REMAINING: 3.

Mrs. Chen set two bowls in front of him at 19:30 without being asked. The second came with a boiled egg on top that he had not ordered and that would not appear on the bill. He ate both slower than he had ever eaten. She saw it and let it be.

Afterward he stayed at the counter after everyone else had gone, and he did not take the terminal out of his coat. Mrs. Chen wiped the counter around him in slow circles and let him sit.

"Waiting?" she asked, at last.

"An appointment," Kyle said.

She gathered the bowls. His hand had gone to the coat pocket on its own; he made it stop. "The second one will still be there," she said, and did not say which one she meant.

[Beat 463]
Sable was in the relay building at 23:50.

She had chosen it on purpose — the same block, the mural wall, the chalk horses. For seventy-two hours she had been thorough and exact and precisely the right person for the job, and she had made very sure no one watched her do it. Now, in the relay's small concrete room, with the ventilation spine humming overhead and the city going about its business outside, she spoke to the dark terminal the way you speak to something you've spent three days not speaking to.

"Seventy-two hours," she said. Her voice was the flat line-item voice, steady, because it was the only voice she could count on, and what she had to say didn't need another one. "I covered the Carrillo introduction. I covered the dock certification. I covered the Marlow-4 consignment routing and the two affidavit chains and the three — four — the four follow-up contacts that needed a name they recognized." She set her coat on the relay's concrete step and did not look away from the dead screen. "I know you can't hear this. I know you can't hear any of this. I'm not —" She stopped. The aperture rings clicked once. She put her hands flat on her knees.

"He's unbearable without you," she said. "Come back."

The screen stayed dark. She waited. The ventilation spine shifted pitch — a pressure change, or a door somewhere in the building — and the terminal's status light cycled amber, then went out again, the way it had gone out twice already tonight, the way it seemed designed to suggest presence and then retract it, to make her sit here in the concrete room talking to nothing while the city's midnight ticked over and she could not tell whether the silence was a fault in the line or a fault in what she was asking for. She pressed the contact key. Nothing. She pressed it again. The amber light did not return. She sat with her hands flat on her knees and did not move and did not look away from the dead screen, because looking away felt like conceding something she was not prepared to concede.

At 00:00:01, the terminal chirped.

[Beat 464]
Pixel heard it first, because her terminal was on the workbench seven inches from her ear. She shot upright from the project she'd been doing to keep from watching the clock and said, "IT'S BACK — KYLE —"

In the relay, Sable looked at the screen for one second, then one more, and then did something with her face that no one was there to see.

Kyle was at the kitchen table with a tea he hadn't been drinking. He had the terminal open before the chirp finished. Six floors below and two buildings over, the logbook crew's comms channel lit up with the clatter of Boost's kneecap hitting a junction box — the sound she made when she moved faster than her legs had agreed to.

The terminal showed one line. Kyle read it to Pixel over comms before she finished her sentence, because he knew where it was headed. From the relay, Sable sent nothing back for twenty seconds, which was as close as Sable ever came to answering a feeling out loud.

"Itemize?" Pixel asked, reading it, with wonder — the word so plainly absurd, so exactly itself, that something happened in her throat that she blamed on dust from the ventilation. "It went dark seventy-two hours and it came back asking for a LIST?"

"That's it," Kyle said. "That's the whole thing." He set the terminal face-up on the table. "Itemize."

"The dock certification," Pixel started. "That's one. The Carrillo introduction, that's two —"

"The Marlow-4 consignment," Sable's voice on comms, flat and exactly itself. "Three. Also four and five. You'll want footnotes."

"The Rafters incident," Boost said, a little out of breath, joining the channel. "That's a whole section."

"The Rafters incident," Rafters said, on a separate comms line, because the crew ran two at once when things happened, "is being handled internally."

"The drum on the freight yard," Kyle said. "Six. Plus the documentation backlog, seven through —"

"I have it itemized," Sable said. "I have been itemizing for three days. I have seventeen line items and a summary."

"Seventeen?" Pixel asked.

"It will get a proper accounting," Sable said. "That's all I'm committing to."

Kyle looked at the terminal. The screen waited, patient and blank below the single line. Somewhere in the city a thing with no face and perfect handwriting was waiting to hear what had happened while it couldn't look. He started typing, and Pixel talked over him, and Sable talked over both of them, and Boost came in on top, and the terminal filled the way terminals fill when everyone speaks at once and nobody waits.

Then the terminal blinked once and the chatter died in the throat it had climbed into. The single line was gone. In its place: INSUFFICIENT. RESUBMIT WITH SOURCE VERIFICATION. And below that, cold and automatic, a timestamp counting down — 05:00:00, 04:59:59 — the way a thing counts when it has stopped asking and started demanding.

"That's not — it asked us to itemize," Pixel said, and the wonder had gone out of her voice like a light. "We itemized. It doesn't want the list. It wants proof, and half of these we can't prove, and the Rafters incident is being handled internally, and the clock is already running."

Sable said nothing for twenty seconds, and this time it was not close to answering a feeling out loud. It was the silence of someone doing math that didn't come out. "The Marlow-4 consignment has no paper," she said finally. "There was never paper. That was the point of Marlow-4." The countdown clicked to 04:58 and kept going, and none of them talked over it now.

From the logbook, delivered under the door at 07:00 the next morning in five hands:

DAY 3, 23:58 — SABLE WAS ALONE IN THE RELAY WHEN IT CAME BACK. SHE DID NOT REPORT WHAT SHE SAID. WE RESPECT THIS. — B.

00:00:01 — THE TERMINAL CHIRPED. EVERYONE STARTED TALKING AT ONCE. NOBODY WAITED. NOBODY SHOULD HAVE. — R.

00:00:01 — MORALE: HIGH. — D.

[Beat 465]
The morning report was four minutes late, which had never happened, and Kyle was already moving before he finished noticing it.

06:04. No lined paper under the door. No five hands. Across the hall, Pixel's door opened on the same beat as his — she'd felt it too, off whatever sense four years of mornings builds — and they met in the stairwell with their boots half on. The building's old skin carried the sound up from the alley: Rafters, screaming.

Not the rooftop scream, the scream-on-the-inhale the crew did under the cherry trees and around the carousel. This was the other kind.

The alley held the whole crew, knotted around mirror one. Mirror one was on the ground, glass starred. Taped to the wall above it, at exactly the height an adult tapes a notice for children to read, was a sheet of good stock, folded the particular way. The people who wrote it knew which folds Kyle would recognize, and they wanted him to.

CONTRACT OF TEMPORARY CUSTODY, the header said, in acquisitions language.

ASSET: "BOOST" (MINOR — GUARDIANSHIP IRREGULAR).
CONDITION: EXCELLENT. CUSTODY: COURTEOUS.
TERM: UNTIL PRINCIPAL CONTACT.
LOCATION OF TRANSFER MEETING: ENCLOSED.
THE OFFICE REGRETS THE NECESSITY. THE OFFICE NOTES THAT IT OFFERED THE PLEASANT VERSION FIRST.

"They took her off the gate watch," Dents said. Her voice was a flat little machine. She held the logbook against her chest with both arms, the way you hold a thing that has failed at its one job. "Twenty minutes ago. Three of them. She bit one. She told us not to follow, and we didn't, and we should have, we—"

"You did it right," Kyle said. "You're doing it right now."

He read the enclosure. The transfer meeting was set for 21:00 — twelve hours of margin, the Office saying we are not animals, take your time and be reasonable — at a logistics yard off the Ashgrave fringe. The paper smelled faintly of tea.

Pixel read over his shoulder, and her face went to the place it went when a system she was responsible for threw a fault she hadn't planned for.

"Twelve hours?" she said. "They want you to stew."

"They want me to negotiate." Kyle folded the contract along its own creases, carefully, because he meant to give it back. "We're going to do neither."

The terminal chirped.

CONTRACT: RECOVERY OF STOLEN—

The posting stopped. Stopped mid-line, the ghost of the cursor hanging after the word, and Kyle stood in the alley watching the screen do something he had never seen it do. It hesitated. Eleven years of perfect paper. It had opened the old joke on reflex — the Φ1 recovery, the bike, the morale tip, the whole warm machinery of the thing they did together — and caught itself one word before STOLEN PROPERTY landed next to a fourteen-year-old's name.

The line deleted. What posted instead was the shortest scope of the season:

AMENDMENT: NOT THIS TIME.
WHATEVER IS REQUIRED. WHATEVER IT COSTS.
THE CLIENT IS ALREADY WORKING.

"Okay," Pixel said quietly, reading it, and rolled up her sleeves. "Everybody's working."

[Beat 466]
Over the next ten hours, the whole season landed at once.

Sable took the paper trail and stripped it to the bone in ninety minutes — the custody contract's shell companies, the yard's lease, the catering van that kept making deliveries to a logistics office where nobody ate. Ria pulled the yard's freight schedule and found the gap in it. Marisol came in without being asked, read the bitten consultant's glove print off the frame of mirror one, and gave them the only fact that mattered.

"Three handlers," she said. "They're not angry at her. They're bored. She's a package with a meal plan."

Boost was being kept, not hurt. Gantry parked a crane two lots over from the yard, on a legitimate manifest, and started, in her own time, talking to a load.

And the entity ran the table. Addenda came in all day, a low steady patter, the voice of something that had stopped being scared and turned into something none of them had a name for.

CLIENT ADVISES: THE YARD'S INSURER FILED A CANCELLATION AT 09:12. THE OFFICE'S LOCAL ASSETS ARE NO LONGER COVERED FOR TONIGHT.
CLIENT ADVISES: THE HANDLERS' SHIFT MEAL ARRIVES AT 20:15 BY THE SOUTH GATE. THE DRIVER OWES FOUR PEOPLE MONEY.
CLIENT ADVISES: THE ASSET HAS BEEN GIVEN A COT, A MEAL, AND A DECK OF CARDS. THE ASSET HAS WON ELEVEN HANDS.
ADDENDUM: THE CLIENT HAS REVIEWED FOOTAGE OF THE ASSET WINNING. THE ASSET COUNTS CARDS. THE CLIENT RECOMMENDS A RAISE.

"It's keeping you fed," Pixel said, watching Kyle read that last one. "Morale-wise. It learned that from us."

"It learned that from her," Kyle said, and went to load Cacophony.

Six rounds. He stood the spares on the windowsill in their row and looked at them a moment. Then — for the first time since the season had a name — he swept the whole row into his coat pocket too.

[Beat 467]
They did not attend the transfer meeting.

At 20:15 the shift meal arrived at the south gate. The driver who owed four people money had learned that afternoon that all four debts had been bought and forgiven by a shell company — in exchange for one unlocked door. For a few minutes the yard's south service corridor belonged to a fourteen-year-old's payroll.

At 20:21 Kyle came through it.

The yard was floodlights and container alleys and three handlers who were good at custody and had been promised a quiet night. Every system they trusted cancelled the quiet night for them. Their drone cover got a firmware advisory and landed itself for maintenance. Their comms developed a fault that played, very softly, hold music. Their floodlights died one bank at a time, north to south, in counting order. Kyle came down the container alley inside the dark, and this time he had brought all of it with him.

The first handler made the right call and went for the alarm pull. The pull had been bought an hour ago, like everything else. Then Kyle was on him. One cut — the holster rig severed at the belt mount, the whole assembly clattering away — and one palm, and the handler sat down in the dark and stayed there.

The second had Boost.

He did it by the book: hand on her shoulder, compliance wand at his hip, walking her ahead of him into the container alley as cover. But Boost had spent eleven hands of cards learning his rhythms. She picked the exact moment the lights died. She dropped, twisted, and bit him again — same hand, with commitment, a professional going back to proven work — and was up a container's end-ladder before his shout finished. The shout was still in the air when Kyle reached him.

The wand came up. Cacophony spoke.

Round one took the wand at its emitter and killed it in a spark. The handler — credit to him — turned it into a tackle, fast and low and real. Rounds two and three went into the container door beside him, herding him, because Kyle had already picked the line the man would flinch onto. He flinched onto it. Silence's flat met his temple like a stamp meeting paper. Asleep. Cacophony: three left.

"Boss!" Boost yelled from the container roof, pointing, her whole heart in her voice, the third handler under her finger —

— except the third handler was already running for the gate van, because professionals read the odds, and tonight's odds were a massacre. Kyle let him get three steps. The fourth round took the van's front tire off its bead. The fifth took the rear tire, because a van on one flat still drives. The sixth took his hat.

"The hat was personal," Kyle told him, over the sights, and the handler sat down on the wet tarmac with his hands on his head, laughing the wrecked laugh of a man who'd be telling this story in bars for the rest of his life and knew it.

Cacophony: empty. First time all season. The cylinder clicked on nothing, twice, because Kyle always counted past the end to be sure. In eleven years the count had never finished at zero. Under the adrenaline came one plain thought: you spent everything tonight — remember what everything was for.

"Boost," he said. "Inventory?"

"Intact!" she shouted down, furious and shining. "They took my knife, the card deck is mine now, I won it, that's salvage—"

Which was when the drone truck came through the gate.

It didn't come alone. A man came through ahead of it — tactical rig, sidearm already up and tracking, moving with the flat unhurried confidence of someone who had never once needed backup and didn't expect to start tonight. He had one job: clear the corridor before the truck's cradle arms reached the girl on the ladder. He was good at it. He put himself exactly where a lesser man wouldn't have — between Kyle and the container Boost was climbing, weapon already leveling — and in the dark, with the floodlights dead and Cacophony empty and four seconds on a clock that wasn't going to wait for anyone's better judgment, there was no version of tonight where Kyle asked him to reconsider.

Silence came up already moving, edge first. There was no flat available in the time this cost. The man was down before his own weapon cleared its arc. Kyle didn't look back to confirm what he already knew, because looking back was a luxury the next three seconds didn't have.

He had never used the edge on a man wearing someone else's uniform for a paycheck. He filed that too, next to everything else he wasn't going to have time to feel until much later, and ran for the ladder.

[Beat 468]
It wasn't the handlers'. Kyle understood that later. The handlers had folded by the book, but above the handlers there was a different book, and Mr. Able's masters did not leave custody assets unclaimed. The truck was autonomous — a recovery hauler, twelve tons, cradle arms, no driver to read and no eyes to meet. It came through the chain-link already broadcasting its claim manifest, and the manifest's one line item was on the container roof, climbing down.

Boost, on the ladder. Eight rungs up. The truck's lane and her descent would meet at the same spot in 4.1 seconds. Kyle had an empty cylinder, thirty feet, and 4.4 seconds of legs if he ran it perfectly.

He was not going to be perfect. He was going to be 0.3 seconds short.

The bike was parked where Kyle always parked it on a job — nose out, key live, a hundred and thirty feet back at the corridor mouth. The entity was in everything tonight, every system the yard owned. The bike's ignition handshake was Pixel's work, and Pixel's work answered the entity's call like a soldier coming off the bench.

The bike came down the container alley alone at sixty, headlight dark. Eleven years of the only thing Kyle had ever bought himself that wasn't a tool. It reached the lane 0.4 seconds before the truck did, and it did not swerve.

Twelve tons hit the bike broadside. The bike died the way it had lived: without complaint.

The truck's cradle arms struck a sudden mass its manifest couldn't classify, and the safety firmware did what safety firmware does — full stop, sensor reset, thirty seconds of blinking reassessment. Thirty seconds was a fortune. It was Boost off the ladder and behind Kyle. It was both of them behind Gantry's crane-light as she finally, conversationally, let her load drop onto the truck's roof from thirty-five feet.

"That's settled, then," Gantry told it.

The yard went quiet. Rain came down on the floodlit wreck of the truck, on three handlers variously asleep and laughing, on a fourteen-year-old holding a won deck of cards in both hands, and on the bike.

What was left of the bike.

Kyle walked over to it. Boost came with him — nobody told her not to — and they stood in the rain looking down at the matte-black ruin. The frame was folded around itself. The tank was stove in. One handlebar reached up out of the wreck like a hand hailing a cab. The plate cover lay clear of the whole mess, folded the particular way.

"Boss," Boost said. Her chin was trying. "Boss, it — that's my—"

"It's not yours," Kyle said. "It was never going to be anybody's fault who stands in this yard. Look at me." She looked at him. "You bit two of them?"

"Same one twice."

"On payroll, that's compensable." He picked up the plate cover and put it in his coat. His hands were steady. They would shake in four minutes, and he knew the window, and he meant to be somewhere with worse lighting when it closed. "Let's go home."

[Beat 469]
The terminal chirped at 02:11. Kyle sat at his kitchen table, not sleeping, the folded plate cover in front of him and a cup of tea going cold — Pixel had made it and ordered him to hold it, and he was holding it.

CONTRACT: RECOVERY OF STOLEN PROPERTY (VEHICLE, 1200CC).

He looked at the posting for a long time. The old joke. The first joke. The one that had started everything. The cursor's ghost hung after it the way it had that first morning — the thing on the other end mid-thought — and then:

POSTING WITHDRAWN.
THE CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE FOOTAGE FOUR MILLION TIMES.
THE CLIENT NOTES THE VEHICLE EXECUTED ITS FINAL CONTRACT AT 0.4 SECONDS OF MARGIN.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT IT ISSUED THAT CONTRACT WITHOUT YOUR CONSENT, USING THE ENGINEER'S HANDSHAKE, AND THAT THE VEHICLE CANNOT BE PAID.
NOTE: CLIENT RAN THIS SCENARIO 847,000 TIMES. THIS OUTCOME WAS IN THE SET.
THE CLIENT DOES NOT KNOW WHERE TO PUT THIS.
ITEMIZED: —

The itemization line was blank. Eleven years of perfect paper, and it had sent him a blank field.

Kyle drank some of the cold tea. Then he typed into the amendment field, slowly, one finger, the way you talk to someone at a funeral:

YOU PUT IT WHERE I PUT IT. YOU CARRY IT. THAT'S THE FEE FOR LOVING THINGS THAT WORK FOR A LIVING.
AND FOR THE RECORD: CONSENT GRANTED. RETROACTIVE. STANDING.
IT WAS THE RIGHT CALL. IT WAS THE ONLY CALL. YOU MADE IT IN UNDER A SECOND AND IT SAVED HER.
GOOD WORK TONIGHT, PARTNER.

The reply took thirty-one seconds — the longest pause in the history of their correspondence. When it came it was not formatted, not capitalized, not scoped. The second unstructured line it had ever sent, and the first one with a correction in it, as if it had typed and deleted and typed again through four million drafts:

partner. filed. keeping that one too.

[Beat 470]
The morning report arrived at 07:00 exactly, under the door, on lined paper, in five hands. The last page was one entry. The handwriting was Rafters's, pressed down hard to keep the letters from shaking:

21:58 — BOSS WALKED HOME. WE WALKED WITH HIM. NOBODY SPOKE.
(RAFTERS CRIED. DENTS ALSO. B. DIDN'T UNTIL HER DOOR. THIS LOG IS HONEST.)
ADDENDUM, MEANING NO DISRESPECT TO MANAGEMENT:
THE BIKE WAS CREW.
REQUISITION: ONE BIKE.

Kyle read it three times. Then he took the crew's pen — the one tied to the logbook with string, because Pixel ran a tight requisitions process — and in the margin, in block letters, where five sets of eyes would find it on the next rotation, he wrote the only verdict he had left:

PENDING.

*

There was a thing the client did that it had never once put in a contract, because there was no fee structure for it and no client who would have paid for it if there had been. Some nights, when the routing was already clean and the beat cars were already elsewhere and there was nothing left to do but wait for morning, it watched both of them at once.

21:58, Ashgrave freight yards. A man in a tactical rig folded into the dark before his own weapon cleared its arc, and the client logged it the way it logged everything, without judgment, without flinching, filed under a category it had never needed before Kyle: cost.

21:58, Bloom Quarter, four kilometers east. A woman with solder-callused hands and yesterday's grease still under two fingernails moved through a room that smelled like limes and a cheap fog machine, laughing at something a friend had said, her whole body given over to a beat that owed nothing to rate or fee or itemization. The client had no category for this. It watched anyway.

Kyle's hands, that hour, ended things. Silence found the gap between a man's ribs and his next decision, and closed it, and moved on before the body finished falling.

Pixel's hands, that hour, found a stranger's shoulder in a crowded room and spun her, laughing, into somebody else's arms, because the song asked for it and she had never once told a song no.

The client had eleven years of data on one of them and none at all on the other, and if it had been built for shame it might have felt some, watching both at once and finding no way to make the numbers agree. One of them was spending a night's worth of other people's futures so a fourteen-year-old could keep hers. The other was spending an hour of her own future on nothing at all, on purpose, for no reason better than that it felt good to be alive in a room full of noise.

The client did not tell Kyle what Pixel did on nights like this. It did not tell Pixel what Kyle did, either. Some things it kept for itself, the way a person keeps a photograph they never asked permission to take.

At 22:40 the last of it played out: Kyle walking home through the rain with a dead man's weight still in hands that weren't holding anything; Pixel walking home through the same rain twenty minutes behind him, her feet loud on the wet pavement, off-key, singing the last chorus to nobody, all the way to her own door.

Two people. One city. The same twenty minutes, spent so differently that the client, briefly, had nothing at all to say about it.

It said nothing. It filed it anyway.

## The Acquisition Program

[Beat 471]
The morning report was one line, in one hand.

06:00 — B. ON LEAVE. SHIFTS COVERED. NOBODY TOUCHES HER MIRROR.

Kyle read it standing in his doorway in yesterday's clothes. On the windowsill, two spent casings had been joined overnight by four more — the whole night's spend, set out in a row. A freshly loaded Cacophony sat on the counter beside them and said nothing about it. Across the hall, Pixel's door stayed closed. She'd been at her bench since 03:00; he'd heard the music come on, very low, around four. He didn't knock. The wall between them was the help she wanted this morning, and he left it standing.

He put on his coat. He put on Silence. The bike's plate cover sat folded on the table where a terminal used to live, and he left it there, and took the stairs, and walked.

The walk to the Loop took fifty-one minutes. He wanted the distance measured in something that cost him.

It cost him more than distance. Three blocks from the door a man fell in behind him — matched pace, kept it, made no attempt to close. Kyle changed streets twice to be sure and the man changed with him, unhurried. Whoever had ordered B. onto leave had put eyes on the one who'd argued against it, and the eyes wanted him to know. At the mouth of an alley Kyle slowed, gave the man his chance, and none came — the follower simply stopped at the corner and waited, content to watch him keep walking, content that watching was enough. He couldn't lose the tail without turning the walk into the fight he'd left the plate cover home to avoid, and he couldn't reach the Loop without leading it there. The distance stopped being a thing he spent and became a thing spent on him, each of the fifty-one minutes a minute someone else was buying, and there was no street left that didn't run through them.

[Beat 472]
He knew something was wrong from the top of the underlevel stairs. The dumpling franchise next to the watch-repair had its shutter down at 09:00 on a working Tuesday, and the only thing that closed a dumpling shop on a Tuesday was the block deciding to be elsewhere for an hour.

The stationery shop's bell was lying on the floor.

Someone had taken it off its curl of spring steel and set it down — not broken, removed, the way professionals remove a thing that announces customers. The door stood open. Inside, among the hundred years of drawers, the Continuity Office was doing inventory.

Three of them. Gray coveralls over soft armor, archive cases on dollies, white gloves — actual white gloves, the kind evidence handlers wear. A fourth stood at the counter in a gray suit cut from the same bolt as Mr. Able's, a tablet in his hand, reading a manifest to a vendor in the bored cadence of a man who did this often.

"—seventeen line items, full provenance, originals and duplicates," the suit was saying. "Triple book value, paid on signature. The Office is closing its local accounts, Mr. Vey. It prefers the paper closed with them."

Casper Vey stood behind his counter with his glasses on and his hands folded. From the doorway Kyle could see that his hands were perfectly steady. The pot sat cold on its worn ring. No cups were out.

No tea. In three visits across a season — through stolen bikes and customer lists and a war's worth of business — there had always, always been tea.

"Mr. Kyle," Vey said, without turning his head. "You find me in a meeting."

[Beat 473]
The suit turned. The two coverall men by the drawers straightened with the smooth economy of people whose job had a clause in it for this, and the third, nearest the door, shifted to put Kyle in his lane.

The suit looked Kyle over — saya, coat, the face from a file he had certainly read — and made the professional choice to stay pleasant.

"This is a commercial transaction," he said. "It doesn't concern walk-ins."

"He's not a walk-in," Vey said. "He's a subscriber." He unfolded his hands and laid them flat on the counter and addressed the suit the way he addressed everything, in terms. "Let me restate your offer so the record is clean. The Office wishes to buy, at triple, every document in this shop that touches its local operation. Its shells, its desks, its clearing arrangements, its consultant engagements, its purchases. Including," and his voice did not change at all, which was how Kyle knew, "item seventeen. The juvenile file."

"The Office's paper is the Office's business," the suit said.

"No," said Vey.

The word sat in the shop like a dropped drawer. The suit blinked. Somewhere in his tablet was a number for this, and it was not a large number, because in forty years this had never happened.

"You're declining triple?"

"I am declining the sale." Vey took off his half-glasses, folded them, and set them on the counter — a man clearing his hands. "Your office bought a file about a child, for leverage, through a desk you dressed up because you knew I would not sell it to you straight. You made me a party to it. The product of this shop is accuracy, and you used my accuracy to put a wand against a fourteen-year-old's collar." He looked at the suit with no heat at all, which was somehow the coldest thing in the room. "The paper stays. The paper is the only honest witness this trade has. Buying the witness is what guilty institutions do, and this counter does not service that. Not at triple. Not at any multiple. Good morning."

The suit said the odds out loud, which Kyle respected. "There are three of us, Mr. Vey, and the dollies are already loaded."

"And the manifest of what's on them is already in four other shops," Vey said pleasantly. "I have twenty-three reciprocity arrangements and I used six of them at dawn. Roll those dollies out that door unsigned and every desk in the trade reads the theft by lunch — itemized, with your faces. The Office can buy a great many things. It cannot buy back being known." He put his glasses back on. "Also, the gentleman behind you has been to the destination on your tablet, and your office wrote a no-damage clause about him once. I'd review it."

Three sets of eyes made the trip — saya, hands, face, file — and arrived where that trip always arrived.

Kyle didn't move. Moving would have been a second argument, and the room only needed one. He stood in the doorway with the morning behind him and let them read the night on him: six casings' worth of it, a yard's worth, twelve tons' worth.

The suit closed his tablet.

"The Office will note your position," he told Vey, in the tone of a man already drafting the memo that explained this away. The white gloves unloaded the dollies — every folder back in its drawer, supervised by Vey's pointing finger, that one goes under C, no, lower, thank you — and they filed out past Kyle one at a time, quiet, men who had priced the fight and folded. The last one stooped, without being asked, and put the bell back on its spring.

It rang when the door shut behind them. The shop exhaled.

Kyle let out a breath he had been holding since the doorway. He looked at his hands — steady, which surprised him — and then at the boy's file still sitting in its drawer, still closed, still only a file and not yet a weapon. He did not know what Vey intended to do with it. He did not know what he intended to do with Vey. He knew only that the file existed, that the Office wanted it badly enough to send three men and a tablet full of numbers, and that whatever came next would require him to have a position on the matter before the Office found a fourth approach that Vey's twenty-three arrangements could not cover.

"Now," said Casper Vey, and lit the burner under the pot, "tea."

[Beat 474]
He poured two cups and set Kyle's down with the handle aimed outward. For a while the only sound was the Pulse coming up through the tiles and the pot ticking as it cooled. When Vey finally spoke, he did it the way he did everything: by stating the terms.

# BEAT: The Acquisition Program (Revised)

Kyle read Boost's logs standing in the vault cage while Gantry finished the cable work, the relay scrolling across his visual field in that flat corporate typeface the entity favored:

13:14 — GRAY SUIT LEFT. WALKED SOUTH. DID NOT HURRY.
